RE: Formal Opposition to the Clark County Comprehensive Growth Management
Plan Update — Request for Party of Record Status

To the Clark County Council and Community Planning Staff:

Please accept this formal written comment as my official opposition to the proposed
Clark County Comprehensive Growth Management Plan (2025–2045) update and its
associated zoning changes.

By submitting these comments into the legislative public record prior to final adoption, I
am explicitly requesting to be designated a Party of Record for all future notices,
updates, and potential administrative or legal appeals regarding this matter.

I oppose the proposed high-density zoning expansions and land-use alterations due to
the severe, unmitigated negative impacts they will introduce to our community,
specifically:




     Increased
     Traffic & Gridlock:
     The infrastructure improvements proposed in the current plan are entirely
     inadequate to handle the projected volume of vehicles. The resulting gridlock will
     compromise neighborhood safety and delay emergency response times.
      Overcrowded
      Schools:
      Local public school districts are already strained. Forcing rapid residential density
      increases without proportional, pre-funded school infrastructure will drastically
      overcrowd classrooms and diminish the quality of education for our children.




      Increased
      Strain on Public Safety & Crime:
      The plan lacks a concurrent, funded strategy to expand local law enforcement
      and emergency services. Higher density without adequate municipal policing
      infrastructure historically correlates with an increase in property crime and a
      strain on emergency resources.




      Devaluation

      of Existing Property:

      The proposed zoning changes fundamentally disrupt the character of established
      residential neighborhoods. Introducing incompatible multi-family or high-intensity
      zoning adjacent to single-family homes will cause a direct, measurable decrease
      in current property

      values for existing homeowners who invested in the area based on its historic
      zoning.




For these reasons, I urge the Clark County Council to reject or significantly amend the
proposed zoning maps to protect the quality of life, financial security, and safety of
Clark County residents.

Please confirm receipt of this letter and verify that my name, email, and physical
address have been formally entered into the Comprehensive Plan Index of Record.

Sincerely,

Rebekah Conklin

Dear Clark County Council and Planning Commission,



I am writing to express my strong opposition to expanding the urban growth boundaries
(UGB) in the current Comprehensive Plan Update. Expanding these boundaries
threatens our valuable agricultural lands, strains existing infrastructure, and accelerates
suburban sprawl. Instead of converting rural and natural areas, the county should
prioritize smart infill development, revitalization, and affordable housing density within
our current urban limits. Please protect Clark County's rural character and hold the line
on the UGB.

To Clark County Council and Planning Commission,

  We the concerned citizens and residents would like to comment on the proposed plan for
more high-density housing to be built. The area being NE 88th St. and NE 94th Ave (corner
lot). Also, would like to include the cumulative impact of the new City of Vancouver
Operations facility, along with any other upcoming developments in our Clark County and
otherwise.

  We are asking the county and all involved to consider and prioritize safety and functional
transit by addressing the follow points:

     •   Emergency Access and Street Width: Our current building codes make it ok for
         narrow streets, with the developments. However, when you add parked cars on
         these narrow streets, it can become impassable for emergency vehicles (ﬁre
         engines, ambulances) and utility vehicles. We would like to have the streets
         widened to accommodate safe two-way traffic, 35’-40’ widths so cars can park
         and have still have space for emergency vehicles to get through. to keep ﬂuid
         movement of all vehicles, including ﬁre and emergency vehicles. Two lanes one
         way and two lanes the opposite way, or turn lanes would be optimal to
         accommodate all of the new traffic that will be happening.
     •   Parking and Driveway Standards: Short unaccommodating driveways and
         insufficient onsite parking with no guest parking. This causes the overﬂow
         vehicles park out on the main highways. We would encourage the county to
         mandate longer driveways and more parking for guests in these developments. In
         this day and age, there are more than two cars in a household at times. That way
         our main roads stay clear and less congested. Sometimes cars are parked in front
         of hydrants, parking half on sidewalks and blocking driveways. Making any
         possible evacuation from homes in emergency situations VERY difficult. Or
         access to homes in emergency.
     •   Ingress/Egress Points: Make more than one entrance/exit for high density
         residential areas. Relying on one way in/out makes for unsafe and dangerous
         bottlenecked traffic. We would like it considered to change or update the current
         codes to reﬂect multiple entrance and exit points for high density developments.
     •   88th and Andresen/ 88th and 94th: 88th needs safe ADA compliant sidewalks to
         accommodate the newbuilds and current going in. I am sure the people that will be
         living and live in our communities would like a safe way to walk, bike, or take their
         electric wheelchairs, to the food and shops in the current Home Depot center and
         other businesses put in with the new apartments/business combo that has been
         built by Andresen, across from the Costco center. As it stands, 88th (from 94th to
         Andresen) does not have a consistent sidewalk. You literally have to walk out, bike
         or take your electric wheelchair out into the road, if you want to get from one point
         to the other. This, with the diesels and speeding traffic up and down 88th is quite
         scary to see. I for one, don’t even walk down that street.

        Also, now this street is no longer a country road, but a throughfare/ short cut to
bypass Padden. Which is better equipped to handle large diesels, but they use our 88th st.
instead. Also, hoping some change for huge trucks coming up our 88th st. (between 94th
st.and Andresen)

     •   Speeding on Andresen/72nd: This too needs to change, by enforcing our speed
         limits. It’s 45 MPH currently, but the line of site and intersection on Andresen and
         88th (Costco/Home Depot sides) make this a very unsafe intersection. As a lot of
         people speed up trying to catch the green lights and green turn lights.



   Our community is expanding, that is inevitable; however, the infrastructure is not
expanding with it. We plop developments here and there and do-nothing infrastructure
wise to support those developments. There is no Masterplan to go along with the other
parts of the city for the infrastructure and all of this building. It’s time to look at not just
building places here, there and everywhere, but look at the effect on our community, roads,
sidewalks etc.

  We do not have much in the way of mass transit. It’s our vehicles that get us from here to
there, it’s time we change our infrastructure to accommodate this. Maybe the builders and
developers can help with some of the cost of this, since they are the only ones beneﬁtting
from this situation.

 We are hoping these and any other safety concerns are addressed in the revised site plans
and future code amendments. Let’s make our community a “Master planned” community,
safe for everyone living in it. It’s time to change our building codes and make it possible for
a safer living environment for all. Title 40 must be changed; lives depend on it. It’s time
to relook at Title 40 and make some changes. Thank you.

Best Regards,

Ina Aparicio

9115 NE. 79th Ct., Vancouver WA. 98662, Ph. 949-697-3714

Cedar Dell Board Member

FOR THE PUBLIC RECORD AND THE COMPREHENSIVE PLAN

Re:  Civil and property rights excluded from permitting process - No net loss of
function and value must apply to all civil rights and protections for private
property rights

Dear Councilor, Commissioners and Staff,

Clark County Citizens United, Inc. has been informed that during an environmental
permit process, no net loss of function and value is required. But this must equally
apply to all civil rights and protections for private property rights according to the equal
goals under (RCW 36.70A.020 Washington State Growth Management Act Goal # 6. The
county's comprehensive growth plan was written over three decades ago. It was very
controversial then and remains so now. Rural families, who hoped managing their
private properties would get easier over time, now realize it is harder, with increased
regulations and more environmental conflicts. Despite the requirement for "science-
based" regulatory actions by state and federal laws. This is only part of the big picture
that has driven sky-rocketing permit fees, costs of housing and declining farm incomes.
 Washington State ranked last in the nation for agricultural profitability, according to the
recent 2025 USDA Economic Research Report.

Across 30 plus years of county comprehensive growth planning, increased
environmental regulations and land use zoning have transformed rural economies.
Common farming practices and how rural families choose to live their lives have been
forever altered. The county turns a blind eye to actions of staff, that resonates and
impact the civil rights of countless rural families.

County staff, when making determinations and mitigating environmental conflicts, have
broken the process and created mis-trust with the citizens they are tasked with helping.
There are no county policies authorizing standards that staff are required to uphold.
 Staff works with little oversight and hold lethal powers over private property and civil
rights. This paints a very bleak picture of the process, and makes it nearly impossible
when permitting any rural project. This includes agricultural structures, common
farming practices and hardship permits. The county is not interested in asking why or
understanding how regulatory overreach is contributing to problems for their farmers,
foresters, equestrians or rural families just trying to build or establishing a home.  

Clark County rejects Federal laws, Washington Dept. of Fish and Wildlife, and
Washington Department of Ecology recommendations for science-based buffers and
exclusions for critical areas. Instead, the county chooses regulatory overburden. The
federal and state recommendations would help open the door to more options for
landowners and protections for private property rights. The county regulatory burdens,
create a breach of trust with all that are forced to co-exist with staff's actions. Rather
than face to face conversations, the process forces permittees to line up an attorney.

This is not how any permitting process is supposed to work. Washington state and Clark
County do not require staff to be qualified as verifiers of critical areas, wetlands and
habitat. This allows for a corrupt process and determinations that fall prey to political
pressures rather than scientific facts and federal laws. It creates uncertainty, and
makes it hard to predict where the next onerous regulation will pop up. Written,
evidentiary standards for county agents are unclear what counts as a "drainage ditch,"
"stock pond," land "depression" or a "hazard tree." As a result, staff wrongly assumes
that every historical man-made disturbance, even common farming practices or a
downed tree, is a "probable" critical area or habitat and needs to be regulated to the hilt.
Common sense, standard practices, health, safety, wellbeing, civil and property rights
all take the back seat in the process. The final determination results in negligible
environmental improvement, but has major financial implications that restrict civil
rights, how rural families live, work and use their private property.

The door is opened when staff are allowed to speculate and make determinations that
require fabricated "buffers", and create "environmental loss" that must be mitigated.
Before the ink is dry on a permit, entire deeds to private properties are burdened with
conservation covenants that extend forever. Staff speculations resonate and directly
conflict with protections for private properties and civil rights obligations. This rampant
activity has been allowed to go unabated. This is where the county permitting process is
predatory and lethal to property and civil rights. This is not how rural permitting is
supposed to work.  

The county has a responsibility to mitigate damages to private property rights and all civil
rights obligations. Staff's work needs to reflect the best biological science, provide
balance and predictability. The county needs to clarify standards, clarify protections for
private property rights, and acknowledge the health, safety and wellbeing of rural
families. We need the permitting process to change, as there are real consequences
that resonate and impact civil rights. The county has a responsibility to take in the whole
picture and not focus on environmental issues alone. All of the GMA 15 mandatory
Goals carry equal importance. Clark County must be compliant to the protection of
private property rights.

Sincerely,

Susan Rasmussen, President

Clark County Citizens United, Inc.

Under Washington's Growth Management Act (GMA), the property rights goal states
that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation, and
landowners must be protected from arbitrary or discriminatory actions. [1]


Property Rights Goal Details
   Just Compensation: Private property cannot be taken for public use without
   payment.
   Arbitrary Protection: Landowner property rights are protected from arbitrary
   decisions.
   Discriminatory Actions: Regulations must avoid discriminatory treatment of
   individual owners.
   Basis for Plans: It serves as a guiding principle for local comprehensive plans
GMA Goals (RCW 36.70A.020)
   1. Urban growth. Encourage development in urban areas.
   2. Reduce Sprawl. Reduce the inappropriate conversion of undeveloped land.
 3. Transportation. Encourage efficient multimodal transportation systems.
 4. Housing. Plan for and accommodate housing affordable to all economic
    segments.
 5. Economic development. Encourage economic development throughout the
    state.
 6. Property rights. Private property shall not be taken for public use without just
    compensation having been made.
 7. Permits. Applications should be processed in a timely and fair manner.
 8. Natural resource industries. Maintain and enhance natural resource-based
    industries.
 9. Open space and recreation. Retain open space, enhance recreational
    opportunities.
10. Environment. Protect the environment and enhance the state's high quality of
    life, including air and water quality, and the availability of water.
11. Citizen participation and coordination. Encourage the involvement of
    citizens.
12. Public facilities and services. Ensure that those public facilities and services
    necessary to support development shall be adequate.
13. Historic preservation. Identify and encourage preservation.
14. Climate change and resiliency. Ensure that comprehensive plans,
    development regulations, and regional policies, plans, and strategies adapt to
    and mitigate the effects of a changing climate.
15. Shoreline management (RCW 36.70A.480)

Comment on the Clark County Growth
Management Plan Update
Submitted by: Mike Eyster, Heights at Pleasant Valley

My name is Mike Eyster, and I live in the Heights at Pleasant Valley. The County’s Growth
Management Plan update introduces zoning changes that, if implemented, will significantly
degrade an extensive area north and south of NE 139th Street between 50th Avenue and 72nd
Avenue. To date, I have been unable to locate any parcel-level zoning detail in the publicly
available materials describing the zoning changes scheduled for a County vote on October 13.
Without this detail, residents cannot determine how these changes interact with existing
infrastructure capacity, transportation limitations, or established development patterns. This lack
of clarity raises serious concerns about the feasibility and compatibility of any proposed
redesignation.

Based on the County’s materials, it appears the area south of NE 139th Street between NE 72nd
Avenue and NE 50th Avenue may be considered for high-density residential zoning. If this is
correct, it would significantly degrade a large, well-established residential district of 300 to 400
acres. These neighborhoods—including the Heights at Pleasant Valley—were intentionally
planned as cohesive communities with moderate-density single-family homes, internal
circulation, pedestrian connections, stormwater systems, and CC&Rs that support long-term
stability and neighborhood quality. These characteristics are not accidental; they reflect decades
of coordinated planning that produced a functional, compatible, and successful residential area.

The area south of NE 139th Street is a distinct residential pocket within the northern Vancouver
Urban Growth Area. Although built over time, the subdivisions share a consistent development
pattern: compatible lot sizes, similar building forms, predictable circulation routes, and a unified
neighborhood structure. This continuity is a major reason the district functions well today and
contributes positively to Vancouver’s overall livability. Introducing high-density zoning into this
location would undermine those established patterns and fundamentally conflict with the
planning framework that has guided this area for decades.

The implications of such a redesignation cannot be evaluated without parcel-level clarity,
infrastructure analysis, and compatibility review. In the absence of such detail in the publicly
available materials, the County has not demonstrated that any increase in intensity would be
compatible with the area’s infrastructure or development pattern. Any increase in density should
be assessed not only by the number of units it produces but also by how well it fits the existing
development pattern, street network, and infrastructure systems. Abrupt changes in density can
create substantial conflicts such as increased traffic on streets not designed for higher-density
use, added pressure on stormwater systems, and incompatibilities between different residential
forms. These issues warrant careful analysis and clear public communication.

R-32 allows three- to four-story multifamily buildings, larger footprints, higher lot coverage, and
reduced setbacks. These forms represent a pronounced increase in height, massing, and density
compared to surrounding single-family neighborhoods. In areas where higher-density uses are
appropriate, they are usually introduced through transitional zoning or design standards that
moderate the interface between different residential types. None of those elements exist here.

Higher-density residential uses are typically placed along major transportation corridors, near
commercial centers, or adjacent to areas already planned for more intensive development. This
approach ensures that increases in height, massing, and population occur gradually and
predictably. The neighborhoods south of NE 139th Street were designed around
moderate-density residential use. Any significant departure from that pattern should be evaluated
carefully to ensure it does not undermine neighborhood stability or functionality.

If the area south of NE 139th Street were redesignated to a high-density category such as R-32, it
would represent a substantial increase in intensity within the center of an established R-7.5
district. Without transitional zoning, buffering, or infrastructure upgrades, such a change would
create an immediate and unmitigated jump in scale. High-density residential uses typically
require enhanced transportation capacity, expanded stormwater facilities, and more robust utility
infrastructure. Placing such uses in the middle of a moderate-density neighborhood—rather than
along a major corridor—risks creating conflicts related to traffic, parking, building scale, and
overall compatibility.

An abrupt shift to R-32 density would destabilize the surrounding neighborhood, permanently
alter its residential character, and create severe, unresolvable conflicts with every adjacent street
and subdivision across a broad, multi-neighborhood area.

NE 72nd Avenue is the primary north–south circulation route for a large portion of the
community, and it already operates at or near functional capacity during peak periods. The
roadway was designed as a neighborhood-scale corridor, with narrow travel lanes, limited
shoulders, no center turn lane, and constrained opportunities for widening without significant
right-of-way acquisition. It currently carries school traffic, local residential circulation, and
regional cut-through volumes that exceed what the original design intended.

Based on data collected by the County, NE 72nd Avenue is already problematic and
dysfunctional. Adding significant housing density at NE 139th Street will exacerbate these issues
and extend them both north and south along the corridor.

NE 72nd Avenue already functions as a major arterial without major-arterial infrastructure.
Existing high-density development between NE 119th Street and NE 134th Street has produced
persistent peak-hour congestion, long queues at signalized intersections and stop-controlled
approaches, multi-cycle delays for left turns, increased cut-through traffic into adjacent
neighborhoods, and conflicts between regional through-traffic and local residential circulation.

Introducing another large concentration of high-density units would further burden an already
constrained corridor, compounding existing congestion and creating additional safety concerns
for pedestrians, cyclists, school traffic, and neighborhood residents. The cumulative effect of
funneling substantially higher traffic volumes onto 72nd Avenue would not only degrade
mobility but also alter the fundamental character and function of the roadway. This classification
does not align with the roadway’s physical design, width, or operational capacity.

A corridor or neighborhood system reaches failure not when one component breaks, but when
multiple stressed components interact. NE 72nd Avenue already exhibits overloaded traffic
volumes, insufficient pedestrian protection, abrupt land-use transitions, ongoing high-density
construction, and no remaining capacity for additional peak-hour demand. Under these
conditions, any additional high-density designation at NE 139th Street would push the corridor
beyond functional failure, creating a system-wide breakdown in mobility, safety, and
neighborhood circulation.

NE 139th Street between NE 50th Avenue and NE 72nd Avenue is classified as a Local Access
Road—the lowest-capacity classification in the County’s transportation hierarchy. It is designed
for short neighborhood trips, low traffic volumes, direct driveway access, and minimal peak-hour
loading. Today it operates as a quiet, rural-scale neighborhood road with narrow lanes, no center
turn lane, no shoulders, limited pedestrian facilities, and multiple residential driveways. Its
design reflects its intended purpose: to serve existing single-family homes at moderate density.

High-density development south of NE 139th Street would overwhelm this corridor. Multifamily
development generates substantially higher daily and peak-hour traffic volumes, including
concentrated morning and evening surges. A Local Access Road is not engineered to absorb
these volumes. The result would be congestion, queueing, turning conflicts, driveway blockages,
and increased cut-through traffic into adjacent neighborhoods. The County’s roadway
classification system makes clear that Local Access Roads are not appropriate locations for
high-density residential zoning, rendering the proposed redesignation incompatible by definition.
Local Access Roads are intentionally designed for the lowest-intensity residential uses; applying
high-density zoning to such a corridor contradicts the fundamental purpose of the roadway
classification system.

The neighborhoods surrounding NE 139th Street represent a stable, intentionally planned
residential district designed for moderate-density single-family living. The built environment,
infrastructure systems, and governance structures were all created to support this level of
intensity, and they function effectively within that framework. Introducing high-density zoning
into the center of this district would disrupt that stability, create incompatible land-use
transitions, and place additional strain on a transportation corridor already operating beyond its
intended capacity. Growth is necessary and welcome, but it must be placed where infrastructure,
context, and planning principles support it. The incompatibility between the proposed zoning and
the area’s infrastructure, street hierarchy, and established development pattern constitutes a fatal
flaw that cannot be mitigated through conditions or design standards. For these reasons, the
proposed redesignation should be withdrawn until a complete, parcel-level analysis demonstrates
that the area can support such intensity — a threshold it clearly does not meet today.

Chair Marshall — Randal Friedman on behalf of the Camas Earth Day Society (CEDS). CEDS
thanks the Council for listening to the concerns of many, including ourselves, in reversing your
approval of 1,200 housing units and adding the Nevin property to Camas’ UGA. We acknowledge
the hard work of the Friends of Clark County, Washington Conservation Action and many others
that helped make this happen. While CEDS applauds this action, our concern remains that the
EIS’s lack of meaningful indirect Impact analysis remains in the record. Beyond those expressed
in our DEIS comments and Mill District Plan, these comments support the Council's denial action.
We also offer thoughts on issues likely created through upgrade of lower Crown Road.



We were asked at the final public hearing to hold up the perfect sign. This picture shows it at an
appropriate locale. The pad-locked, barb-wired North Gate access to the shuttered Kraft Pulp Mill
foretell Camas’ current destiny. The buildings may come down, but not the foundations and a
cleanup beyond industrial. This is hardly working for our kid’s future.



Your action is a step towards making Camas’ future not one of continued sprawl, but one of smart
downtown growth after the mill property’s proper remediation.



CEDS exists to acknowledge and honor the legacy of Camas and Clark County to Earth Day’s
creation. Denis Hayes grew up the son of a Camas Mill worker. His childhood was one of
observing fish kills, clear cutting forests to wasteland, and pollution so thick they always had a
sore throats. Out of this childhood he was called to be the National Director of the effort which
created the first Earth Day. He then took it worldwide. It is the largest secular event in the world.
You can read about it here.




  Denis Hayes, one of Earth Day’s founders 50
  years ago, reflects
  news.harvard.edu


Earth Day created simple principles to live by: clean land, clean water and clean air. These are our
oxygen. We believe Earth Day’s legacy should return back to its Camas root and show a future
pathway respective of these principles. In this light, the inclusion of the Nevin property was
incompatible with Earth Day's basic principles.



Our EIS comments, as well as the Mill District Plan, speak to a different path. The concept is
simple: as hundreds of acres of mill property are properly planned for remediation, that land is
added to the vacant lands inventory. It is available in the future for what the MTCA calls “future
social use.”



Alternatively there's a future where Camas, courtesy of Koch Industries, exists with a large
brownfield next to its Historic Downtown. History has not been kind to towns facing this
situation.



Your action on the Nevin property has stopped sprawl in its tracks. What would have been the
inevitable bulldozer march overtaking Fern Praire is turned off. The Fern Praire Market is spared
the destiny of another soulless strip mall. Thankfully, these significant indirect impacts, never
identified, considered or mitigated, are moot.



Camas relied on your EIS for its SEPA compliance. Our EIS comments shed light of how Camas’
use is deficient for the granulation required at the city level. Beyond these direct impacts, what
about the required indirect impact analysis?



The Nevin property involved 160 acres of “bait and switch” before the Camas community.
Eighteen days after the County’s draft EIS was published for comment, Camas’ preferred land use
map showed the Nevin property designated rural land outside Camas’ city limits. It was in the
country with the majority of its street frontage on land used for ag uses. Camas' county effort for
the UGA expansion was hidden from Camas’ more stringent public participation requirements.
We were one who was never informed. You have righted this wrong.


Alan Peters, Camas’ Community Development Director, told Camas’ Planning Commission
Tuesday something needed for your record. Once the Nevin property was within the UGA, the
city must start planning for the urban services needed to serve 1,200 homes. He mentioned three
roads as needing upgrading. One was Crown Road. Some discussion of Crown Road issues
follows.

Our overall point continues that no one knew the answers to these questions. There was no
consideration of the actual combined traffic impact from the likely induced growth. The County's
SEPA document actually suggested the opposite: the Nevin property was part of an Alternative 3
that on the county-scale reduced traffic. Thankfully you saw through this.

Mr. Peters inferred in his preface to this Council’s final public hearing that development would
somehow stop at the Nevin's property. He further suggested, at the last minute, that Camas would
not annex the Nevin property until a TDR program was in place. These words have no legal basis
and make no irrevocable commitment. Four votes on the Camas City Council and any
commitment goes poof. These words are not a substitute for the robust direct and indirect impact
analysis required to support the proposed UGA expansion itself.


Given the owner’s new rights identified by Camas’ Community Development Director, TDRs are
not a reason to place the Nevin property in a UGA. If a future TDR program is up and running,
and legally enforceable, perhaps the question can be revisited on a regional scale. Until then it is
vaporware.



Let’s hope Camas by then will have an approved plan that follows the GMA by focused growth
downtown as part of the emerging HWY14 urban corridor.



In sum, your staff correctly noted the Nevin property is not needed for future growth at this time.
It is the wrong place for a number of reasons, including wild land fire risk sadly demonstrated by
the recent destruction in Spokane.



Thankfully your action avoids the dark future discussed in our DEIS comments. On behalf of our
kid’s better future as was asked on the sign, Camas can now move towards plan worthy of its
Earth Day heritage.



Respectfully,

    ISSUES ARISING FROM INCREASING THE TRAFFIC CAPACITY OF
                          CROWN ROAD

Crown Road is the County's responsibility. Is the county expected to make necessary upgrades to
support the development made possible by approval of Camas’ request? What about Crown
Road’s long-term maintenance? Would other jurisdictions involved expect the county to pony
up?

Consider what would be involved in creating this capacity. One thousand feet of lower Crown
Road is wedged between a slope supporting homes and Lacamas Creek. There is around 90
horizontal feet from the western edge of the pavement to the creek with an elevation drop of 60
feet. The second photo shows encroachment on an existing four-plex above Crown Road.




The road must include needed bicycle and walking connections to 3rd where a future shuttle
service might stop. What’s the required width to serve the complete future traffic created by
Camas’ request including indirect impacts? Will Crown Road need four lanes? Will Lacamas
Creek be impacted, e.g. put in a concrete channel? The engineers in Los Angeles made the Los
Angeles River a filming location for dystopian movies through the use of concrete. Let’s not
aspire to that.

Development marches on regardless of obstacles like Camas’ namesake creek.

Will there be stability issues with the upslope homes?

Technical Memo

Subject: HCM Segment v/c — NE 119th Street EB corridor (Upstream: NE 117th Ave →
Downstream: NE 124th Ave) — 2029 PM Buildout
From: Craig Kathol, Engineer II
Date: September 18, 2026
Methods: Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7th Edition — Chapter 18 (Urban Street
Segments) segment v/c check using downstream boundary intersection inputs;
downstream capacity basis per HCM Chapter 19 (Signalized Intersections)/Chapter 20
(TWSC) conventions.



1) Purpose

Document the eastbound (EB) segment v/c for NE 119th Street between NE 117th Ave
(upstream) and NE 124th Ave (downstream) for the 2029 PM peak hour and conﬁrm the
corridor is ≤ 0.90 v/c, following HCM methodology:

   •   In Chapter 18, the v/c screen for an urban street segment uses the downstream
       boundary intersection’s demand and (optional) capacity ﬁelds for the subject
       direction; this is where the segment “exits” and thus the controlling boundary for
       v/c.

   •   At a Two-Way STOP-Controlled (TWSC) downstream intersection, the major-street
       EB movements (through & right) operate with priority/free and are not
       capacity-limited by signal control. Consequently, the v/c denominator can be
       represented by a free-discharge capacity per EB lane (i.e., saturation ﬂow per lane),
       rather than a signal green share.



2) Corridor orientation (EB)

   •   Upstream boundary: NE 117th Ave / NE 119th St

   •   Downstream boundary: NE 124th Ave / NE 119th St (TWSC; NB approach is
       stop-controlled; EB on the major street is priority).
       This orientation matches HCM Chapter 18 practice: the downstream boundary
       provides the demand input for the segment v/c screen and the appropriate capacity
       representation for the subject direction.




                                                                         EXHIBIT 111
3) Inputs (2029 PM buildout — EB at downstream boundary)

   •   Downstream EB demand at NE 124th Ave:

          o   EB through = 682 veh/h (p. 164/180 of the TIA)

          o   EB right = 185 veh/h (p. 164/180 of the TIA)

          o   EB left: not provided (and not needed for the major-street EB exit of this
              segment)

Under TWSC, the major-street EB through and right are Rank 1 priority movements; the
HCM TWSC method focuses v/c/delay on minor-approach movements, while
major-approach movements are typically considered free/priority for control purposes. For
the segment v/c denominator we therefore use the lane saturation ﬂow (free-discharge) per
EB lane.



4) Capacity basis (HCM-consistent)

   •   Saturation ﬂow per lane (planning default):
       𝑠𝑠0 = 1,900 pc/h/lnfor large metro areas when local measurement is unavailable.
       (HCM encourages local calibration; if measured, substitute the local value.)
       [mctrans.ce.uﬂ.edu]

   •   EB lane count at the downstream boundary: not speciﬁed; by default, assume
       one EB lane. (If two EB lanes discharge through/right, capacity doubles and v/c
       drops proportionally.)

Note: When signal control applies, HCM Chapter 19 deﬁnes capacity as 𝑐𝑐 = 𝑠𝑠 ⋅ (𝑔𝑔/𝐶𝐶) ⋅ 𝑁𝑁.
Here the downstream boundary is TWSC (major EB is free), so 𝑔𝑔/𝐶𝐶 ≈ 1.0conceptually and
capacity reduces to𝑐𝑐 ≈ 𝑠𝑠0 ⋅ 𝑁𝑁. [fhwa.dot.gov], [hcm-calculator.com]



5) Calculations (Chapter 18 segment v/c using downstream EB approach)

5.1 Downstream EB approach demand (hourly)

                𝑉𝑉EB,down = EB through + EB right = 682 + 185 = 867 veh/h


5.2 Downstream EB approach capacity (free-discharge, TWSC major)
With one EB lane:

                           𝑐𝑐down = 𝑠𝑠0 ⋅ 𝑁𝑁 = 1,900 ⋅ 1 = 1,900 veh/h


5.3 Segment v/c (hourly, HCM Chapter 18)

                                                    867
                                 v/csegment,EB =         = 𝟎𝟎. 𝟒𝟒𝟒𝟒𝟒𝟒

Optional: If a peak-15-minute equivalent is required and a PHF is available for this
boundary, form 𝑣𝑣𝑝𝑝 = 𝑉𝑉hr /PHFand compute 𝑣𝑣/𝑐𝑐15 = 𝑣𝑣𝑝𝑝 /𝑐𝑐. (Chapter 18’s v/c check itself is
hourly; peak-15 is an intersection convention.) [hcmguide.com]



6) Compliance

   •   NE 119th Street EB segment v/c (hourly): 0.456 → Meets v/c ≤ 0.90 with
       substantial margin.

These calculations follow Chapter 18 (downstream boundary inputs) and
TWSC/Chapter 20 conventions for the major-street EB exit capacity (free-discharge per
lane), which is appropriate since the downstream boundary is stop-controlled only on the
minor approach.

   f rame. This correction is given because it does not appear that the document making that correction as a part of

   As this open record period relates to the volume-to-capacity analysis for PLD-2025-00114, it is staff’s position that
   the use of CCC 40.350.020(F)(9) allows concurrency staff to consider other factors that the Public Works Director
   has determined could have an impact on the operating level of the transportation corridors or intersections. Since
   the Public Works Director’s determination of other f actors and subsequent direction to staff in the 2014 time f rame,
   concurrency staff has used the intersection level-of-service and queuing, along with existing roadway influences
   and, where applicable, potential mitigation options such as Transportation System Management (TSM) or
   Transportation Demand Management (TDM) strategies may be considered in whole or in part when determining
   compliance with or determining acceptable levels-of-service under CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a). Based on the
   evaluation method that has been applied and practiced since the 2014 time f rame, the regionally significant
   corridors evaluated as a part of PLD-2025-00114 Heartwood North Subdivision provide operational capacity to
   support the proposed development under existing and buildout conditions. Theref ore, staff recommends the
   Hearing Examiner approve PLD-2025-00114 Heartwood North Subdivision with conditions of approval as listed
   in the concurrency staf f report (Exhibit 54).

      • Email dated June 10, 2026, prepared by Steve Thalberg (Ex 62)

   The County’s responses will be shown without italics.

   “1. Clark County staff states that a failed volume to capacity ratio does not represent roadway
   deficiencies, but rather corridor mobility is facilitated with good intersection level of service.” (Ex 62)

   As provided in Exhibit 68, when “corridor v/c ratio thresholds may appear to be exceeded even when
   intersection operations remain within acceptable limits. In such cases, higher corridor volumes indicate that
   intersections are operating ef f iciently enough to allow more vehicles to pass through with minimal delay,
   thereby increasing the overall throughput of the corridor.”



For other formats, contact the Clark County ADA Office: 564.397.2322 / 711 or 800.833.6388 / ADA@clark.wa.gov

                                                                                                     EXHIBIT 113
“2. No matter how the Clark County staff tries to reword or reinterpret Clark County Code, it is in error,
and they don’t have that authority – only the Clark County Council or the Superior Court can do that.”
(Ex 62)

“If no code authority can be identified for the intersection substitution methodology and no compliant
cumulative analysis can be demonstrated, deny the project on the grounds that the concurrency
finding in the staff report is not supported by the adopted code.” (Ex 89)

Application of CCC 40.350.020 requires that the corridor and intersection operations must be determined
under CCC 40.350.020(F) Determination of Operation Levels bef ore compliance is tested under CCC
40.350.020(G) Level of Service Standards.

When reviewing the f actors under CCC 40.350.020(F), it has been determined by the Public Works Director
and the Transportation Division Manager that other f actors have an impact on the operating level of
transportation corridors that require f urther evaluation when a prescriptive evaluation of v/c exceeds a 0.9.
CCC 40.350.020(F)(9) grants the Public Works Director the authority to make that determination.

Staf f ’s application of this code section is not to reword, or to reinterpret the code but to make sure that the
f actors that can have impact on an operating level (existing operational characteristics of the roadway) are
more accurately represented when evaluating development related impacts. This type of analysis ensures
that the required v/c ratio of 0.9 is not exceeded. CCC 40.350.020(F)(9) provides f lexibility to identif y other
f actors f or consideration through the Public Works Director’s authority.

“3. CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a) states each roadway segment shall not exceed the volume to capacity
ratio of 0.9.” (Ex 62)

“VIII. The Corridor V/C Standard Is Binding, Not Discretionary” (Ex 64)

This 0.9 v/c ratio is the concurrency level-of -service threshold that was established and codified in compliance
with the Growth Management Act.

“4. For traffic capacity, Clark County Code does not allow intersection findings to substitute for
corridor roadway segments.” (Ex 62)

“Require county staff to identify, by specific code citation, the legal authority that permits substitution
of intersection delay analysis for segment volume-to-capacity compliance under Clark County Unified
Development Code Section 40.350.020(G)(1)(a) before making a finding of concurrency compliance for
this project.”(Ex 89)

Staf f ’s evaluation of corridor roadway segments does not substitute intersection f indings f or corridor level of
service. Intersection operations is one of the characteristics used in the evaluation of how a corridor is
operating. Roadway operations breakdown/degrade at intersections because of poor levels-of-service and/or
queueing issues.

“5. According to CCC 40.350.020, there is no intersection mobility standard that overrides the volume
to capacity ratio for road segments.” (Ex 62)

Intersection operations is one of the characteristics used in the evaluation of how a corridor is operating. It
should be noted that the applicant could volunteer mitigation to offset the impacts of their development. This
is allowed under CCC 40.350.030(B)(6). While the applicant has not volunteered mitigation, it is something
the county could consider when the 0.9 v/c has been determined to be exceeded.

“6. The Heartwood North project is using very newly invented methodology to get concurrency
approved.” (Ex 62)

“The applicant’s own traffic study documents the eastbound segment of NE 119th Street between SR-
503 and NE 124th Avenue at a volume-to-capacity ratio of 1.09 in the 2029 evaluation year, with 119th
Street Station included in the baseline as required by Clark County Unified Development Code Section

What Concurrency Is For
Concurrency is a Growth Management Act requirement: roads must meet the adopted standard, or a
financial commitment must be in place to complete the fix within six years, before development is
approved. The staff who presented the 2014 corridor standard told the Board so, and the Council wrote
it into its findings.

What that design means for this case:
   •   Two separate tests, each able to stop a development. A corridor that fails is a failure. A corridor
       that passes can still fail on a problem intersection. Nothing the Board adopted provides a third
       outcome: corridor fails, intersections pass, approve.
 •     The protection runs one way. Intersection standards were kept to catch problems a passing
       corridor would miss. Staff now use them to excuse a corridor that fails.
 •     The Board retired the travel-speed standard on purpose. Under the speed standard,
       intersection delay fed into corridor travel time, so a corridor could be judged through its
       intersections (Exhibit J; Exhibit N, § 3). The Board replaced that with a capacity test and kept
       intersection standards separate. Clearing NE 119th and NE 99th on intersection performance
       brings back the speed-era approach the Board retired.
 •     Intersection effects are already in the capacity. The Board was told intersection spacing goes
       into the capacity figures. Using intersection performance again to clear a segment counts it
       twice, only toward approval.
 •     The code reflects the design. The 2014 amendment replaced the corridor measure in (G)(1)(a)
       with a v/c ratio, separate from the intersection standards in (G)(1)(b) and (c). Staff concede
       “each subsection of section G represents different elements … County code has established
       individual levels of service for each” (Exhibit J).

Point 4 — (F)(9) Adds an Input. It Does Not Override (G)(1)(a)
(F)(9) is the ninth item in a list of things that make up the operating level. It reads: “Any other factors
that the Public Works Director has determined could have an impact on the operating level of the
transportation corridors or intersections.” It lets the Director capture traffic the first eight items miss. It
says nothing about capacity, the 0.90 standard, or approval. It also predates the v/c standard: the 2014
ordinance carried Section (F), including (F)(9), over unchanged from the travel-speed code, with an
amendment history running from 2007 to 2011 (Exhibit H, p. 6). It was not adopted as part of the 0.90
standard.
An attorney’s analysis already in the record works through Section (F) item by item and reaches the
same conclusion (Ex. 73, pp. 2–5). Neither staff’s response nor the applicant’s addresses it. Bryan
Telegin of Telegin Law, writing in the 174th Street matter, sorted each (F) factor by what it feeds:

   •     Different conditions, one objective number. A participant (0:16:21): the capacity standard is

   •      The stamp is the professional standard. The code requires a professional engineer to prepare or
          supervise the study ((D)(3)), and the 2011 Manual requires it to be “prepared and stamped” by a
          Washington PE (Exhibit A, p. 5). State law requires that “[p]lans, specifications, plats, and
          reports prepared by the registrant shall be signed, dated, and stamped,” and that the stamp
          “shall constitute a certification by the registrant that the same was prepared by or under the
          registrant’s direct supervision” (RCW 18.43.070).
   •      Unlicensed staff may do engineering work only under a licensee’s responsibility. These rules
          bind the County. A public agency that performs engineering “shall perform its duties and
          responsibilities in the same manner as an individual” (WAC 196-25-080). The engineering
          registration law excepts the work of an unlicensed employee only where “such work does not
          include final design or decisions and is done under the direct responsibility, checking, and
          supervision of a person holding a certificate of registration” (RCW 18.43.130(2)). Direct
          supervision means “[m]aintaining control over those decisions that are the basis for the findings,
          conclusions, analyses, rationale, details, and judgments required for the preparation of
          engineering … reports,” and review “after preparation without involvement in the design and
          development process as described above cannot be accepted as direct supervision” (WAC 196-
          25-070(1), (5)).
   •      The record shows no licensed engineer taking responsibility for this work. Recalculating
          corridor capacity with Highway Capacity Manual factors is engineering analysis, and a
          concurrency determination under (E)(3) is a decision. None of Exs. 54, 111, 112 or 113 is
          stamped or notes review, checking or supervision by a licensed engineer. Exs. 111–112, the
          calculations that changed the result, note no review at all. The Director is a licensed engineer,
          but nothing in the record shows he performed, checked or supervised Exs. 54, 111, 112 or 113.
          And no record delegates the Director’s authority to the staff who did it (Point 7).


                                                       Page 14
   •     The result. A corridor failure reported in a study stamped by two licensed engineers was set
         aside by an engineering judgment that the record does not show any licensed engineer made or
         checked.
Staff’s claim that they can change the road capacity the code assigns is new. It first appeared on May
21, 2026, in the middle of the 174th Street hearing. Until then, staff cleared failing corridors by pointing
to intersection LOS, and the capacities in Table 40.350.020-1 were not questioned in any finding
reviewed. Starting May 21, staff claimed they could adjust the capacity itself with HCM “real-world”
factors, and tied that claim to the Director’s long-standing direction.

In 2014–2017 the record shows corridors were expected to have ample room before failure, and the
County’s concurrency work was about intersections.

  •    The corridor standard was built with ample room before failure. The Board’s example corridor
       was at 50%: “if the LOS standard is 90%, we’re not in failure” (Exhibit D, 0:04:39). It “has 40
       more percent points to go before it goes into failure” (Exhibit E, 0:05:08). Corridors were to be
       color-coded, with green meaning “there’s plenty of capacity left, highly unlikely it will fail
       anytime soon” (Exhibit D, 0:05:09).
  •    The 2014 standard was adopted as a package with a smaller capital plan and lower impact
       fees. The ordinance says so: “because the change in the concurrency standards will impact
       traffic impact fee (TIF) rates, the new concurrency standards will go into effect the same time
       the revised Capital Facilities Plan (CFP) is adopted” (Exhibit H, p. 1). The new standard was
       expected to “reduce the CFP,” after which “you would recalculate the traffic impact fees based
       on that lower level of CFP.” Schulte: “Right. That’s correct.” (Exhibit C, 0:37:58, 0:39:01). Staff
       “set out to cut about 150 million from the bottom line” (Exhibit D, 0:48:15). The advisory board
       was told “Traffic Impact Fee (TIF) rates will decrease when a revised CFP is adopted later this
       year,” and that “[t]he BOCC approves of the VTC ratio and the downsized CFP” (Ex. 75, minutes
       pp. 1–2).
  •    Concurrency money was aimed at intersections. Schulte: “this table helps keep mobility on the
       links, on the segments. We still have issues at individual intersections not having capacity…
       Urban arterial intersections. We’re proposing about $20 million a year that would be money we
       could move to fix intersections if they do begin to fail” (Exhibit D, 0:28:17).
  •    The 2016–2017 code work was about individual intersection approaches, not corridors.
       Mr. Jardin showed the Council “a large development using the current exemptions to justify
       compliance”: a stop-controlled approach at LOS F with a v/c of 0.62, and “no mitigation was
       required” (Exhibit F, 0:26:54). The problem was that “the projected volume-to-capacity ratio of
       0.9 is very difficult to achieve,” so “we may have some missed opportunities to require or get
       mitigation from development” (0:32:21). The Council closed that gap by ordinance (Exs. 79, 80,
       85).
  •    Nothing in the record from that period mentions a corridor override. In 2016, staff and the
       Director were before the Council specifically to fix how a v/c test let developments avoid
       mitigation. If corridors over 0.90 had been cleared by Director direction since 2014, that practice
       would have been directly relevant. It was not mentioned at the 2016 session.
  •    The 2014 plan for failing corridors was monitoring and prioritization, not an override. The new
       standard was expected to “reduce the CFP” (Exhibit C, 0:37:58), and staff “set out to cut about
       150 million from the bottom line” (Exhibit D, 0:48:15). In place of the dropped projects, the
       Board was promised an annual status report “so you will know when … road segments are
       nearing failure, and then we can move monies around as needed to resolve those issues”
       (Exhibit E, 0:06:37). That reporting has not continued: a records request for the Council’s annual
       corridor reviews returned nothing for six years (Exhibit M). Mr. Jardin described the test as
       comparing existing volumes “to the capacity that’s allowed” (Ex. 75, minutes p. 1). The record
       shows no need for an override in 2014.
Three conclusions follow:
  1.    If a Director ever directed staff to judge corridors by their intersections, it fits only the pre-2014
        travel-speed standard, where intersection delay was part of the corridor measure. That standard
        was repealed in 2014.
  2.    In 2014 Mr. Jardin was the Concurrency Engineer and helped prepare the Board presentation
        materials (Exhibit J, p. 1). Staff told the Board the opposite of what he now says they were
        directed to do that same year.


                                                   Page 18
   3.    When a concurrency provision did not work, Mr. Jardin took it to the Board. The record does not
         show that he did for this one. Nothing in the record shows the practice was ever authorized; the
         record shows no challenge before the 174th Street hearing.

The one record the County did produce shows how Public Works actually delegates. It is a written
form (24FORM-DEL-PW), names the specific code sections, requires the Director’s approval, is “for
delegating authority which exists within the current laws and regulations of the county,” and states: “No
additional authority may be assumed that is beyond the authority expressly granted herein” (Ex. 106,
pp. 2, 4). It also states that “Delegation is for the individual, not the position,” that “Sub-delegation of
this authority is prohibited,” and it withholds a decision the code assigns solely to the County Engineer
(Ex. 106, pp. 3–4). The County produced no equivalent instrument for CCC 40.350.020. The request
named no employee. It asked for “the document from the Public Works Director providing authorization
for Staff to use F(9) of the Concurrency code (or other authorization without citing the code) to
recommend concurrency approval for developments with v/c ratios above .9” (Ex. 106, p. 1). The County
identified one record, the Development Engineering delegation, and stated “there are not any additional
known responsive documents” (Ex. 106, p. 1). Asked a follow-up, it replied that “[t]he previously
provided policy is responsive” and that “[t]he PRA does not require that I answer questions about the
provided responsive records” (Ex. 106, p. 11). If an authorization exists, it has not been made public and
is not in this record. A member of the public should not need to know the County’s organization, or
guess which employee to name, to learn who is authorized to run a state-mandated concurrency
program. The code requires the method to be published ((N)(3)), the County’s own form requires
delegations to be in writing (Ex. 106, pp. 2–4), and the applicant bears the burden of showing the
standards are met (Ex. 110, pp. 1–2).
Nothing connects the Director’s authority to the staff who acted here. CCC 40.350.020 assigns its
determinations to the Public Works Director. The only delegation the County produced was granted by
Jeremy Provenzola to Dan Kaler, with approval by Public Works Director Ken Lader. It covers
construction plans and road modifications, not CCC 40.350.020, and it prohibits sub-delegation (Ex. 106,
pp. 2–4). Nothing in this record, and nothing the County produced in response to a records request,
delegates concurrency authority from any Director to Mr. Jardin or Mr. Kathol. Yet Mr. Kathol prepared
the concurrency report and the capacity calculations, and Mr. Jardin approved the report and issued the
response (Exs. 54, 111–113).
Even a proper delegation or manual could not do what staff are doing.

Point 9 — The Traffic Study May Understate the Problem
Two licensed engineers report different results for the same corridors, and Kittelson’s are lower. That
suggests traffic may be missing from the operating level. If so, the failures shown are a floor, not a
ceiling.

                                                            Page 22
   •       The operating level must include all approved, unbuilt development. Section (F)(5) requires
           “the traffic impacts of other approved developments not yet fully built-out,” and (E)(2) tests
           applications in order of their fully complete dates. Kittelson used the 16 in-process
           developments “provided by Clark County staff” (TIA pp. 16–17, Table 5). Nothing in the record
           shows that list is complete, or reconciles it with the other studies.
   •       Stumpf’s figures come from other developments’ traffic studies. His memo draws on 27 studies
           prepared over five to eight years (Ex. 65, p. 2). Different studies counted different in-process
           traffic and found higher ratios on the same roads.
   •       Kittelson tested corridors in the PM peak only. Stumpf reports NE 99th and SR 503 failing in the
           AM as well. The Manual says “any peak traffic period during the day can be tested” (Exhibit A,
           p. 4).
   •       Staff checked in the wrong direction. Before relying on any finding, staff should confirm that
           every approved, unbuilt development is counted. Instead, they recalculated capacity upward.
           Any missing traffic makes these corridors worse, not better.
   •       The study area was chosen, not set by the code. In practice, studies select which intersections
           and corridors to analyze instead of covering the radius the code requires (Ex. 64, § I). Ex. 113
           defends the narrower scope by asking whether the County could find a “nexus” to require
           mitigation or deny the project (p. 3). That is the wrong question. The study area exists to find
           concurrency problems early, by analyzing “the projected impact of the proposed development
           upon the current operating level” of each affected corridor ((D)(2)(b)), not to decide what a
           developer can be charged.
   •       Small increments add up, and no one is looking. Ex. 113 treats locations receiving “5 or less
           trips” as having “minimal impact” and leaves them out of the study (p. 3), and (G)(1)(c) does not
           require a development to mitigate at a failing approach unless it adds at least five trips. Applied
           one development at a time, with background growth layered on ((F)(8)), these rules mean a
           location that many developments each add a few trips to is never studied and never mitigated.
           It degrades in increments that no single study captures. The code’s safeguard is the Council’s
           annual review of corridor standards and operating levels ((G)(3)). A records request returned no
           such review in six years (Exhibit M).

Point 10 — The TIA Did Not Evaluate SR 503 as a Corridor, Though the Code
Requires It
(G)(1)(a) requires that corridor “measurements shall also be made for state highways of regional
significance.” Kittelson’s own study says County performance requirements apply “at the study
intersections along SR 503,” and it measured SR 503 only at those intersections. Heartwood trips
heading west on NE 119th and NE 99th reach SR 503, and the County has known for more than a
decade that SR 503 is a problem.

   •    The applicant’s GMA arguments are for another forum, as its counsel recognized. Whether a
        development regulation complies with the GMA is decided by the Growth Management
        Hearings Board, and adopted regulations are presumed valid (RCW 36.70A.280, .290, .320(1);
        Woods v. Kittitas County, 162 Wn.2d 597, 174 P.3d 25 (2007)). Whether the standard should
        change is for the Council. Applicant’s counsel said as much in June when he asked for time to
        pursue a code fix (Ex. 110, pp. 4–5).
  •     No code change has come. None was adopted. What came back instead was Exs. 111–113.
  •     Staff recommend; the Examiner decides. Ex. 54 and Ex. 113 are staff recommendations. As the
        Examiner explained, the question is whether there is “sufficient credible evidence to
        demonstrate that each of those standards is met” (Ex. 110, p. 1).
  •     The question returns to the code as adopted. The Examiner observed on September 10 that the
        (F)(9) catch-all is “so like open ended so that it’s almost an exception that consumes the rule”
        (Ex. 114, p. 9). Applying CCC 40.350.020 so the 0.90 standard keeps its effect answers the
        question actually before him.
Denial is not a countywide moratorium. It is concurrency working as intended, applied to this
application.
Applicant’s counsel argued on September 10 that denial would be a “de facto moratorium” because
other corridors in the County also exceed 0.90 (Ex. 114, p. 9). That is not the question before the
Examiner.
   •     The Examiner decides this application, on this record. Whether another development passes or
         fails is decided in its own review, on its own traffic study. A moratorium is a legislative act the
         Council alone may take under (G)(4) and RCW 36.70A.390. A denial of one application is not.



                                                         Page 26
  •     Concurrency is road-specific. A finding that NE 119th, NE 99th and SR 503 exceed 0.90 is a
        finding about those roads. The memo counsel relies on (Ex. 65, p. 3) lists specific corridors in
        specific areas, not the whole County.
  •     Other applicants still have paths forward. The code allows volunteered mitigation ((E)(5); CCC
        40.350.030(B)(6)(a)), credits improvements funded and scheduled for completion of
        construction within six years ((F)(6)), and lets a development proceed once capacity is built. Ex.
        113 (p. 2) itself says the applicant “could volunteer mitigation.”
  •     The code itself says denial is available. CCC 40.350.030(B)(6): “nothing in this section shall be
        construed to preclude denial of a proposed development where off-site road conditions are
        inadequate to provide a minimum level of service as specified in Section 40.350.020.” Staff
        quote this provision in their own findings (Exhibit T, pp. 4, 11, 19, 26).
  •     The County has dealt with this before, area by area. Schulte told the Board in 2013 that the
        County’s concurrency history was “dominated by Pipeline 1” and two more events “in Salmon
        Creek in ’04 and ’07” (Exhibit C, 0:02:38). On September 10 the Examiner recalled that the
        pipeline projects “were forced to stall and … come up with a comprehensive mitigation plan”
        (Ex. 114, p. 10).
  •     This is the result the Council wrote into the code. The code “attempts to delay development in
        areas served by roads failing concurrency until the condition can be improved or mitigated”
        (Ords. 2016-10-11 and 2017-04-13, Exs. 80, 85, recitals). The Board was promised annual
        monitoring so money could be moved before roads reached failure (Exhibit E, 0:06:37). That this
        did not happen is a reason to fund fixes, not to approve development on failing roads.
  •     Counsel identified the remedy himself. On June 11 he asked for time to pursue a code change
        (Ex. 110, pp. 4–5). Changing the standard is for the Council, not this hearing.

Requested Decision
Deny PLD-2025-00114 under CCC 40.350.020(C), (E)(1), (E)(3) and (G)(1)(a). Three corridor segments
exceed 0.90 on the operating level the code defines, so a concurrency approval cannot issue.
Find that Exhibits 111–113 are not a lawful basis for approval, because they:
  1. replace the capacities fixed by (G)(1)(a) and Table 40.350.020-1 with staff’s own numbers;
  2. use volumes lower than the Section (F) operating level, without explanation;
  3. rely on (F)(9), which adds inputs and does not override (G)(1)(a); and
  4. rest on a Director determination that no one can identify, date, or produce.
The decision should also address three other failures in the record. The denial rests on (G)(1)(a). But
the record also shows:
  1.   NE 124th and NE 132nd Avenues at NE 119th operating below the LOS D standard that applies
       where signal warrants are met ((G)(1)(c); Point 5);
  2. SR 503, which the code requires to be measured as a corridor, not evaluated by the TIA
       ((G)(1)(a); Point 10); and
  3. a study area set by the consultant’s choice of locations rather than the code’s radius, with no
       (D)(8) determination in the record, under a practice that lets locations degrade through small
       increments no single study captures (Point 9).
Each shows that the concurrency review in this case did not apply the code as written.

                                       Measuring the Leap
   Supplemental Submission — Heartwood North (PLD-2025-00114) — Submitted by Heidi Pozzo —
                            Before Hearing Examiner Daniel Kearns
                                               October 8, 2026

Summary
Staff are replacing the corridor standard with their own practice, one development at a time. Exhibit
113 is not another step. It is a leap.
Before October 1, 2026, the County’s filings on the corridor standard took two forms. Some claimed that
staff’s practice complied with the code. Others admitted it operated “outside of the code’s prescriptive
measures.” Both treated the code’s own measurement as showing a ratio over 0.9. Ex. 68 called that
result an exceedance that “may appear” when intersections are working. The dispute was whether staff
could look past it.
Exhibit 113 drops the premise. It is the first County filing in this record to say that these segments do not
exceed 0.9 at all, and the first to show a calculation that gets there by computing its own capacity. In the
same filing, staff retreat from the summer’s admissions, describe the code as the “conservative” option
among several, state that (F)(9) “does not dictate how staff evaluates” the factors, and describe as
practice “since the 2014 time frame” a capacity calculation dated September 18, 2026 and first entered
in this record on October 1.
Nothing remains of the code. Over the summer, staff called the standard “not binding” and applied
factors “in lieu of the code-prescribed threshold values.” Exhibit 113 brings the 0.9 back only after
everything it is applied to has been made to vary. Staff choose the volume, compute the capacity and
select the method, case by case.
The people the code puts in charge have been written out. The Council adopted a fixed, objective
standard, and staff told the Council in 2016 that standards are set “by approval through the board.” This
practice was never brought to it. The code makes the Public Works Director responsible for the method
and the approval, yet nothing from any Director has been produced, in this record, in the 174th Street
record, or in response to a public records request for the Director’s authorization (Ex. 106). Staff decide.
And it is spreading where it can least be undone. Staff are already offering the method to new
applicants before their studies are written. It is being applied where the County lifted the overlay that
held development back until the roads were built, and where the County’s own budget shows its road
program is short.
This supplement is filed with my Concurrency Submission and cites its exhibits (A–X).

I. Where the Window Stood Before Exhibit 113
Through September 10, the record conceded that the ratio, measured as the code directs, was above
0.9. The County’s own filings differed only in how they described the authority to look past it.
