That was the edge of the window on September 10. The County claimed authority to look past a failing
ratio, and over the summer described its work as an analysis outside the code’s prescriptive measures,
performed under (F)(9). None of these County statements said the segments were below 0.9.
In just over five months, the County’s position has moved from no code authority, to claimed code
authority, to admitted departure from the code’s measures, to a claim that the code’s own result is
merely the cautious version of staff’s.

II. The Moves in Exhibit 113
1. The exceedance is erased, not excused.
Exhibit 113 reports NE 119th Street eastbound at 0.46 and NE 99th Street at 0.46 and 0.73, and
concludes: “The result of the HCM analysis showed that NE 99th Street and NE 119th Street did not
exceed the code required 0.9 v/c” (Ex. 113, p. 3).
Its closing conclusion, that the corridors “provide operational capacity to support the proposed
development under existing and buildout conditions” (Ex. 113, p. 1), is the same sentence that ended Ex.
68 in the 174th Street case. There the sentence followed an acknowledged ratio over 0.9. In Exhibit 113
the same sentence rests on a claim that there is no exceedance. Exhibit 113 does not acknowledge that
the staff report and staff’s testimony on September 10 said the ratio was over 0.9.
Item 1 of Exhibit 113 repeats Ex. 68’s claim that higher corridor volumes “indicate that intersections are
operating efficiently enough to allow more vehicles to pass through with minimal delay, thereby
increasing the overall throughput of the corridor” (Ex. 113, p. 1). Under (G)(1)(a), a higher volume
produces a higher ratio. The code treats it as a step toward failure, not as evidence of efficiency.




                                                        Page 2
2. A retreat from the summer’s admissions.
On May 21, the County claimed code authority for the practice (Ex. 54; Ex. 68). From June through
August, its filings described the same practice as an analysis “outside of the code’s prescriptive
measures” that “was performed in compliance with CCC 40.350.020(F)(9)”; as “not binding or a ‘flat
prohibition’”; and as factors “applied in lieu of the code-prescribed threshold values.” Exhibit 113 keeps
the code-authority framing that Ex. 68 and the June 4 letter both used, drops the June–August
admissions, and goes further:
  •     “Staff has not used invented methodology. Staff has used application of code and authorities
        granted by code to ensure that the 0.9 v/c roadway capacity is not exceeded” (p. 3).
  •     “Staff’s application of this code section is not to reword, or to reinterpret the code” (p. 2).
  •     “Staff’s application of the code does not override the 0.9 v/c ratio concurrency level-of-service
        threshold” (p. 4).
The description retreated while the method expanded. The summer filings admitted working outside the
code’s prescriptive measures while citing (F)(9). Exhibit 113 replaces the code’s capacity, a larger
change, and calls it application of the code.
3. The code becomes the “conservative” option.
Exhibit 113 lays out three paths: “whether development seeks to pursue a conservative approach to the
concurrency code and follow it prescriptively, or a more robust analysis using existing real-world
roadway influences in an HCM analysis is performed, or volunteering mitigation” (p. 3). It adds that “if
the traffic study can show that it meet the prescriptive, more conservative threshold the more robust
analysis is not necessary” (p. 4).
The 2014 standard was not conservative. It set the line at 90 percent of “full capacity, theoretical
capacity” (Exhibit E, 0:05:08), and the County built its road plans around it. The ordinance tied the new
standard’s effective date to the revised capital facilities plan because the change “will impact traffic
impact fee (TIF) rates” (Exhibit H, p. 1), and staff told the Board they “set out to cut about 150 million
from the bottom line” (Exhibit D, 0:48:15). The program was built so road capacity would not be
exceeded, and so that if it were, “county funds [would be] available to mitigate failures” (Ex. 75, minutes
p. 2).
Calling that standard “conservative” implies a large margin above it. Exhibit 111 then claims one: it
treats a lane the code rates at 900 vehicles an hour as carrying 1,900, more than twice the code. Staff
are not applying a cautious version of the rule. They are writing a new rule as they go, under which the
road holds more than twice what the code allows.
4. A failing result becomes a trigger, and (F) absorbs (G).
The idea that a failing result opens a second analysis began with the corridor language staff introduced
on May 21. That language recast the code’s capacities as “baseline service levels under ideal conditions”
and asserted “real-world influences that also affect roadway capacity” (Ex. 54, p. 5; Ex. 67, pp. 4–5). On
June 4, Mr. Jardin made the connection explicit: if a traffic study showed the prescriptive thresholds
exceeded, “additional corridor analysis could be performed to determine acceptable operation outside
of the prescriptive thresholds identified in the code” (Exhibit J, p. 2). Exhibit 113 completes it. It states
that the other factors “require further evaluation” when a prescriptive evaluation exceeds 0.9 (p. 2), and
that the HCM analysis “will always be in response to a potential 0.9 v/c exceedance” (p. 4). A result over
0.9 is no longer a failure to be excused. It is the event that unlocks an alternative calculation, and the
code’s own measurement is relabeled a “potential” exceedance.


                                                   Page 3
Exhibit 113 supplies the structure that makes this possible: “the corridor and intersection operations
must be determined under CCC 40.350.020(F) Determination of Operation Levels before compliance is
tested under CCC 40.350.020(G)” (p. 2). Subsection (G)(1)(a) assigns only the volume to (F) and fixes
capacity itself through Table 40.350.020-1 (Exhibit H, pp. 6–7). By placing the whole operating level
under (F), Exhibit 113 brings capacity within the factors staff evaluate. That is the move that lets 900
become 1,900.
5. The standard is described by its required outcome.
Three times Exhibit 113 describes staff’s work by the result it must produce. The analysis “ensures that
the required v/c ratio of 0.9 is not exceeded” (p. 2); staff act “to ensure that the 0.9 v/c roadway
capacity is not exceeded” (p. 3); staff work “as we seek to ensure the 0.9 v/c ratio is not exceeded”
(p. 4). A standard is ordinarily a test applied to a measurement. Exhibit 113 describes the analysis by the
outcome it is meant to secure, not as a measurement of what the road carries.
6. The Public Works Director is written out of the code.
The code puts the Director at every decision point in this process. The Director issues the concurrency
approval ((E)(3)) and decides whether to accept volunteered mitigation ((E)(5)). The Director determines
any “other factors” that affect the operating level ((F)(9)). And the Director “shall establish and adopt
the methodology and criteria to be used to … evaluate the operating level for each transportation
corridor” and “shall publish and regularly update an administrative manual setting forth the
methodology and criteria adopted” ((N)(1), (N)(3)). The standards “shall be applied and interpreted as
stated in the administrative manual” ((G)(2)), and where the manual and the code conflict, the code
controls ((N)(5)).
Staff’s reports speak in the Director’s voice. The corridor finding in this case opens: “In accordance with
CCC 40.350.020(F)(9), the Public Works Director acknowledges that a variety of factors can influence the
operating performance of transportation corridors,” and says those factors “allow the Public Works
Director and supporting staff to create an affirmative finding of compliance” (Ex. 54, p. 5). The same
language opens the corridor findings in other reports (Exhibits K, W, X). Ex. 68 says the Director and the
Transportation Division Manager “directed concurrency staff to use intersection performance … in the
evaluation of v/c ratio compliance” (Ex. 68, p. 1). Exhibit 113 says the factors were “determined by the
Public Works Director and the Transportation Division Manager” (p. 2), then adds: “Although (F)(9)
provides this authority for the Public Works Director, it does not dictate how staff evaluates the other
factors” (p. 4).
Nowhere in the materials does the Director appear. No determination, adopted method, manual
update, signature or testimony from any Public Works Director has been produced, in this record, in the
174th Street record, or in response to a public records request for the Director’s authorization (Ex. 106).
The reports that speak for the Director were prepared and approved by staff (Ex. 54). Every description
of the Director’s role comes from Mr. Jardin (Ex. 68; Exhibit J; Ex. 113). The most recent manual is from
2011 and contains no HCM capacity method (Exhibits A, B), and Exhibit 113 does not mention Section
(N) or the County’s manual. A records request for the Director’s authorization returned only an
unrelated delegation (Ex. 106, pp. 1–4, 11). The code makes the Director responsible for the method and
the approval. The practice leaves the Director as a name staff write into their own findings.
7. Compliance factors added that the code does not contain.
On May 21, Ex. 68 listed what staff consider “in whole or in part when determining compliance with or
determining acceptable levels-of-service under CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a)”: “the intersection level-of-
service and queuing, along with existing roadway influences” (Ex. 68, p. 2). On June 4, the same


                                                   Page 4
sentence added “and, where applicable, potential mitigation options such as Transportation System
Management (TSM) or Transportation Demand Management (TDM) strategies” (Exhibit J, p. 1). Exhibit
113 repeats the June 4 version (p. 1).
TSM and TDM appear nowhere in CCC 40.350.020. In fourteen days, by staff letter, the list of things that
may establish compliance grew to include strategies the code does not mention. They are framed as
considerations in determining compliance, not as mitigation an applicant volunteers and is conditioned
on under (E)(5).
8. A new calculation is presented as long-standing practice.
Exhibit 113 says the corridors pass “[b]ased on the evaluation method that has been applied and
practiced since the 2014 time frame” (p. 1). The method it actually relies on, a recalculated segment
capacity with the calculation shown, first appears in Exhibits 111 and 112, dated September 18, 2026
and entered in the record on October 1 with Exhibit 113:
  •      The practice described in earlier filings was clearing segments on intersection level of service.
         The staff report here did that and said “no further analysis is required” (Ex. 54, p. 6).
   •     My June 11 submission noted that the HCM factors were “cited, not applied” (Ex. 64). None of
         the fourteen findings from June 2023 through August 2026 that I reviewed shows an HCM
         capacity calculation or a recalculated ratio (Exhibit M).
   •     On September 10, staff told the Examiner, “So I’m not extremely familiar with all of the factors”
         (Ex. 114, p. 6). Exhibits 111 and 112 are dated eight days later and were not filed until October
         1.
9. The intersection rationale is disavowed and replaced.
The staff report cleared these corridors because of “good intersection LOS” (Ex. 54, p. 6). The
intersections are not performing well: the applicant’s own study shows LOS F at NE 117th Avenue and
NE 119th Street, with approach delays of two to three minutes (Concurrency Submission, Point 5).
Exhibit 113 now disavows the rationale the staff report relied on: “Staff’s evaluation of corridor roadway
segments does not substitute intersection findings for corridor level of service” (p. 2). In its place comes
a new corridor measure, a capacity staff computed.
That capacity is built from intersection inputs. Exhibits 111 and 112 take the demand on one approach
at the downstream intersection, and that approach’s signal timing or stop control, and treat them as the
segment (Ex. 111, pp. 1–2; Ex. 112, pp. 1–2). The 1,900 vehicles an hour assigned to NE 119th is the
HCM’s base saturation flow rate, which the applicant’s licensed engineers describe as “a factor used to
assess operations at signalized intersections in the Highway Capacity Manual methodology” (Ex. 107,
p. 4). The substitution has not stopped. It has moved inside the capacity number.
10. The language of necessity: concurrency recast as a path to approval.
Exhibit 113 presents its analysis as accuracy and best practice. Staff’s purpose is to make sure the factors
“are more accurately represented when evaluating development related impacts” (p. 2). The HCM is “a
nationally accepted comprehensive engineering reference document for capacity analysis” (p. 3). Staff
“strive to ensure use of best engineering practices to ensure that development is in compliance with
CCC 40.350.020” (p. 3), and “using the HCM and other best engineering practices provides the
operational characteristic staff can test against the 0.9 v/c threshold” (p. 4). Staff produce the number
they then test.
It presents an exceedance as a reason to consider mitigation, not denial: “the applicant could volunteer
mitigation … While the applicant has not volunteered mitigation, it is something the county could


                                                   Page 5
consider when the 0.9 v/c has been determined to be exceeded” (p. 2). Denial appears once, as the
alternative to a mitigation demand that requires “nexus”: it “would be very difficult for the county to
find nexus of development impacts to say the development needs to volunteer mitigation or deny the
project” (p. 3). Nexus is the test for charging a developer for impacts. It is not the concurrency test. The
conclusion is that “we believe staff has shown that this development can comply” (p. 4), not that it does.
The code asks whether the roads meet the standard before development is approved (CCC
40.350.020(A); (E)(3)). Exhibit 113 asks how to reach approval.
11. An exception becomes a standing rule.
Exhibit 113 states that the HCM analysis “would not be a part of a routine analysis” (p. 4). In the weeks
before Exhibit 113 was submitted to the record, staff had already written it into pre-application
comments for two new projects near 179th Street (Cedar Vista, PAC-2026-00246, Exhibit Y, Sept. 23,
2026; The Commons at Whipple Creek, PAC-2026-00247, Exhibit Z, Sept. 30, 2026). Before any study
existed, both memos predicted that some corridor segments “may exceed the 0.9 threshold in the
buildout year using the prescriptive method” and told applicants that if so, they “may choose to mitigate
per CCC 40.350.030(B)(6) or the traffic study may include discussion and/or calculations for the volume-
to-capacity ratio using the methodology as outlined in the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM).” Denial is
not listed. Both memos come from Mr. Kathol and direct applicants to the Concurrency Administrative
Manual, which contains no HCM capacity method (Exhibits A, B).
Together these moves replace the code with staff judgment.

III. What Is Left of the Code
Set against the code and the County’s own earlier position, the change looks like this:

Exhibit 113 says the 0.9 still governs: staff’s application “does not override the 0.9 v/c ratio” (p. 4). Over
the summer, staff had already set it aside. The standard was “not binding or a ‘flat prohibition’” (Exhibit
J, p. 3), and the factors were applied “in lieu of the code-prescribed threshold values” (Exhibit L, p. 20).
Exhibit 113 brings the number back only after everything it is applied to has been made to vary. The
volume varies: staff used a different number than the applicant’s engineers, and different studies of the
same corridors have counted different amounts of approved, unbuilt traffic (Concurrency Submission,
Points 5 and 9). The capacity varies: staff computed a different value for each segment, none of them
the Table’s. The method varies: intersection LOS in the staff report, an HCM recalculation in Exhibit 113,
chosen case by case, and (F)(9) “does not dictate how staff evaluates” it. Exhibit 113 does not cite Table
40.350.020-1, which fixes capacity, or Section (N), which requires the Director to adopt and publish one
method. A threshold applied to inputs staff choose each time is not a standard. Nothing remains of the
code.




                                                     Page 7
IV. Where This Is Happening
NE 119th Street, NE 99th Street and SR 503 lie in the SR 503/east county area. Mr. Stumpf’s failing-
corridor memo lists all three among the corridors over 0.90 (Ex. 65, p. 3). In 2007, this area carried an
Urban Holding overlay that restricted development pending infrastructure investment (Exhibit AA).
Between NE 119th and NE 99th, the current Comprehensive Plan shows that overlay gone (Exhibit BB).
The figure below shows the same area, at the same scale, on each map.




                                                  Page 8
This is happening where the consequences cannot be reversed: in the area where the County lifted the
overlay that held development back until the roads were built. The record shows no improvement to
these segments funded or scheduled for completion within six years (Concurrency Submission, Point 1).
Once a development is approved on a recalculated capacity, its traffic is permanent. Once approved and
built, the development and its traffic stay. The County has not funded the capacity.
The County’s own budget shows its road program is short. The Public Works Director’s October 7, 2026
budget presentation to the Council states that the Road Fund available for capital “diminishes each
year,” that even with a levy increase the six-year Transportation Improvement Program “is projected to
dip into Road Fund reserves by the end of the 6-year period,” and that the result is “reduced ability to
meet capital commitments” (Exhibit CC, p. 2). The six-year Transportation Improvement Program is the
County’s plan for what it will build, and it must be balanced to available revenue. The County will have
to find more money or drop projects. The record identifies no project in it that adds capacity to these
segments (Concurrency Submission, Point 1).
Concurrency exists to prevent exactly this: approval first, with no road to carry it.

V. What the Examiner Is Being Asked to Accept
The Examiner asked for a segment-specific professional opinion explaining why these roads function
adequately “despite the volume to capacity problem” (Ex. 114, p. 9). That opinion has to be one the
code allows, and the analysis the code calls for is already in the record (Concurrency Submission, Points
1 and 5). Exhibit 113 does not offer an opinion within the code. It offers an alternative the code does not
provide for. Nor does it explain why a failing segment is acceptable. It says the failure does not exist.
Accepting that answer would mean finding:
  1.    that a segment the code’s own measure puts over 0.9 does not exceed 0.9;
  2.    that staff, not the Council, set the capacity of a road, and may set it differently in each case;
  3.    that the code’s measure applies only when it passes, and a second measure applies when it fails;
  4.    that a calculation dated September 2026 and first entered in this record on October 1 has been
        practiced since 2014;
  5. that a standard the Council adopted as fixed and objective can be replaced by a practice never
        brought to the Council, though staff told the Council in 2016 that standards “are established, uh,
        uh, by approval through the board” and that staff bring proposed changes to it (Exhibit F,
        0:01:57); and
  6. that the Public Works Director made the determinations staff attribute to him, though nothing
        from any Director has been produced in this or any other record, or in response to a public
        records request for it.
The Council set the standard, and the code makes the Director responsible for how it is applied. Under
the practice, neither one decides. Staff do (Concurrency Submission, Points 3, 6 and 7).
The County is already treating the result as settled. It is offering the same route to new applicants near
NE 179th Street before their studies are written. If the Examiner adopts Exhibit 113’s framing, the next
filing will begin from there, and the question will no longer be whether a failing corridor may be
excused, but whether any corridor can be found to fail at all.

Dear Councilors and staff
Attached please find comments from the City of Vancouver following your recent deliberations
on the Clark County Comprehensive Plan in advance of your scheduled October 13 consent
adoption. Thank you.
October 8, 2026

RE: Clark County Comprehensive Plan follow up

Honorable Chair Marshall and County Councilors Yung, Belkot, Fuentes and Little:



This letter is provided in follow up to the County Council deliberations on October 2 and 5
towards the final adoption of the Clark County Comprehensive Plan. We support your
preliminary decisions pertaining to the Vancouver UGA, and offer the below for going forward:

1. We appreciate your decision to have upcoming workplans address the lack of commercial
   or employment zoning in parts of the VUGA, which does not require the development of
   full subarea plans. Formal subarea plans like Highway 99 generate a wide range of issues,
   goals, and action steps, which isn’t necessary to add opportunities for commercial and
   employment uses. Our request is to consider some small-scale rezones- this will require
   review and notification of properties but not a lengthy process like creating a full subarea
   plan. We look forward to resuming discussion on this issue in 2027.

2. We support your decision to modestly reduce minimum density requirements for
   apartment zones in the VUGA, but wish to emphasize that this represents only a small
   portion of the overall residential capacity. In future years it will be important to monitor
   high density development using complete data, and to consult with high density apartment
   developers. However, while higher density residential zoning in the VUGA is needed for the
   County to meet below market housing requirements of HB 1220, it is only a small part of
   accommodating total housing capacity. Appendix N of the County materials shows that
   zones where the 40 unit per acre minimum density were proposed accounted for just 8% of
   the VUGA’s overall buildable land for housing, and just 17% of its total housing unit
   capacity.

3. We commend your decision not to pursue late market factor assumption increases which
   would have had significant negative consequences for this update process and its
   outcomes. Going forward we urge that changes to growth assumptions not be advanced
   without proper analysis. The recently proposed market factor increase would have added
   many months or longer to the already overdue schedule by having to revisit the EIS to
    include not just the new growth assumption, but also new mapping of greatly increased
    UGA expansions of multiple square miles that would be triggered by the assumption
    change. 1

    If adopted, the market factor increase would be very unlikely to survive a legal challenge,
    since GMA caselaw requires local market factor choices to be justified if challenged, with
    data showing why the assumed amount is not likely to develop during the planning period.
    No data was provided in this case to support the proposed new 20% and 40% market
    factors. No data was provided to demonstrate that the existing 10% and 30% factors that
    were recommended almost unanimously by the Buildable Land Project Advisory Committee
    in 2020 is no longer appropriate. As noted by County staff at the October 2 deliberations,
    many of the changes in conditions since 2020 have added flexibility and options for
    development. 2

    Increasing market factor also appears unnecessary from a policy perspective as the GMA
    already contains several safeguards to ensure that long term housing and land supplies are
    established at adequate levels, and will not come close to running out:
     Counties may adopt countywide population forecasts to drive local plans that are
         higher than what the state projects is most likely to occur. Clark County has already
         taken this step in this update, adopting a countywide forecast that is about 20,000
         persons higher than the state has estimated.
     The state housing unit targets that flow from the adopted local population forecast
         come with large built-in housing vacancy assumptions, as noted by County staff.
     The 20-year land supplies that local plans adopt must be re-stocked based on new
         growth forecasts at minimum in 10 years, half-way through the planning period. The
         law further allows full updates sooner than that if needed, which Clark County did in
         2007 by adopting an entirely new plan after only three years.

    These safeguards should be considered in any realistic discussion about land supply
    adequacy in our view.

    The proposed market factor increase is also inappropriate because if more land for housing
    is desired, it should be done transparently by increasing growth forecasts and allocations to
    account for the additional growth that will likely occur. Counties also have more legal
    latitude in choosing and allocating growth forecasts within the OFM range than they do
    with market factor and other development assumptions, and can calibrate the growth

1
  Appendix N shows 6447 acres or 10 square miles of otherwise buildable land is currently removed from the
countywide inventory for market factor. Increasing from 10% vacant and 30% underutilized deductions to 20% and
40% deductions would likely result in an increase to 15 square miles or more of otherwise developable land being
removed for market factor. Deducting 15 square miles from the inventory would turn what Exhibit 4 of the County
materials reports as surplus capacity of 10,498 housing units countywide into a deficit of many tens of thousands
of units, triggering the need for UGA expansions of several square miles.
2
  Thurston County v. Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board, 164 Wn.2d 329, 190 P.3d 38
(2008)

    increase precisely to match the land use. We are not advocating for this action which would
    still require revisiting the EIS, but believe it is preferable to an unsupported increase in
    market factor assumptions which would completely derail the countywide land use
    planning process and substance that has been completed to date.

    Thank you again for your extensive work in getting the process to this point. We look
    forward to continued collaboration as we all move to implementing our new
    Comprehensive Plans.

RE: 2025-2045 Comprehensive Plan Update — Comments Ahead of the October 13 Adoption

Dear Chair and Members of the Council:
Viking Homes LLC is a homebuilder / developer and a member of the Building Industry
Association of Clark County (BIA). We build in Clark County, and the decisions you make in
the Comprehensive Plan Update will shape our ability to build homes that local families can
afford for the next 20 years. We support adopting a Comprehensive Plan. We write ahead of
your October 13 vote to ask that the final plan rest on analysis that can withstand scrutiny and
on costs that Clark County homebuyers can actually carry.
We have seen firsthand how long permitting timelines in Clark County can put
homeownership out of reach. Members of our own family were priced out of building their
homes here, largely because of the extended wait to get their projects approved. Every month
of delay adds carrying costs, interest, and rising material prices, and those costs fall directly on
families and builders.
We'd like to propose a solution: tie a portion of compensation for Clark County building and
planning staff to how efficiently permits move through the system. This would reward staff for
their productivity, offer them meaningful bonus opportunities, and save developers and
homeowners significant time and money.
We respectfully ask the Council to address the following before adopting the plan:
1.. Validate the land capacity assumptions before relying on them for 20 years. The Vacant
Buildable Lands Model applies never-to-convert assumptions of 10 percent for vacant
residential land, 30 percent for underutilized residential land, and 0 percent for commercial,
business park and industrial land. We have not seen evidence that these percentages have been
tested against what has actually developed in Clark County. If they overstate buildable
capacity, every urban growth area and zoning decision built on them is less reliable, and
harder to fix after adoption than before. Please direct staff to complete a documented market-
factor sensitivity and validation analysis before the final capacity determination is relied upon.
2. Consider the combined cost of new fees — and who ultimately pays them. Higher school
impact fees, new fire district impact fees, and higher land use and wetland review fees were
approved separately within weeks of one another.. The Council should see the stacked total
per home, not a series of isolated votes. Builders and developers write the check at the permit
counter, but the homebuyer pays the bill, in the price of the home and in the mortgage they
carry for decades. We also ask the Council to confirm that the new fire district fees rest on a
clear showing that each charge is tied to the cost of growth-related fire service impacts.
3. Size urban growth area expansions to real, near-term demand and available infrastructure.
Battle Ground, Camas, La Center, Ridgefield and Yacolt each have expansion requests in this
plan. Each should be judged on demonstrated housing need and existing or funded
infrastructure, not treated as a one-time opportunity to add land regardless of how much the
market can absorb. Oversized or misplaced expansions can lock up land in the wrong places
for two decades while under-serving the places where housing is actually needed.
4. Make sure permitting and infrastructure capacity keep pace with planned growth. Capacity
on paper means little if permit review timelines, water and sewer capacity, and roads cannot
support the development the plan assumes. Every month a project waits in review adds
carrying costs that ultimately land on the buyer.
5. Keep the County’s middle housing code consistent with the cities’. The County’s Housing
Options Study and Action Plan governs unincorporated urban growth areas, while HB 1110
separately governs the cities. If standards, densities or review processes diverge meaningfully
across the line, builders face different rules project to project and buyers face uneven housing
choices. We ask the Council to confirm the County’s code aligns in substance with what its
cities are required to do.
6. Build in a way to correct course. If the assumptions behind this plan turn out to be wrong,
the County should not have to wait a full planning cycle to find out. Please include a defined
monitoring and mid-cycle review trigger tied to actual permit and absorption data.
7. State the affordability impact before you vote. Every fee increase and every acre of
constrained capacity has a measurable effect on the cost of a home. We ask that the effect be
stated plainly in the record for the decisions that make up this plan, not just discussed in
general terms.
We are not asking the Council to delay or reject the Comprehensive Plan. We are asking that
the record and the methodology be strong enough that the plan stands up to review and to the
next 20 years without reopening these fights. Thank you for your service and for considering
our comments. We would welcome the opportunity to share more about our experience with
you or your staff.
Respectfully,
Zeke Ketola

Viking Homes LLC

buildwithviking@gmail.com
Member, Building Industry Association of Clark County

Thank you

Comment on the Clark County Growth
Management Plan Update
Submitted by: Mike Eyster, Heights at Pleasant Valley

My name is Mike Eyster, and I live in the Heights at Pleasant Valley. The County’s Growth
Management Plan update introduces zoning changes that, if implemented, will significantly
degrade an extensive area surrounding NE 139th Street between 72nd Avenue and east of 50th
Avenue.

County planning materials propose a dramatic escalation in residential density within this area,
far beyond what the neighborhood’s established development pattern can support. These
neighborhoods—including the Heights at Pleasant Valley—were intentionally planned as
cohesive communities with moderate density single family homes, internal circulation,
pedestrian connections, stormwater systems, and CC&Rs that support long term stability and
neighborhood quality. These characteristics are not accidental; they reflect decades of
coordinated planning that produced a functional, compatible, and successful residential area.

This is a distinct residential pocket within the northern Vancouver Urban Growth Area. Although
built over time, the subdivisions share a consistent development pattern: compatible lot sizes,
similar building forms, predictable circulation routes, and a unified neighborhood structure. This
continuity is a major reason the district functions well today and contributes positively to
Vancouver’s overall livability. Introducing high density zoning into this location would
undermine those established patterns and fundamentally conflict with the planning framework
that has guided this area for decades.

The County has not demonstrated that an increase in intensity would be compatible with the
area’s infrastructure or development pattern. Any increase in density should be assessed not only
by the number of units it produces but also by how well it fits the existing development pattern,
street network, and infrastructure systems. Abrupt changes in density can create substantial
conflicts such as increased traffic on streets not designed for higher density use, added pressure
on stormwater systems, and incompatibilities between different residential forms. These issues
warrant careful analysis and clear public communication.

R 36 allows three to four story multifamily buildings, larger footprints, higher lot coverage, and
reduced setbacks. These forms represent a pronounced increase in height, massing, and density
compared to surrounding single family neighborhoods. In areas where higher density uses are
appropriate, they are usually introduced through transitional zoning or design standards that
moderate the interface between different residential types. None of those elements exist here.

Higher density residential uses are typically placed along major transportation corridors, near
commercial centers, or adjacent to areas already planned for more intensive development. This
approach ensures that increases in height, massing, and population occur gradually and
predictably. The neighborhoods south of NE 139th Street were designed around moderate
density residential use. Any significant departure from that pattern should be evaluated carefully
to ensure it does not undermine neighborhood stability or functionality.

If the area surrounding NE 139th Street were redesignated to R 36, it would represent a
substantial increase in intensity within the center of an established R 7.5 district. Without
transitional zoning, buffering, or infrastructure upgrades, such a change would create an
immediate and unmitigated jump in scale. High density residential uses typically require
enhanced transportation capacity, expanded stormwater facilities, and more robust utility
infrastructure. Placing such uses in the middle of a moderate density neighborhood—rather than
along a major corridor—risks creating conflicts related to traffic, parking, building scale, and
overall compatibility.

An abrupt shift to R 36 density would destabilize the surrounding neighborhood, permanently
alter its residential character, and create severe, unresolvable conflicts with every adjacent street
and subdivision across a broad, multi neighborhood area.

Increasing the density to R 36 in this area is inconsistent with the climate planning requirements
established under HB 1181. The legislation requires counties to adopt land use strategies that
reduce greenhouse gas emissions and lower per capita vehicle miles traveled (VMT). This
location cannot support those outcomes. The area is physically isolated, lacks transit service, and
has no walkable access to employment, groceries, medical services, childcare, or other daily
needs. In this context, residents of a large R 36 development would be required to drive for
nearly all trips—work, school, shopping, medical appointments, and basic services. Rather than
reducing VMT, high density development in this location would increase it, because every
additional household adds vehicle trips to an area with no multimodal alternatives. HB 1181’s
climate and VMT reduction goals rely on concentrating growth in walkable, transit served,
infrastructure ready areas. This location does not meet those criteria, and the proposed density
would move the county further from compliance with the intent of the legislation.

NE 72nd Avenue is the primary north–south circulation route for a large portion of the
community, and it already operates at or near functional capacity during peak periods. The
roadway was designed as a neighborhood scale corridor, with narrow travel lanes, limited
shoulders, no center turn lane, and constrained opportunities for widening without significant
right of way acquisition. It currently carries school traffic, local residential circulation, and
regional cut through volumes that exceed what the original design intended.

Based on data collected by the County, NE 72nd Avenue is already problematic and
dysfunctional. Adding significant housing density at NE 139th Street will exacerbate these issues
and extend them both north and south along the corridor.

NE 72nd Avenue already functions as a major arterial without major arterial infrastructure.
Existing high density development between NE 119th Street and NE 134th Street has produced
persistent peak hour congestion, long queues at signalized intersections and stop controlled
approaches, multi cycle delays for left turns, increased cut through traffic into adjacent
neighborhoods, and conflicts between regional through traffic and local residential circulation.
Introducing another large concentration of high density units would further burden an already
constrained corridor, compounding existing congestion and creating additional safety concerns
for pedestrians, cyclists, school traffic, and neighborhood residents. The cumulative effect of
funneling substantially higher traffic volumes onto 72nd Avenue would not only degrade
mobility but also alter the fundamental character and function of the roadway. This classification
does not align with the roadway’s physical design, width, or operational capacity.

A corridor or neighborhood system reaches failure not when one component breaks, but when
multiple stressed components interact. NE 72nd Avenue already exhibits overloaded traffic
volumes, insufficient pedestrian protection, abrupt land use transitions, ongoing high density
construction, and no remaining capacity for additional peak hour demand. Under these
conditions, any additional high density designation at NE 139th Street would push the corridor
beyond functional failure, creating a system wide breakdown in mobility, safety, and
neighborhood circulation.

NE 139th Street between NE 50th Avenue and NE 72nd Avenue is classified as a Local Access
Road—the lowest capacity classification in the County’s transportation hierarchy. It is designed
for short neighborhood trips, low traffic volumes, direct driveway access, and minimal peak hour
loading. Today it operates as a quiet, rural scale neighborhood road with narrow lanes, no center
turn lane, no shoulders, limited pedestrian facilities, and multiple residential driveways. Its
design reflects its intended purpose: to serve existing single family homes at moderate density.

High density development south of NE 139th Street would overwhelm this corridor. Multifamily
development generates substantially higher daily and peak hour traffic volumes, including
concentrated morning and evening surges. A Local Access Road is not engineered to absorb
these volumes. The result would be congestion, queueing, turning conflicts, driveway blockages,
and increased cut through traffic into adjacent neighborhoods. The County’s roadway
classification system makes clear that Local Access Roads are not appropriate locations for high
density residential zoning, rendering the proposed redesignation incompatible by definition.
Local Access Roads are intentionally designed for the lowest intensity residential uses; applying
high density zoning to such a corridor contradicts the fundamental purpose of the roadway
classification system.

The neighborhoods surrounding NE 139th Street represent a stable, intentionally planned
residential district designed for moderate density single family living. The built environment,
infrastructure systems, and governance structures were all created to support this level of
intensity, and they function effectively within that framework. Introducing high density zoning
into the center of this district would disrupt that stability, create incompatible land use
transitions, and place additional strain on a transportation corridor already operating beyond its
intended capacity. Growth is necessary and welcome, but it must be placed where infrastructure,
context, and planning principles support it. The incompatibility between the proposed zoning and
the area’s infrastructure, street hierarchy, and established development pattern constitutes a fatal
flaw that cannot be mitigated through conditions or design standards. For these reasons, the
proposed redesignation should be withdrawn until a complete, parcel level analysis demonstrates
that the area can support such intensity — a threshold it clearly does not meet today.

I am writing to express concern about the zoning changes being considered as
part of the Clark County Growth Management Plan update. The neighborhoods
surrounding NE 139th Street represent a stable, intentionally planned
residential district. Introducing high density zoning into the center of this area
would disrupt that stability, create incompatible land use transitions, and
place additional strain on transportation corridors that are already over
capacity.

Proposed changes are inconsistent with the climate planning requirements of
HB 1181. Instead of reducing vehicle miles traveled (VMT), VMT would increase
significantly if the current plan is implemented

Transportation capacity is a major concern. NE 72nd Avenue is the primary
north–south circulation route for a large portion of the community, and it
already operates at or near functional capacity during peak periods. The road
was built as a neighborhood scale corridor with narrow lanes, limited
shoulders, and no center turn lane. It currently carries school traffic, local
residential trips, and regional cut through traffic that exceed what the roadway
was designed to handle. Adding highdensity zoning at NE 139th Street would
increase traffic volumes and worsen existing congestion and safety issues.

NE 139th Street is classified as a Local Access Road, the lowest capacity
designation in the County’s transportation system. It is intended for short
neighborhood trips and low traffic volumes. High density residential
development generates substantially higher daily and peak hour traffic, which
this type of road is not designed to absorb. Applying high density zoning to a
Local Access Road contradicts the purpose of the County’s own roadway
classification system.

Any significant increase in residential intensity will overwhelm the systems
that support it, violate the intent of HB 1181, and degrade the surrounding
neighborhood forever.

The proposed redesignation should not move forward until the County
demonstrates that the area can support an increase in residential intensity.

                 Comment on the 2025 Comprehensive Plan Update
                   Vancouver Urban Growth Area Zoning Map
To: Clark County Council
From: Heidi Pozzo
Date: October 11, 2026

Summary
The Vancouver Urban Growth Area (VUGA) zoning map accounts for nearly nine of every ten
parcel changes in this update, yet it received very little discussion. The result is significant new
density at the outer edges of the growth area, away from jobs and on roads not built for it.
  • There was extensive discussion of the Comprehensive Plan in general, in-depth discussion
    of agricultural land, and discussion of the methodology for the plan. There was very little
    discussion of the VUGA mapping.
  • The VUGA accounts for 8,221 of the 9,281 parcel changes (89%) listed in the County's
    Parcel Number Detail for the adopting ordinance.
  • Density was increased in three ways: consolidation of the medium- and high-density zones
    (by far the largest impact), site-specific requests, and a third group of changes for which the
    Parcel Number Detail shows how the density increases were applied, but nothing identifies
    what originated them.
  • County staff stated on the record that the urban medium zones are the only land base
    available to meet the income targets, and that a detailed analysis of the available parcels
    had not been done. Significant density was placed at the outside edges of the growth area,
    where there is little commercial land or employment.
  • Land that has not yet been through the development process is being upzoned in areas
    where roads already exceed the County's capacity standard. In the 179th Street area, the
    developer-commissioned traffic studies show the roads failing even with the planned
    improvements credited as complete, and those improvements are not funded (Table 6;
    March 1, 2026 comment, Sections 4 and 7). Adding density in these areas is not
    appropriate.
  • The 179th Street area is one example. Staff stated on October 5, 2026 that the zone changes
    there will apply to the remaining parcels that have not developed, including vacant land in
    the OR-36 area. The Council Chair said bringing in the area without the planning and
    funding for infrastructure “was not our best effort,” and Councilor Yung said there was no
    “real way to unwind that.” The upzoning was left in place.
  • The same conditions exist elsewhere but were not discussed in the Council's October 2 and
    5 deliberations. Along 119th Street east of SR-503, R-36 and R-50 parcels sit at the edge of
    the growth area, and both 119th Street and SR-503 are above the County's capacity
    standard (Table 6).
  • The roads serving these edge areas lack capacity for this level of development, and the
    RTC regional transportation analysis would not have picked up these gaps.
   • As a result, the plan does not balance housing, jobs and transportation, and vehicle miles
     traveled (VMT) will increase. The GMA requires that balance and internal consistency
     when the plan is adopted. Deferring commercial land and road capacity to later work plans
     does not meet that requirement.

4. How the VUGA Map Was Approved
   • The July 30, 2026 Planning Commission work session on the housing code covered the
     code changes only. The zoning map changes and parcel selections were not presented.
   • The County posted updated maps showing the proposed zoning and urban growth area
     changes. The maps were not discussed to show where zoning changed within the VUGA or
     where density increased, and no parcel table was available until October 9, 2026.
   • At the January 29, 2026 Planning Commission hearing, Vancouver UGA items 2.K through
     2.W were bundled into a single motion and approved 7–0 with no discussion (Minutes, pp.
     34–36).
   • At the September 3, 2026 Planning Commission hearing, maps were available only “as-
     needed” (Minutes, p. 6).
   • At that hearing, the first part of the Decision Table received extensive discussion: the urban
     growth area expansions and agricultural land (Items 1–10, Minutes pp. 6–29) and the zone
     consolidation (Item 11, pp. 30–36), each with its own vote. The motion to approve Item 11
     as presented failed 3–4.
   • The remaining Vancouver UGA map items were then grouped. Items 12 through 17 were
     approved in a single 7–0 vote with no discussion, and the descriptions of Items 12, 13 and
     14 were not read aloud (pp. 40–41). Items 18, 19 and 21 through 24 were approved in a
     second grouped vote (p. 43). The only Vancouver UGA site-specific request discussed was
     Item 20, after a commissioner asked to see it on the map (pp. 43–45).
  • At the Council hearing on October 2, 2026, the urban growth area expansions and
    agricultural land (Items 1–9) took most of the day. The Chair noted the time as 2:30 after
    Item 9. Items 10 through 24 were then taken up before the afternoon break at about 3:10.
  • When Item 12 was moved at the Council, Councilor Yung asked what it was “actually
    changing to” and noted that it “doesn't say what it's changing to.” The Chair responded
    “Close enough,” and Item 12 passed 5–0 with no parcels or map identified. Before Item 23,
    the Chair asked to refer to the remaining items by number only.
  • On October 5, 2026, the Council completed the code items, approving Items 67, 69–73,
    75–86 and 88–91 in grouped votes.

6. Result
Multifamily placed at the edges
 • Significant density is placed at the outside edges of the growth area, including the 179th
     Street area, formerly in urban holding, and the SR-503/119th Street area (Clark County
     2025 Comprehensive Plan zoning map, clark.wa.gov; County Council hearing, October 5,
     2026).
  • On the 2025 zoning map, R-36 and R-50 parcels sit directly across the urban growth
    boundary from rural and agricultural zoning, including along 119th Street east of SR-503
    (Clark County 2025 Comprehensive Plan zoning map, clark.wa.gov).
  • The Land Use Element requires that areas planned for Urban Medium density “shall be
    located near commercial uses and transportation facilities” and that Urban High density
    areas “shall be located in transit corridors and near commercial and employment
    centers…while providing easy access to employment.” Future amendments to the plan map
    must be consistent with these descriptions (Chapter 1, Council work session draft, July 22,
    2026, p. 11, lines 21–23 and 32–34; p. 8, lines 38–41).
  • Policy 1.1.15 calls for higher densities along transit corridors and lower densities in
    “neighborhoods on the fringes of the urban area.” Policy 1.3.1 calls for “less intensity in
    areas where urban development is of lower density or has not yet occurred, or in areas
    where urban services do not yet exist.” Policy 1.4.9 states that higher intensity uses should
    be located on or near streets served by transit (Chapter 1, pp. 25, 30, 31).
  • The Land Use Element also states that the land use map “must not specify a land use
    development pattern which cannot be adequately served by transportation and other
    services” (Chapter 1, p. 2, lines 13–15).
  • These areas have little commercial land nearby. The City of Vancouver asked for a
    commercial component along 119th Street for Item 18, Councilor Yung stated that
    properties had been upzoned without access to amenities, and mixed-use land along SR-
    503 is being converted to multifamily because it drew no commercial interest (Table 5:
    County Council hearing, October 2, 2026, Item 18; Planning Commission work session,
    July 30, 2026, 35:36).
Roads lack capacity
  • The draft code lists the factors to be considered in applying the R-24, R-36 and R-50
    districts to a site, including proximity to major streets and the available capacity of these
    streets, vehicular and pedestrian traffic circulation, and proximity to commercial services
    (CCC 40.220.020(A)(1)(b), July 15, 2026 Draft, p. 12).

     if the standard is applied as written (Exhibit 100, pp. 2–3, 10). It was submitted to the
     Comprehensive Plan record on May 20, 2026, with a transmittal identifying Mr. Stumpf as
     the traffic engineer for the 174th Street Subdivision.
  • SR-503 is a state highway (Exhibit 100, Table 1, p. 3). Access to it is controlled by the
    State, and the County does not control whether lanes are added to it (County Council
    hearing, October 2, 2026, Item 20; Planning Commission hearing, September 3, 2026,
    Minutes, p. 44).
  • The widening of 179th Street between 29th and 50th Avenue is not on the Reasonably
    Funded Project List and is scheduled for 2031–2033. The I-5/179th Street interchange
    reconstruction is a WSDOT project with an earliest completion of 2031 (March 1, 2026
    comment, attached summary, Section 1).
  • Under CCC 40.350.020(G)(1)(a), roads not built to county standard carry lower capacity,
    600 to 800 vehicles per hour per lane, than a road built to standard.
RTC analysis would not have picked up the gaps
  • The regional model assumed construction of the projects on the 2024 Regional
    Transportation Plan 6-year and 20-year project lists (Final EIS, Vol. 1, Section 3.9.2(A)).
    The modeled network is the existing network plus RTP improvements (Chapter 5, Planning
    Commission draft produced August 4, 2026, p. 50, lines 12–14).
  • Intersections with Transportation Improvement Program projects were excluded from the
    deficiency screen. Road segments with TIP or RTP projects were coded as built in the 2045
    model network, so they cannot show a deficiency (Final EIS, Vol. 1, Section 3.9.2(B), pp.
    132–134).
  • RTC staff stated that regional travel demand models are not operational traffic models:
    demand can exceed capacity, and the excess demand does not queue and spill onto
    downstream links (County responses to DEIS questions, Q15–Q16).
  • The DEIS transportation consultant stated that a comparison of the RTC regional model to
    individual subarea or corridor studies was not part of the DEIS (County responses to DEIS
    questions, Q12 and Q14). The developer traffic studies in Table 6 show the failures the
    regional model does not.
  • RTC staff stated that the 2045 Regional Transportation Plan assumes no fixed-route transit
    service on 179th Street; growth in the corridor has automobile access only (County
    responses to DEIS questions, Q25).
Housing, jobs and transportation are not balanced
  • The GMA requires the plan to be internally consistent when adopted (RCW 36.70A.070),
    and the plan's own policy requires urban growth areas to provide a balance of industrial,
    commercial and residential lands (Chapter 1, Policy 1.2.2, p. 29). Since November 2024,
    the City of Vancouver has repeatedly asked the County to add commercial or employment
    land near upzoned areas, stating that VMT reduction is “likely impossible” otherwise. It
    asked for a commercial component on large upzone proposals and for supportive
    commercial or employment zoning in a number of upzoned areas (City of Vancouver
     letters, November 6 and 26, 2024, Index of Record; DEIS comment, November 10, 2025,
     Final EIS comment index 59; letter of September 29, 2026). The Council adopted the
     upzoning and deferred the commercial land to the 2027 work plan. Deferring to a later
     work plan does not meet that requirement.
  • Placing large amounts of housing at the edges of the growth area, far from jobs and
    services and with no fixed-route transit planned, lengthens trips and increases VMT. HB
    1181 requires the greenhouse gas emissions reduction subelement of the climate element to
    identify actions that will result in reductions in per capita vehicle miles traveled (RCW
    36.70A.070(9)(d)(i)(B)). Clark County is one of the 11 counties required to adopt that
    subelement (RCW 36.70A.095).
  • The housing element must consider housing locations in relation to employment location
    (RCW 36.70A.070(2)(d)(iii)).
  • The plan elements are not balanced between housing, jobs and transportation. The Growth
    Management Act requires the plan to be internally consistent and the transportation
    element to be consistent with the land use element (RCW 36.70A.070 and RCW
    36.70A.070(6)).
Please enter this comment into the Index of Record for the 2025 Comprehensive Plan Update.

I am writing to express concern about the zoning changes being considered as part of the Clark
County Growth Management Plan update. The neighborhoods surrounding NE 139th Street
represent a stable, intentionally planned residential district. Introducing high density zoning
into the center of this area would disrupt that stability, create incompatible land use transitions,
and place additional strain on transportation corridors that are already over capacity.

Proposed changes are inconsistent with the climate planning requirements of HB 1181. Instead
of reducing vehicle miles traveled (VMT), VMT would increase significantly if the current
plan is implemented.

Transportation capacity is a major concern. NE 72nd Avenue is the primary north–south
circulation route for a large portion of the community, and it already operates at or near
functional capacity during peak periods. The road was built as a neighborhood scale corridor
with narrow lanes, limited shoulders, and no center turn lane. It currently carries school traffic,
local residential trips, and regional cut through traffic that exceed what the roadway was
designed to handle. Adding high density zoning at NE 139th Street would increase traffic
volumes and worsen existing congestion and safety issues.

NE 139th Street is classified as a Local Access Road, the lowest capacity designation in the
County’s transportation system. It is intended for short neighborhood trips and low traffic
volumes. High density residential development generates substantially higher daily and peak
hour traffic, which this type of road is not designed to absorb. Applying high density zoning to
a Local Access Road contradicts the purpose of the County’s own roadway classification
system.

Any significant increase in residential intensity will overwhelm the systems that support it,
violate the intent of HB 1181, and degrade the surrounding neighborhood forever.

The proposed redesignation should not move forward until the County demonstrates that the
area can support an increase in residential intensity.

Regards

Cynthia Lynch

VVancouver, WA 98686

                                                               Appendix D1 – Growth Targets and the Urban Growth Area
                                                                                     Attachment G to Ordinance 19881


I.       Abstract
This appendix provides an analysis of the amount of growth King County and cities in King County are
planning for within the Urban Growth Area (UGA) for the 20-year planning period of the 2024
Comprehensive Plan, and the capacity available to accommodate it. It also provides a similar analysis for
urban unincorporated King County. The purpose of these analyses is to ensure that the UGA is
appropriately sized to accommodate the housing and employment projected during the planning period of
the Comprehensive Plan.

Appendix D was originally prepared for the 1994 Comprehensive Plan in support of the creation of King
County’s UGA Boundary and has been supplemented with new appendices in periodic and major updates
since 2004, including this 2024 Appendix. Those supplements incorporate the 1994 Appendix D by
reference but do not address issues already covered by the original, such as delineation of the Urban
Growth Area. Therefore, they supplement but do not replace the 1994 Appendix D.

The key inputs to the analysis in this appendix are housing and employment growth projections adopted as
growth targets in Table DP-1 of the 2021 King County Countywide Planning Policies and estimates of
developable capacity contained in the 2021 King County Urban Growth Capacity Report. 1 The growth
targets adopted in the Countywide Planning Policies are consistent with the Growth Management
Population Projections developed by the Washington State Office of Financial Management (OFM), and the
Puget Sound Regional Council’s VISION 2050 Regional Growth Strategy. 2 The Urban Growth Capacity
Report 3 contains the required review of the UGA and urban patterns of development compared to
planning objectives and goals.The 2021 King County Urban Growth Capacity Report was accepted by the
Washington State Department of Commerce in June 2021.

King County’s UGA is sized to adequately accommodate projected growth while also accounting for
unpredictable circumstances that could alter the calculated supply of urban growth capacity or the number
of housing units needed to accommodate projected population growth. The location of the UGA includes
areas of the county that already have urban services or have solid commitments for future urban services,
and as a result, would be inconsistent with the criteria for rural or Natural Resource Lands. The most recent
developable capacity information, analyzed in the 2021 King County Urban Growth Capacity Report affirms
the adequacy of the existing UGA to accommodate all the county’s projected growth through 2044. This is
true both for the entire UGA and for the unincorporated portions of the UGA.



II.      Background
A foundational element of growth management planning in Washington state is the designation of urban,
rural, and natural resource lands. Urban land is composed primarily of incorporated cities and towns, and
secondarily of portions of unincorporated King County. Certain mapped urban lands may also be subject to
the sovereign governmental authority of Indian tribes. Rural and Natural Resource Lands are portions of
unincorporated King County, certain sub-portions of which are owned by, or held in trust for, Indian tribes.
The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires the delineation of urban lands by establishment of the urban
growth area (UGA), and of rural and natural resource lands by designation pursuant to comprehensive land
use and zoning. While the GMA requires coordination of local plans, and population and employment
projections are tacitly inclusive of tribal growth, Indian tribes have historically not been included in
discussions about allocating urban growth within King County. King County recognizes that urban, rural,

  2021 King County Countywide Planning Policies [LINK]; 2021 King County Urban Growth Capacity Report, ratified 2022 [LINK]
2
  Washington State Office of Financial Management, Growth Management Act County Projections, 2022 [LINK]; Puget Sound

and natural resource lands are inclusive of certain lands held and governed by Indian tribes, and King
County will coordinate with Indian tribes as a part of County and countywide planning processes.

The 1992 Countywide Planning Policies established a framework UGA for King County. The County initially
designated the UGA in its 1994 Comprehensive Plan based on this framework. Each city or town within King
County is responsible for determining, through its comprehensive plan, land use within its borders,
including accommodating the broad range of residential and nonresidential uses associated with urban
growth. King County is responsible for establishing land use in the unincorporated portion of the UGA
through its comprehensive plan.

Key factors used in setting the UGA size include population and employment projections, growth targets,
and land capacity. Population and employment projections are predictions about likely future growth based
on past trends. Growth targets are a jurisdiction's policy statement on the quantity of net new housing units
and jobs it plans to accommodate over the 20-year planning period based on projections and the
jurisdiction’s rolein the regional growth strategy. Land capacity is derived from an estimate of vacant land
plus the redevelopment potential of land already partially developed or underutilized. Discount factors are
applied to the estimate of land capacity to account for probable constraints and likelihood of developing
the land over the 20-year planning period.

Population and employment projections are useful as an indicator of the potential future demand for land
capacity. Growth targets follow the development of specific goals and objectives for future growth, and
under the GMA, they must be supported by commitments of funds, incentives, and regulations. Discounted
capacity is a market-constrained estimate of how much growth may be accommodated in a geographic
area.

Under the GMA, each county is required to plan to accommodate 20 years of population growth in its
comprehensive plan. Counties are to establish a UGA "within which urban growth shall be encouraged and
outside of which growth can occur only if it is not urban in nature." 4 Further, based on OFM population
projections, the GMA requires the UGA to “include areas and densities sufficient to permit the urban growth
that is projected to occur in the county for the succeeding twenty-year period.” 5 As part of the county’s
planning, it must accommodate housing and employment growth targets, including institutional and other
nonresidential uses. All cities are places for urban growth and, by law, must be included within the UGA. 6 In
addition, unincorporated areas may be included within the UGA "only if such territory already is
characterized by urban growth or is adjacent to territory already characterized by urban growth." 7 The UGA
must also include greenbelt and open space areas. Several GMA goals, such as those dealing with
affordable housing, economic development, open space, recreation, and the environment, also have an
important bearing on these UGA requirements. These goals need to be balanced with those which
encourage efficient urban growth and discourage urban sprawl.

The concurrency goal for public facilities and services in the GMA directs jurisdictions to ensure that "those
public facilities and services necessary to support development shall be adequate to serve the development
at the time the development is available for occupancy without decreasing current service levels below
locally established minimum standards." 8 King County also coordinates with school districts to ensure that
schools are able to plan for projected growth. Ensuring adequate land capacity for industrial and
commercial development and providing enough land capacity to allow for choices in where people live can
help advance economic development and maintain housing affordability. If the UGA is adequately sized,
then pressures to develop on environmentally constrained land and areas setaside for open space are
reduced.

III. Size of the Urban Growth Area
A.          Growth to be Accommodated
As shown in Figure 1: Growth Targets Development Process below, establishing the amount of
population, housing, employment growth to be accommodated countywide and in individual King County
jurisdictions begins with countywide and regional forecasts. Growth is allocated to King County and to
groups of jurisdictions called “Regional Geographies” via VISION 2050’s Regional Growth Strategy, and
population growth is then converted to housing growth. Finally, jurisdictions grouped by Regional
Geography collaboratively determine jurisdictional-level housing and employment growth targets based on
local factors and input.


Figure 1: Growth Targets Development Process




       PAA means Potential Annexation Area



1.          Projected Countywide Growth
Forecasted population growth is generally sourced from the most recent OFM growth management
population projections, which are prepared at a countywide level. The OFM projections from 2017 were the
most current forecast available during the target setting process in 2020 and 2021. The OFM projections
contain “high,” “medium,” and “low” series of projected growth. King County has planned for the medium-
series population growth projections in past Comprehensive Plan updates. In December 2022, OFM
published a new population projection based on updated Census data and forecast assumptions. The 2022
medium series is approximately 1,000 persons greater from the 2017 medium series in the year 2044 (the
last year in the planning period). Because of the limited differences between the 2017 and 2022 projections,
the current countywide growth allocations adopted in the Countywide Planning Policies and the
Comprehensive Plan are consistent with the 2022 projections.

In 2017, in preparation of VISION 2050, the Puget Sound Regional Council (PSRC) produced a regional
forecast for its jurisdiction, which includes King, Kitsap, Pierce, and Snohomish Counties, forecasting
population and employment through 2050. This forecast was used as the source for projected employment
growth in past Comprehensive Plan updates. The PSRC forecasted population is comparable to the 2017
OFM population projection medium series for the four-county PSRC region. Because of the similar
population projection, the use of the PSRC employment forecast for determining employment growth
targets, and the primacy of VISION 2050’s Regional Growth Strategy in allocating growth within the region,
King County utilized the PSRC forecast as the source for countywide growth allocations in developing 2019-
2044 growth targets.

As the PSRC forecast is at a regional scale, countywide shares of population and employment growth are
applied to the regional totals to project growth for King County alone. These shares derive from VISION
2050’s Regional Growth Strategy. 9 The resulting population and job growth form King County’s projected
countywide growth allocations for the 2019-2044 period. Figure 2 below shows how countywide growth
allocations were determined.

VISION 2050’s Regional Growth Strategy apportions 50 percent of the region’s population growth and 59
percent of the region’s employment growth to King County. For comparison, in 2020, King County housed
53 percent of the region’s population and 67 percent of the region’s jobs. 10 The Regional Growth Strategy
shares reflect King County’s role within the region and includes policy choices aimed at improving the
regional balance of jobs and housing among the four PSRC counties. The Regional Growth Strategy
disperses employment growth traditionally concentrated in King County but retains a similar share of
population growth.

Finally, before sub-county allocations are made, the countywide employment growth number is adjusted to
remove construction and resource sector employment. While the contributions from these sectors are
essential to King County’s economy, construction and resource jobs are less likely to have a fixed worksite,
e.g., an office or storefront, and resource sector jobs are generally less urban. These jobs are removed from
the countywide allocation.

2.                 Allocation of Population, Housing, and Job Growth within King County
With the countywide population and employment growth allocations established, the next step is to allocate
population, housing, and jobs to jurisdictions within King County. Growth is allocated to VISION 2050
Regional Geographies before being allocated to individual jurisdictions. Regional Geographies are groups
of cities and urban unincorporated areas that have similar characteristics, such as designated regional
growth centers or high-capacity transit infrastructure. 11

The policy goals of VISION 2050 and the 2021 Countywide Planning Policies define how growth is allocated
to Regional Geographies. Metropolitan and Core Cities have regional growth centers and existing or
planned high-capacity transit investments, and collectively are planned to accommodate the greatest share
of projected growth. High Capacity Transit Communities are cities and urban unincorporated areas with
planned high-capacity transit investments that will allow these jurisdictions to accommodate a larger share
of future growth. 12 Cities and Towns and the Urban Unincorporated areas accommodate the least amount of

3.       Allocation of Projected Growth to Cities and Urban Unincorporated King
         County
The final phase of the growth target setting process allocated growth to cities and potential annexation
areas in urban unincorporated King County. This was a two-step process. First, Regional Geography
allocations were apportioned into an initial range of growth target scenarios for individual cities and PAAs.
Each scenario within the range is based on a proportional allocation of Regional Geography growth to cities
and potential annexation areas based on relevant data, including existing capacity from the Urban Growth




                                                           D1-7
                                                                                     2024 King County Comprehensive Plan
                                                                    Appendix D1 – Growth Targets and the Urban Growth Area
                                                                                          Attachment G to Ordinance 19881

Capacity Report, existing development and recent growth, the number of regional growth centers, and
number of transit station areas.

The initial growth target ranges provided the foundation for the second step of this stage of the process,
where planning staff representing the 39 cities and unincorporated King County were convened by their
VISION 2050 Regional Geography to negotiate the set of draft growth targets. Each Regional Geography
group met approximately five times. Groups discussed the preliminary target ranges created in the previous
step, weighing the merits and relevancy of capacity, existing development, transit and transportation
connections, growth rates, and other supplied data to allocate growth targets within their Regional
Geography. Groups worked iteratively, collectively identifying a baseline set of housing and employment
targets from the preliminary target ranges as a starting place for negotiation, and then individually working
with other jurisdictional staff and elected officials to develop a jurisdictional position on the baseline. King
County staff then assembled the individual positions from jurisdictions and convened the Regional
Geography groups again to collectively review and attempt to close any gap between the individual growth
target positions and the Regional Geography growth allocation.

The ultimate result of this process are the growth targets adopted by the King County Council and ratified
by the cities in the 2021 King County Countywide Planning Policies. 13 Figure 5 displays the adopted housing
and employment growth targets for 2019-2044.

4.       2019-2044 Urban Unincorporated Growth Targets
As shown in Figure 5, growth targets for urban unincorporated King County are divided across two Regional
Geographies. Growth targets for the Federal Way PAA, North Highline, and Renton PAA are in the High
Capacity Transit Communities Regional Geography, reflecting the planned transit investments in these
areas. 14 Targets for other PAAs and unaffiliated urban areas are included in the Urban Unincorporated
Regional Geography. Per the Countywide Planning Policies, growth targets were allocated to PAAs in the
Urban Unincorporated Regional Geography proportionately based on their relative capacity. 15 Growth
targets for the PAAs in the High Capacity Transit Communities geography were also allocated relative to
their existing capacity to be consistent with the intent of the Countywide Planning Policies, but not directly
proportional to the capacity of urban unincorporated King County given the other jurisdictions in the group.


B.       Land Capacity in the UGA
1.       Countywide
The GMA requires King County and the cities in King County to include land area and densities sufficient to
accommodate projected growth over the 20-year planning period within the UGA. 16 Through the review
and evaluation program, King County ensures that sufficient urban capacity for growth persists during the
planning period and beyond, ensuring a stable UGA boundary. In 2021, King County completed the Urban
Growth Capacity Report, its fourth edition of the required evaluation. 17 King County’s previous reports have
consistently reported sufficient capacity within the UGA for projected growth.

The Urban Growth Capacity Report assesses patterns of development within the UGA and uses assumptions
to estimate a more “market-based” capacity for growth, to test whether capacity is realistically available for
future development. 18 Available land supply is identified by its likeliness to re-develop. Densities used to
calculate capacity are informed by recent development in a zone, rather than the base or maximum
densities expressed in zoning. A “market factor” is applied to the calculated capacity to discount capacity
unlikely to develop during the planning period. Therefore, capacity calculated under the Urban Growth
Capacity Report is generally a more conservative estimate than the total amount allowed by zoning.

The Urban Growth Capacity Report found that King County had capacity for over 400,000 housing units and
600,000 jobs within the UGA. 19 This was ample capacity to accommodate the remaining projected growth
from the previous, 2006-2035 growth targets, and sufficient to accommodate the projected growth under
the 2019-2044 growth targets, as reported in Figure 5.

Amendments to the GMA in 2017 ushered in new requirements for the review and evaluation program. 20
The amendments formalized how assumptions about infrastructure gaps and market factors should be
considered and expanded the purview for when “reasonable measures” would be required to correct for
measured inconsistencies to include the achievement of growth targets and urban densities. The Urban
Growth Capacity Report reported on these additional indicators, as a part of its assessment of the patterns
of development with the UGA.

The Urban Growth Capacity Report analyzed progress made by cities and urban unincorporated King
County towards achieving 2006-2035 growth targets. Because past reports had not focused on this specific
outcome before, the 2021 report examined growth since 2006 and through 2018. Over this period, urban
King County grew at a rate to achieve its adopted growth targets. Approximately 41 percent of the previous
