Countywide, development trends analyzed under the Urban Growth Capacity Report showed that urban
densities were being achieved within the UGA. While there is not a stated definition of “urban” growth
stated as a density goal, 70 percent of residential development during the period analyzed by the report
was developed at densities of at least 48 dwelling units per acre, and about 17 percent of development
occurred at densities less than 10 dwelling units per acre. 98 percent of residential development was over
four dwelling units per acre.

While the Urban Growth Capacity Report found that sufficient capacity was available in the UGA for
projected growth, that urban densities were being achieved, and that urban King County was on track to
achieve its 2006-2035 growth targets, a small number of cities lacked sufficient capacity for projected
growth or were not growing at a rate to achieve their targets. The Urban Growth Capacity Report noted the
cities where inconsistencies were identified and recommended that the cities evaluate whether reasonable
measures were required to be taken in the 2024 periodic update to comprehensive plans to correct for the
inconsistency.

Figure 6 lists these cities and the observed inconsistencies. Some inconsistencies may have been corrected
by adopting revised growth targets for the 2019-2044 planning period. The observed inconsistency for the
City of Sammamish related to an infrastructure deficiency that has since been resolved. Following the
adoption of comprehensive plans in 2024, each jurisdiction will be required to monitor progress toward
resolving the inconsistency, with regular reporting to the Growth Management Planning Council.

2.          Unincorporated King County
The Urban Growth Capacity report found sufficient capacity for the remaining portion of the previous
housing growth targets, with a shortfall of capacity for the remaining employment target. The evaluation
revealed capacity for 7,383 housing units and 2,207 jobs, with 7,339 housing units and 4,343 jobs remaining
of the previous period’s 2006-2035 growth targets. The 2006-2035 urban unincorporated employment
targets included a target of over 4,000 jobs for the Bear Creek Urban Planned Development, a fully
contained community surrounded by the rural area. The target was a reflection of estimates of commercial
space planned for the community. As the development built out in Bear Creek in the last decade, the
community added 1,100 jobs between 2006 and 2020, approximately a quarter of the anticipated growth
there. 21 Because of the nature of the development in a fully contained community constrained by developer
agreements and subdivision controls, additional growth is not expected to reach the originally targeted
level. The 2019-2044 growth targets reflect reduced expectations for employment growth in the urban

apparent capacity shortfall.

For the 2019-2044 planning period, King County is planning for a total of 5,412 housing units and 3,340
jobs in the urban unincorporated area. The land capacity analysis performed to support the development of
the 2024 update to the Comprehensive Plan found capacity for 29,600 housing units and 62,900 jobs under
current zoning at base densities.

Zoned capacity is higher than the capacity calculated in the Urban Growth Capacity Report, particularly for
employment. This reflects the differences seen in recent development, which strongly influenced the
capacity calculated in the Urban Growth Capacity Report, and what is allowed under the zoning code. The
significant difference in non-residential capacity also owes to the imprecision in estimating a job-based
capacity, as the quantity of employees varies across businesses and workplace types and is not directly
controlled by the zoning code or land use designations.

in the Black Diamond PAA, and other PAAs with higher proportions.

Surplus residential capacity exists within other portions of urban unincorporated King County, particularly in
areas that have access to transit and are more centrally located within the UGA. King County will work with
the Growth Management Planning Council to reallocate growth targets within urban unincorporated King
County to address the capacity shortfall in a manner consistent with planning goals and the VISION 2050
Regional Growth Strategy.


IV. Conclusion
The UGA is sized appropriately to accommodate the projected growth in housing and employment over the
2019-2044 planning period. As demonstrated in the 2021 King County Urban Growth Capacity Report,
patterns of development within the UGA have been urban in nature and growth has been occurring at a rate
to achieve growth targets. Urban unincorporated King County has sufficient capacity under the current
zoning to accommodate its growth targets for the 2019-2044 period.

KITSAP COUNTY LAND CAPACITY ANALYSIS

Kitsap County is a Growth Management Act (GMA) jurisdiction and must plan for the accommodation of
growth within its boundaries, with most growth focused into urban growth areas (UGAs) where urban services
are available or can be made available. Per RCW 36.70A.110 and WAC 365-196-310, a Land Capacity
Analysis (LCA) is a necessary component in this planning as it quantifies the housing units, population, and
employment growth that can be accommodated within urban areas under existing development regulations.

The Residential LCA identifies vacant, partially underutilized and underutilized parcels in residential zones to
calculate available capacity for development of housing units and associated population.

                                          Step 1.5 of the LCA methodology identifies Under-Utilized
                                          Properties. Under-utilized properties contain some amount of
                                          existing development, but there is a strong possibility that the
                                          existing use will be converted to a more intensive use during the
                                          planning period. For example, a single-family home on a property
                                          with multifamily or commercial zoning could be considered under-
                                          utilized.

                                            Step 4 of the LCA methodology is for identifying future roads/right of
                                            way needs. This deduction is intended to address future
                                            infrastructure needs by new development and market conditions.
Roads, right of way, and traffic mitigation are necessary for new development, particularly undeveloped
properties. Road and right-of-way deductions necessary for a given development project can depend on a
variety of factors, including level of service for roadway segments and intersections, site characteristics,
environmental features, and permitting requirements. Following a The standard deduction used here is
based on review of permit trends and code requirements for vacant land in unincorporated Kitsap County, a
standard dediction of 20% was calculated and was conservatively used for all parcels (vacant, partially
underutilized and underutilized. However, as underutilized properties already contain existing development,
they are already served by roads and right of way networks, thereby reducing the need for new roads or offsite
improvements. Following industry principles, t. The standard deduction for future roads/rights-of-way for
vacant and infrastructure gap areas remains at is 20% for unincorporated Kitsap County, and the deduction
for underutilized properties is reduced to. Developable land in urban areas may already be served by
established road networks, thereby reducing the need for new roads or off-site improvements, the
roads/rights-of-way reduction for under-utilized properties is 5%.

This change added 294 detached single-family units to the land capacity supply and 1,070 multi-family units.
These changes are shown in the relevant population and housing tables of the 2024 Comprehensive Plan.

                              UGA Land Capacity Analysis
                                  Technical Report
                                 December 4, 2024

                                          Introduction


The Growth Management Act (GMA) requires Urban Growth Areas (UGAs) to be reviewed at least
every ten years to ensure that they are capable of accommodating the urban growth projected to
occur in the county during the succeeding 20-year period. In response, the county’s 2024 plan
update establishes a new plan horizon that extends to the year 2044. The county and the cities
must therefore demonstrate that a sufficient supply of land exists within the UGA to
accommodate projected urban growth to the year 2044. Both residential and employment land
needs must be evaluated in this assessment of UGA land capacity.

This report describes the results of Snohomish County’s updated residential and employment land
capacity analysis for unincorporated portions of the UGA adopted by the County Council on
December 4, 2024 under Amended Ord. No. 24-033 as part of the county’s 2024 GMA plan review
and update, required under GMA by December 31, 2024. Using the adopted future land use map,
the report compares the estimates of population, housing, and employment capacity with the
population, housing, and employment target projections to 2044 for each unincorporated UGA in
Snohomish County. This is also done for each unincorporated Municipal Urban Growth Area
(MUGA) within the SW County UGA.

The analysis is consistent with previous capacity analyses conducted by the county for its original
GMA plan adoption in 1995, and for its major plan updates in 2005 and 2015. It is consistent with
relevant Washington State Department of Commerce guidance documents for UGA sizing and land
capacity analyses. It also continues and builds upon the data sources and methodology developed
by the county and cities for the 2002, 2007, 2012 and 2021 Snohomish County Buildable Lands
Reports 1.

1
 Technical guidance documents used for this capacity update include:
• Washington State Department of Commerce’s report entitled “Issues in Designating Urban Growth
   Areas (Part I): Providing Adequate Urban Area Land Supply,” released March 1992;
• Snohomish County Tomorrow’s Working Paper: Land Capacity Methodology for Residential Land,
   approved February 1993;
• Washington State Department of Commerce’s report entitled Buildable Lands Program Guidelines,
   released June 2000;
• Snohomish County Tomorrow’s Recommended Methodology and Work Program for a Buildable Lands
   Analysis for Snohomish County and its Cities (Procedures Report), approved July 2000;
• Washington State Department of Commerce’s Urban Growth Area Guidebook, released September
   2012;


                                                 2
The county’s previous Buildable Lands Reports (BLRs) analyzed the urban development densities
that occurred since adoption of the first GMA comprehensive plans, or since the previous
buildable lands report. Using this information, the reports evaluated the adequacy of the land
supply within the UGA to accommodate the remaining portion of the projected urban growth
anticipated in adopted plans based on the densities observed under GMA plans and development
regulations. In that sense, the Buildable Lands Reports “look back” and compare planned vs.
actual urban densities under city and county GMA plans in order to determine whether the
original plan assumptions pertaining to assumed densities and the adequacy of the urban land
supply to the plan horizon year were accurate (see RCW 36.70A.215).

The current UGA land capacity analysis differs from the GMA Buildable Lands Report requirements
by focusing on the reestablishment of a 20-year urban land supply for accommodating the new
2044 urban growth targets. As such, it fulfills a separate GMA “show your work” requirement for
the sizing of UGAs for projected growth, by demonstrating the adequate provision of land for
future population, housing, and employment uses (see RCW 36.70A.110 and RCW 36.70A.115).

Cities in Snohomish County have the same December 31, 2024 GMA deadline as the county for
updating their comprehensive plans. As part of their local GMA plan update efforts, each city is
responsible for updating its own land capacity analysis for areas within its jurisdiction, while the
county is updating its estimates for unincorporated areas within the UGA.

To do this, the county and most cities have started with the capacity work accomplished for the
2021 Buildable Lands Report effort, but have also added in potential additional capacity associated
with (1) the longer 2044 timeframe for estimating developable land capacity and (2) any updated
future land use/zoning designations they may be considering 2. For the county, this updated land
capacity work has been accomplished using the future land use map for the unincorporated
portion of the UGA adopted by the County Council on December 4, 2024 under Amended Ord. No.
24-033. With cities currently in the process of updating their comprehensive plans before the end
of the year, this report uses the initial 2044 population, housing, and employment targets adopted
into the Countywide Planning Policies (CPPs) as the basis for placeholder city capacity estimates at
this point in time.3

    5254, approved June 24, 2020.

  The latter includes measures that are designed to increase residential and employment capacity

use and regulatory changes that are estimated to increase capacity within the unincorporated
UGA).

  Placeholder capacity estimates are used since, as of this writing, cities have not yet adopted

demonstrating how they are able to accommodate the preferred targets. In January 2024, County


                                                   3
As the cities get closer to evaluating and selecting preferred alternatives for the plan updates due
in December 2024, county staff will again compile city preferred target and capacity estimates,
and update the city information results accordingly. The updated 2044 capacity information from
cities will be combined with the county’s 2044 unincorporated UGA capacity results to arrive at
final composite (city plus unincorporated) UGA land capacity/growth target comparison, and will
be shown in an updated UGA Land Capacity Analysis technical report.




staff did however reach out to the cities and towns and requested information about the status of
their plan updates, whether they are planning for the adopted initial 2044 growth targets, and
information about significant reasonable measures they are considering. Those jurisdictions are in
various states of progress, and of those that responded, nearly all of them expect to adopt plans
consistent with the initial targets. One, the City of Marysville, a city identified for higher growth
under the PSRC VISION 2050 regional growth strategy because of planned high-capacity transit
service, is considering growth targets higher than the initial targets. None of the cities or towns
that responded identified that they are considering lower growth targets. This indicates that cities
and towns either had sufficient capacity documented in the 2021 BLR or are considering
reasonable measures to accommodate their growth targets.

                                                                                                                       19
                                   Methodology:
       Summary of Updates to the Unincorporated UGA Capacity Analysis since the
                             2021 Buildable Lands Report

The unincorporated UGA capacity analysis uses the results from the 2021 Buildable Lands Report
for Snohomish County as a starting point for the 2024 plan update land capacity analysis. It then
introduces two key enhancements that address the new 2044 plan horizon and the future land use
plan designations contained in the 2024 plan update adopted by the County Council under
Amended Ord. No. 24-033 on December 4, 2024.

Please refer to the 2021 Buildable Lands Report for Snohomish County, adopted by the Snohomish
County Council on September 8, 2021, for a detailed description of the methodology used to
develop the buildable lands capacity estimates for UGAs as of April 1, 2019. These estimates were
developed using a 2035 plan horizon timeframe in order to compare with the adopted 2035
population, housing, and employment growth targets in the Countywide Planning Policies for
Snohomish County.

For the purposes of estimating UGA population and employment capacity to the new plan horizon
year of 2044, the 2021 BLR results (which were applicable only to a 2035 plan horizon) needed to
be updated to:

(1) Add the capacity from parcels not considered to be developable by 2035, but which could be
    potentially redevelopable or partially-used to support additional development at potentially
    higher densities by 2044. By adding 9 years to the plan horizon, during which time urban land
    market changes could be expected to generate greater demand for more intensified use of the
    remaining urban land, more parcels could be considered under-utilized and thus candidate
    sites for redevelopment/additional development. 4
(2) Reflect the future land use designation changes adopted by the County Council on December
    4, 2024 under Amended Ord. No. 24-033 for areas within the unincorporated UGA. These
    changes are intended to support a land use strategy of higher density infill development and
    redevelopment in certain areas of the unincorporated UGA to 2044. Locations for these
    proposed redesignations were mainly within the Urban Core Subarea Plan portion of the
    unincorporated SW County UGA. The subarea is generally located between the cities of
    Everett, Mill Creek, Lynnwood, and Mukilteo. This area will be served in the future by light rail
    transit as part of Sound Transit’s Everett Link extension. The Urban Core Subarea Plan
    proposes amendments to the FLU designations and rezones in many parts of the subarea to
    encourage more development at higher densities that is supportive of and served by current
    and planned high-capacity transit in the area. (See the county’s 2024 Reasonable Measures
    Report for more detail on the amendments to the FLU designations and rezones contained in
    County’s 2024 plan update.)

4
 Table 7 below provides descriptions of the specific capacity enhancements implemented in the
2024 plan update UGA land capacity analysis as they relate to revisions associated with the longer
plan horizon to 2044 compared with those used in the 2021 Buildable Lands Report.

A reasonable measure which has emerged as an important source of new capacity within the UGA
since adoption of the 2021 Buildable Lands Report is the Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) provision.
The county’s 2024 Reasonable Measures Report provides the following description of ADUs a small
but increasingly important source of housing capacity within the unincorporated UGA (pages 8-9):

        Permit Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) in single family zones

        State law requires certain jurisdictions to allow ADU construction. Snohomish County has long
        allowed ADUs in single family zones in the unincorporated area. ADUs primarily serve as permanent
        housing, either as rental units or for multi-generational living. ADUs are considered to have the
        potential to serve as low-income housing. On June 19, 2021, the County adopted Amended
        Ordinance No. 22-018 to further encourage ADU construction. The following are some of the
        significant changes to regulations:

            •   ADUs are permitted outright, rather than as a conditional use, in all zones that allow single
                family dwellings.
            •   Urban lots are allowed up to two ADUs, if one is attached and the other detached.
            •   ADUs are allowed on substandard lots in urban zones if there is a legally established single
                family dwelling.
            •   Parking requirements were eliminated for ADUs in urban zones.
            •   There is no longer an owner-occupancy requirement.

        There have been subsequent amendments to ADU provisions that mainly affect the rural area.
        Following the adoption of the revisions described above, ADU construction increased in the urban
        area in 2022 and 2023 as shown below:

        Table 2.A-1. Accessory Dwelling Units permitted in the unincorporated UGA, 2017-2023
                                      2017       2018     2019           2020      2021       2022       2023
        Urban ADUs Permitted            3         12        2             10        8          19         19
        Source: Snohomish County Issued Permits Data, 2017-2023

        The passage of House Bill 1337 in 2023 will require the County to consider additional changes to the
        ADU regulations to meet new requirements in state law to allow two ADUs per lot without requiring
        that one must be attached and the other one detached. In addition, as a result of the review of
        barriers to low-income housing development required under House Bill 1220 adopted in 2021,
        amendments could be considered to remove design requirements and to reduce permit times for
        ADUs.

        Based on recent data and the expectation of further enhancements to the County’s ADU regulations,
        ADUs are expected to contribute a small but increasing amount of residential development each year
        to meet the 2044 residential growth targets within the UGA.

The land capacity analysis for the county’s 2024 Plan Update assumes an annual rate of ADU permitting in
the unincorporated UGA of 30 ADUs per year from 2020 through 2044.

       Re:     2025 Comprehensive Plan Periodic Update – Submission in Support of Site-Specific
               Request: APN 193085000

Dear Mr. Orjiako:

This office represents BGround LLC, the owner of Assessor’s Parcel No. 193085000, located at
21708 NE 72nd Ave in the Dollars Corner neighborhood, about one mile west of Battle Ground (the
“Property”). The Property is currently designated Rural Commercial in the Comprehensive Plan and
zoned CR-2, Rural Commercial.

With the existing rural commercial development on and around the Property, this area is clearly
characterized by urban growth. Nearby businesses include a drainage contractor, equipment rental, a
garage door contractor, two auto mechanics, and an RV repair company. Nearby civic uses include a
Moose Lodge and Clark-Cowlitz Fire Rescue Station 26. These uses are illustrated on the Google
aerial photo which is enclosed as part of the attached GIS Fact sheets.

Excellent transportation access to Interstate 5 is provided by SR 502, located just one parcel north of
the Property. Sanitary sewer service is available in the City of Battle Ground. Potable water is
available from the Battle Ground Water District in the city as well. Battle Ground School District will
accommodate nearby residents. And Clark-Cowlitz Fire and Rescue provides emergency services,
with Station 26 located just across NE 72nd Ave. These urban facilities are also shown on the
attached GIS Fact sheets which provide maps from Clark County’s own MapsOnline. This data
demonstrates the Property and Dollars Corner are characterized by urban development.

The proposed Battle Ground UGA expansion would extend the city to the west along the SR 502
corridor, by adding 161 acres, including the Dollars Corner neighborhood. The Property will be
designated Commercial with an Urban Holding overlay on the Comprehensive Plan Map. The zoning
will be Regional Commercial. This letter is to support those changes, and will explain why the
opposition to them lacks merit, both as a matter of land use planning and as a matter of Washington
law.



                                                                                    57789-83715 4924-7342-3832.1


Portland | Bend | Vancouver, WA | jordanramis.com
October 12, 2026
Page 2


Opponents argue that the existing Battle Ground UGA has sufficient capacity for employment uses.
However, as correctly noted by planning staff in Issue Paper 5, “The GMA does not dictate a data
source that must be considered in planning for future employment.”1 In other words, Clark County has
flexibility to plan for urban employment uses. Table 6 of that paper allocates future employment to
various areas within the county, and allocates 7,449 jobs to Battle Ground. The table notes the 2023
VBLM capacity is only 5,544, which leaves a deficit of 1,905. Opponents do not provide an alternate
data source, or otherwise explain why the 2023 VBLM is inaccurate regarding current and future
employment capacity for Battle Ground. Therefore, the argument that Battle Ground does not need
additional land for employment uses lacks merit.

RCW 36.70A.115(1) requires Clark County to “provide sufficient capacity of land suitable for
development within their jurisdictions to accommodate their allocated housing and employment
growth[.]” It is appropriate and lawful for Clark County to rely on the 2023 VBLM as the data source to
justify expansion of the Battle Ground UGA. It is the right choice to use the existing rural commercial
properties around Dollars Corner as the land suitable to remedy that deficit, because urbanization will
allow increases in employment density. This new UGA lies between Battle Ground and Interstate 5,
and along SR 502. This location leverages the existing state route infrastructure and reduces out of
direction travel, with all the consequent benefits for reduced fuel consumption and reduction of
greenhouse gases.

We support the designation of the Dollars Corner neighborhood for expansion of the Battle Ground
UGA, and appreciate your support for the future employment uses which will be developed.

Very truly yours,

JORDAN RAMIS PC



Jamie D. Howsley

Re: 2025 Comprehensive Plan Periodic Update and Surplus Land Needs

Dear Mr. Orjiako:

This office represents several property owners. They are concerned that Clark County may set aside
too little land for housing in the 2025 Comprehensive Plan Periodic Update. This concern applies to
proposed Urban Growth Area changes for Vancouver, Ridgefield, Battle Ground, La Center, Camas,
and other parts of the County.

The County’s current model assumes a 10 percent never to convert rate1 for residential land and a 30
percent underutilization rate2. There was a motion to increase those percentages but it was not
adopted. The present assumptions are too low. If more land remains unavailable, the County will
not have enough usable land for homes people want and can afford.

We urge the Council to plan for a 20 percent never to convert factor in new residential UGAs
and a 40 percent underutilization factor in already developed residential areas.

The discussion noted that the Housing Options Plan allows accessory dwelling units, middle housing,
and greater density on some properties. These changes may increase housing capacity on paper.
But the record does not show whether there is enough market demand for these housing
types or how much of that added capacity is reasonably likely to be built during the planning
period. The County should therefore consider both the new zoning options and the continued
demand for single-family homes when estimating future housing capacity.

New zoning rules allow more homes in existing single-family neighborhoods, including accessory
dwelling units and middle housing. But many owners will choose not to add homes to their property,


1
  A never to convert rate or factor is an allowance for land that is vacant and designated for
development, but will not fully develop during the planning period.
2
  An underutilization rate or factor is an allowance for land that is already developed or partially
developed, where zoning allows more housing than is likely to actually be built.


                                                                                      55152-80934 4915-3648-2007.1


Portland | Bend | Vancouver, WA | jordanramis.com
October 12, 2026
Page 2


and other limits may prevent building. As a result, unused housing capacity will grow. These zoning
changes may allow more housing, but they may also lead to a higher underutilization rate.

The following example shows why allowed housing capacity can be much higher than the housing
actually built: Assume a neighborhood has 100 homes. Then the neighborhood is rezoned to allow
each lot to add a second unit (that’s up to 200 homes if each lot builds the second unit). If only 15 lots
add a second unit, the neighborhood has 115 homes—not 200—leaving 42% of the
neighborhood’s capacity “unused”.

This is consistent with Councilor Yung’s recommendation of 40 percent. A minor error in the
underutilized rate will mean a shortage of thousands of housing units of the types and in the locations
that Clark County residents are seeking. Given the general housing shortage, the Council should err
on the side of securing enough residential land for the housing type that residents prefer; not the
types we hope will be built.

State rules recognize that not all developable land will be put to its maximum use because of things
such as owner preference, cost, stability, quality, location, and changing market forces. And they do
allow local governments to consider their own circumstances when establishing this market factor, as
other counties have done.

In 2024, Snohomish County’s executive recommendation was for a multifamily vacancy rate of 12.5
percent. Its UGAs have capacity for more than 18,000 more people than needed to hit their adopted
growth target in addition to the areas added to the UGA in 2024. In total, its UGAs are about 6.3%
over capacity. The county expanded UGAs in 2024 based on employment needs (in Marysville) and
needs for specific housing types (Monroe, Bothell MUGA, etc.). One of the UGAs with the largest
amount of excess capacity is the Snohomish UGA, which has a growth target of 405 people, leaving it
with excess capacity for an additional 1,600 people.

King County similarly provides for a surplus of residential land capacity. For its 2024 Comprehensive
Plan, it established Growth Targets and the Urban Growth Area, as shown in the attached report. On
pages 11-13 it addresses the targets and capacity for the unincorporated areas of the county
(including those that are potential annexation areas and those that are unaffiliated or not identified by
a city for future annexation). King County’s housing Target is 5,412 new housing units against a
capacity of 29,600 (about 546% more capacity than needed).

Kitsap County also provides for surplus residential land. Its Land Capacity Analysis is attached. Page
2 shows that for the Preferred Alternative, the county has excess capacity for 8532 people and a
population growth target of 28,825 for 2022-2044. This provides 30 percent surplus capacity.

We urge the County Council to recognize the importance of designating surplus residential Urban
Growth Areas because many portions of the designated areas will not develop housing within the
planning period for reasons that are beyond the control of county planners and residential developers.
The county must aim high to reach the actual target which lies twenty years in the future. The county
should plan for 20 percent vacancy in new Urban Growth Areas and 40 percent
underutilization of the zoned capacity in the existing developed residential areas.

Executive Summary
   1. The proposed Mill Creek Estates project will include the construction of a residential
      subdivision on two properties located at 3511/3619 NE 174th Street in unincorporated
      Clark County, Washington. The proposal will include the construction of a 43-lot
      subdivision, where one existing house will be removed and second existing house will be
      retained. Access to the site will be provided via NE 174th Street to the east of the site and
      NE 171st Way to the south. Note that the remaining existing house will be served access
      via the private road segment of NE 174th Street. This private segment of NE 174th Street
      will serve as emergency vehicle access only for all other proposed houses until the
      private segment is redesigned and reclassified as a public street.
   2. The trip generation calculations show that the proposed subdivision is projected to
      generate 29 net new AM peak hour trips, 38 net new PM peak hour trips, and 373 net
      new average weekday trips.
   3. The intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 50th Avenue is projected to operate at LOS E
      during the PM peak hour under 2028 post-development conditions. While not necessarily
      operating in excess of County standards, it is expected that future operation may
      eventually degrade to LOS F. The applicant will be volunteering to install a dedicated
      northbound left-turn lane at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 50th Avenue as part
      of this proposed development application. This volunteered mitigation is intended to
      demonstrate improved LOS D operation and to add additional capacity to the critical
      minor street approach and turning movement of the intersection.
   4. All other study intersections are currently operating acceptably per Clark County
      standards and are projected to continue operating acceptably through the 2028
      development year of the site. No operational mitigation is necessary or recommended at
      these study intersections as part of the proposed development application.
   5. The roadway segment of NE 10th Avenue between NE 179th Street and NE 189th Street is
      projected to exceed Clark County’s roadway segment v/c ratio threshold under year 2028
      conditions. Although projected to operate with a v/c ratio in excess of 0.90 during the PM
      peak hour, no mitigation as part of the proposed development application is
      recommended for the following reasons:
          a. During the PM peak hour, the northbound travel direction of the roadway segment
             operates with a v/c ratio of 0.921 and the southbound direction operates with an
             acceptable v/c ratio of 0.551. The proposed development is projected to add 0 PM
             peak hour trips to the northbound travel direction of the roadway segment.
             Therefore, the proposed development will not impact or increase the v/c ratio of
             the failing travel direction of NE 10th Avenue.


MILL CREEK ESTATES SUBDIVISION                                                             6/9/2026
TRANSPORTATION IMPACT STUDY                                                            PAGE 1 OF 32
          b. This segment of NE 10th Avenue is projected to operate with v/c ratios above 0.90
             under year 2028 conditions without impacts from the proposed development,
             noting the proposed development does not impact this movement. Therefore, the
             proposed Mill Creek Estates project does not cause this roadway segment to
             exceed the 0.90 v/c ratio threshold.
          c. The study intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue is projected to
             operate at LOS A during the AM and PM peak hours under year 2028 post-
             development conditions. Therefore, the high roadway v/c ratio is not expected to
             create operational issues at the relevant/applicable study intersections.
   6. All other relevant roadway segments are projected to operate acceptably per Clark
      County standards through the 2028 development year of the site during both the AM and
      PM peak hours. Accordingly, no roadway capacity-related mitigation is necessary or
      recommended as part of the proposed development application.
   7. Under 2028 post-development conditions, a total of 142 single-family detached houses
      are expected to utilize and add 1,291 average daily trips to NE 40th Avenue on a typical
      basis to access the greater transportation system. This number of trips generated is below
      the design volume threshold of a Neighborhood Circulator. Accordingly, the increase in
      traffic volume on NE 40th Avenue will not exceed its design volume threshold.
   8. Aside from the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue, which is experiencing
      a high crash rate nearing 1.00 crashes per million entering vehicles, no significant trends
      or crash patterns were identified at any of the study intersections that are indicative of
      safety concerns. Planned improvements at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th
      Avenue are expected to reduce the overall number of recurring crashes at the intersection.

      Creek Estates application.

      access intersection to allow for safe and efficient operation along NE 174th Street. No
      sight distance related mitigation is necessary or recommended.

       the site. No new turn lanes are necessary or recommended as part of the proposed

       at NE 50th Avenue or NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue, under year 2028 post-

Section A – Project Description

Introduction
The proposed Mill Creek Estates project will include the construction of a residential subdivision
on two properties located at 3511/3619 NE 174th Street in unincorporated Clark County,
Washington. The proposal will include the construction of a 43-lot subdivision, where one
existing house will be removed and second existing house will be retained. Access to the site will
be provided via NE 174th Street to the east of the site and NE 171st Way to the south. Note that
the remaining existing house will be served access via the private road segment of NE 174th
Street. This private segment of NE 174th Street will serve as emergency vehicle access only for
all other proposed houses until the private segment is redesigned and reclassified as a public
street.
Based on correspondence with Clark County staff, the report conducts safety and capacity/level
of service analyses at the following intersections:
   1. NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue
   2. NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue
   3. NE 179th Street at NE 50th Avenue
   4. NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue
   •   Future Site Access at NE 174th Street (Sight Distance and Turn Lane Warrant Analysis
       Only)
The purpose of this study is to determine whether the transportation system within the vicinity of
the site is capable of safely and efficiently supporting the surrounding existing and proposed
uses, and to determine any mitigation that may be necessary to do so. Detailed information on
traffic counts, trip generation calculations, safety analyses, and level of service calculations is
included in the appendix to this report.

Location Description
The project site is located north of NE 171st Way, south of NE 174th Street, and west of NE 40th
Avenue in unincorporated Clark County, Washington. Located within a developing residential
area of the County, the site is immediately surrounded by a residential subdivision to the south,
and low density residential/undeveloped land in all other directions.
The site consists of two properties (assessor parcels 181674000 and 181754000) which
encompass an approximate total of 10 acres. Two single-family detached houses and ancillary
storage structures are currently built on-site, all of which will be removed except for one house
following site redevelopment. The site is currently served by individual lot driveways along a
currently private road section of NE 174th Street to the west of NE 40th Avenue.
Figure 1 presents an aerial image of the nearby vicinity with the project site outlined in yellow.

Section D – Operations Analysis

Intersection Capacity Analysis
A capacity and delay analysis were conducted for the study intersections per the signalized and
unsignalized intersection analysis methodologies in the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM)4.
Intersections are generally evaluated based on the average control delay experienced by vehicles
and are assigned a grade according to their operation. The Level of Service (LOS) is a qualitative
measure of traffic operational conditions, and can range from LOS A, which indicates little or no
delay experienced by vehicles, to LOS F, which indicates a high degree of congestion and delay.
The volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio is a measure that compares the traffic volumes (demand)
against the available capacity of an intersection or roadway.

Performance Standards
According to Clark County’s Unified Development Code, Title 40.350 – Transportation and
Circulation, Clark County’s performance standards require unsignalized intersections to operate
at LOS E or better unless traffic signal warrants are met. If traffic signal warrants are met, the
intersection is required to operate at LOS D or better. Individual movements at signalized
intersections of regional significance are to operate with average delays of less than two cycle
lengths or 240 seconds, whichever is less.

Delay and Capacity Analysis
The study intersections were analyzed utilizing methodologies and parameters detailed in the
WSDOT Synchro & SimTraffic Protocol document. Of specific note, the following peak hour
factors (PHF) were incorporated in the analysis models:
      •    For existing year conditions, a PHF of no less than 0.80 was applied to each study
           intersection.
      •    For future year conditions, for study intersections where count data recorded a PHF of
           0.90 or greater, the PHF was increased to 1.0.
      •    To better avoid showing a future year scenario with lower delays than under existing
           conditions, for study intersections where count data recorded a PHF of 0.89 or less the
           PHF was increased to 0.92.
Due to the lane configuration at the signalized study intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th
Avenue (i.e., non-NEMA phasing), the HCM 7th Edition methodology utilizing Trafficware’s
Synchro 12 software does not provide capacity outputs for this intersection under existing
conditions. Therefore, the reported results at this intersection are based on HCM 2000
methodologies.


4
    Transportation Research Board, Highway Capacity Manual, 7th Edition, 2022.

MILL CREEK ESTATES SUBDIVISION                                                                6/9/2026

179th Street at NE 29th Avenue were modeled as roundabouts. In accordance with the WSDOT
Synchro & SimTraffic Protocol and WSDOT Sidra Policy Settings documents, the roundabout
study intersections were modeled using Sidra Intersection 11 software.

NE 40th Avenue Daily Volumes
NE 40th Avenue is classified as a Neighborhood Circulator, where according to Table
40.350.030-3, the design volume of a Neighborhood Circulator is 3,000 average daily trips. At
the time of writing the following existing houses, approved subdivisions, and proposed
development are/will take direct access to the area roadways of NE 40th Avenue, NE 37th
Avenue, NE 165th Circle and/or NE 174th Street.
   •    Existing Houses along NE 40th Avenue, NE 37th Avenue, and NE 165th Circle: 28 houses.
   •    Existing Houses along NE 174th Street: 16 houses
   •    M&H Subdivision: 72 houses

MILL CREEK ESTATES SUBDIVISION                                                             6/9/2026
TRANSPORTATION IMPACT STUDY                                                           PAGE 22 OF 32
   •    Mill Creek Meadows: 40 houses (removing 1 existing house along NE 174th Street).
   •    Viers Subdivision: 84 houses
   •    Proposed Mill Creek Estates:43 houses (removing 1 existing house along NE 174th Street
        and noting only 42 houses will add trips to NE 40th Avenue).
Unlike NE 174th Street, NE 40th Avenue does not provide an outlet or alternative connection to
the greater transportation system. Additionally, no commercial, institutional, or major
recreational uses are currently developed along NE 40th Avenue, NE 37th Avenue, NE 165th
Circle and NE 174th Street. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume all residential trips generated by
the aforementioned land uses will travel to/from the east along NE 174th Street toward the
intersection of NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue. On this basis it is assumed that only the
following residential uses may add trips to NE 40th Avenue:
   •    Existing Houses along NE 40th Avenue, NE 37th Avenue, and NE 165th Circle: 28 houses.
   •    M&H Subdivision: 72 houses
   •    Proposed Mill Creek Estates: 42 houses.
Only a nominal, or de minimis, number of vehicular trips are expected to be added to NE 40th
Avenue by Mill Creek Meadows, the Viers Subdivision, and other existing houses with direct
access to NE 174th Street for the reasons described above. Motorists typically do not travel out-
of-direction without a good reason for doing so, noting there is no reason for residents of Mill
Creek Meadows or the Viers Subdivision to travel out-of-direction along NE 40th Avenue. Both
subdivisions will have fully improved access roads connecting directly to NE 174th Street at
locations east of NE 40th Avenue, which provides a shorter and only path to access the greater
transportation network via NE 50th Avenue. Residents of Mill Creek Meadows and Viers
Subdivision have no reason for traveling west along NE 174th Street unless they choose to visit
another resident within the M&H or Mill Creek East subdivision, noting that the M&H and Mill
Creek East transportation studies have already accounted for this. Once the Viers Subdivision is
constructed, NE 40th Avenue will have a second public street access connection to NE 174th
Street through the Viers Subdivision via NE 45th Avenue. To the extent the Viers Subdivision
has any impact on NE 40th Avenue the effect will likely be a reduction of trips on NE 40th
Avenue since:
    •   Very few motorists from the Viers Subdivision will travel out-of-direction to use NE 40th
        Avenue; and
    •   It is more likely that motorists from the M&H subdivision would drive through the Viers
        Subdivision to reach NE 174th Street (thus bypassing NE 40th Avenue).
Therefore, the Viers Subdivision is expected to have no impact on NE 40th Avenue, but rather
will likely create a small reduction in trips on the roadway.

Section E – Safety Analysis

Crash History Review
Using data obtained from the Washington Department of Transportation (WSDOT) Crash Data
and Reporting Branch, a review of the most recent available five years of crash history (January
2021 to December 2025) at the study intersections was performed. The crash data was evaluated
based on the number of crashes, the type of collisions, the severity of the collisions, and the
resulting crash rate for the intersection.
Crash rates provide the ability to compare safety risks at different intersections by accounting for
both the number of crashes that have occurred during the analysis period and the number of
vehicles that typically travel through the intersection. Crash rates were calculated using the
common assumption that traffic counted during the PM peak hour represents approximately 10
percent of the annual average daily traffic (AADT) at the intersection. Crash rates in excess of
1.00 crashes per million entering vehicles (CMEV) may be indicative of design deficiencies and
therefore require a need for further investigation and possible mitigation.
Regarding crash severity, WSDOT classifies crashes in the following categories:
   •   No Apparent Injury (NA)
   •   Possible Injury (P)
   •   Suspected Minor Injury (SM)
   •   Suspected Serious Injury (SS)
   •   Fatality or Fatal Injury
Table 7 provides a summary of crash types while Table 8 summarizes crash severities and rates
for each of the applicable study intersections. Crash data is included in the technical appendix to
this report.

Additionally, the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue was found to be nearing a

movement or angle type crashes. The intersection is currently undergoing reconstruction as a

indicative of safety concerns. Planned improvements at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE
29th Avenue are expected to reduce the overall number of recurring crashes at the intersection.
Therefore, no crash-related mitigation is necessary or recommended as part of the Mill Creek
Estates application.

Sight Distance Evaluation
Sight Distance Definitions and Methodologies
Intersection and stopping sight distances were measured at the proposed emergency vehicle site
access along NE 174th Street, located approximately 125 feet west of the project site’s east
boundary line. Sight distances were measured and evaluated at the intersection in accordance
with standards established in A Policy of Geometric Design of Highways and Streets6, as well as
per Clark County standards.
Intersection sight distance is an operational measure, intended to provide sufficient line of sight
along the major street so that a driver can enter the roadway without impeding the flow of
through traffic. For intersection sight distance, the driver’s eye is assumed to be 15 feet from the
near edge of the nearest travel lane (or traveled way) of the intersecting street and at a height of
3.5 feet above the minor street approach pavement. The oncoming vehicle driver’s eye height
along the major street approach is assumed to be 3.5 feet above the cross-street pavement.




5
  Traffic Safety Methods | WSDOT. 2 February 2026, https://wsdot.wa.gov/travel/traffic-safety-
methods/roundabouts.
6
  American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), A Policy on Geometric Design
of Highways and Streets, 7th Edition, 2018.

MILL CREEK ESTATES SUBDIVISION                                                                     6/9/2026
TRANSPORTATION IMPACT STUDY                                                                   PAGE 27 OF 32
Stopping sight distance is considered the minimum requirement to ensure safe operation of an
intersection with respect to sight lines. This distance allows the driver of a vehicle traveling on
the major street to react to a turning vehicle or other object in the roadway and, if necessary,
come to a complete stop to avoid a collision. To ensure safe operation, the extent of available
intersection sight distance must at least equal the minimum required stopping sight distance. For
stopping sight distance, the major street approaching driver’s eye height is 3.5 feet while an
object height of 2 feet above the street pavement is used.
According to Clark County Unified Development Code section 40.350.030.B.8, the minimum
recommended intersection sight distance is based on ten times the posted/statutory speed of the
roadway. However, alternative standards may be considered provided intersection sight distance
cannot reasonably be met. Stopping sight distances were based on Table 40.350.030-7 of the
County’s code.
Based on a posted speed of 35 mph along NE 174th Street, the following minimum intersection
and stopping sight distances are applicable to the proposed site access intersection:
   •   Intersection Sight Distance: 350 feet to the east and west.
   •   Stopping Sight Distance:
           o 235 feet to the east, considering the major street uphill eastbound approach grade
             of approximately 4.4% over a 275-foot distance
           o 250 feet to the east, considering the major street westbound approach grade is less
             than 3.0% over a 260-foot distance.

Sight Distance Measurements
Field measurements were conducted at the proposed site access intersection on Monday, May 12,
2026. Intersection and stopping sight distances to the east of the site access location were
measured to be in excess of 350 feet, while sight distances to the west were measured back to the
end of a turnaround/cul-de-sac along the private road section of NE 174th Street. Accordingly, no
sight distance related mitigation is necessary or recommended.

Analysis Summary
Based on the sight distance analysis, adequate intersection and stopping sight distances are
available at the proposed site access intersection to allow for safe and efficient operation along
NE 174th Street. No sight distance related mitigation is necessary or recommended.

Section F – Warrant Analysis

Left-Turn Lane Warrants
Left-turn lane warrants were examined for the proposed emergency vehicle site access along NE
174th Street, located approximately 125 feet west of the project site’s east property line. A left-
turn refuge lane is primarily a safety consideration for the major street, removing left-turning
vehicles from the through traffic stream. To evaluate left-turn lane warrants, section 1310.02(13)
Left-Turn Lanes and Turn Radii and Exhibit 1310-9 Left-Turn Storage Guidelines: Two-Lane,
Unsignalized from the WSDOT Design Manual were referenced. Turn lane warrants were
evaluated based on the number of advancing and opposing vehicles, the number of turning
vehicles, the travel speed, and the number of through lanes.
To determine the combined major street peak hour traffic volumes at the site access intersection,
volumes were balanced with those projected at the intersection of NE 174th Street at NE 50th
Avenue under year 2028 post-development conditions. This is expected to provide a highly
conservative evaluation of major street volumes at the site access intersection when considering
the following:
   •   NE 174th Street terminates as a cul-de-sac near the west edge of the project site; and
   •   None of the major street volumes were assumed to originate/terminate at intermittent land
       uses along NE 174th Street, NE 40th Avenue, or other adjoining roadways.
For the site access intersection along NE 174th Street, the combined eastbound and westbound
design hour volumes are below 300 vehicles per hour under year 2028 post-development
conditions for both the AM and PM peak hours (i.e., 204 and 251 AM and PM peak hour
volumes, respectively). Therefore, the WSDOT volume thresholds for warranting a left-turn lane
will not be met at the intersection. No left-turn lane is necessary or recommended.

Preliminary Traffic Signal Warrants
Preliminary traffic signal warrants were examined for the unsignalized intersections of NE 179th
Street at NE 50th Avenue and NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue to determine whether the
installation of a new traffic signal will be warranted by the 2028 post-development year. These
warrants were not evaluated at the other unsignalized study intersections since these intersections
will be reconstructed as roundabout intersections according to the Clark County 2026-2031 TIP.
Based on a preliminary review of Warrants 1 and 2 in the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control
Devices, or MUTCD, traffic signal warrants are not projected to be met at the intersections of NE
179th Street at NE 50th Avenue or NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue, under year 2028 post-
development conditions. Therefore, no new traffic signals are necessary or recommended as part
of the proposed development application.




MILL CREEK ESTATES SUBDIVISION                                                             6/9/2026
TRANSPORTATION IMPACT STUDY                                                           PAGE 29 OF 32
Note that a review of Warrant 3 was not considered as part of this analysis. According to the
MUTCD regarding Warrant 3:
       This signal warrant should be applied only in unusual cases, such as office complexes,
       manufacturing plants, industrial complexes, or high-occupancy vehicle facilities that
       attract or discharge large numbers of vehicles over a short time.
These study intersections are not located near land uses that are expected to generate this type of
traffic impact on a consistent basis. Therefore, it was concluded that Warrant 3 would not be
applicable to the analyzed study intersection.

Introduction
This memorandum details a proposed scope of work for a Transportation Impact Study (TIS)
related to the Mill Creek Estates project. The project site is located on two properties (assessor
parcels 181674000 and 181754000) addressed at 3511/3619 NE 174th Street in unincorporated
Clark County, Washington. The proposal will include the construction of a 43-lot subdivision,
where one existing house will be removed and second existing house will be retained. Access to
the site will be provided via NE 174th Street to the east of the site and NE 171st Way to the south.

Council (RTC) transportation system model. Both the Viers Subdivision and the project site are
located in Transportation Analysis Zone (TAZ) #1983 (formerly #525), for which a select zone
analysis was run to determine the distribution of site trips entering and exiting the zone. The
following trip distribution is estimated:
    •    Approximately 3% of site trips will travel to/from the north along NE 10th Avenue, north
         of NE 179th Street.
    •    Approximately 35% of site trips will travel to/from the west along NE 179th Street, west
         of NE 15th Avenue.
    •    Approximately 1% of site trips will travel to/from the south along NE 15th Avenue, south
         of NE 179th Street.
    •    Approximately 4% of site trips will travel to/from the north along NE 50th Avenue, north
         of NE 179th Street.
    •    Approximately 15% of site trips will travel to/from the east along NE 179th Street, east of
         NE 50th Avenue.
    •    Approximately 33% of site trips will travel to/from the south along NE 50th Avenue,
         south of NE 159th Street.
    •    Approximately 9% of site trips will travel to/from the east along NE 159th Street, east of
         NE 50th Avenue.

Proposed Study Intersections
According to the project’s Pre-Application Final Report:
        Any development generating 10 or more peak hour trips is required to complete a
        transportation impact study. A general outline is provided in the concurrency
        administrative manual. A traffic impact study shall analyze impacts according to the
        following:
                 - 50 or less new peak hour trips; one mile from site
                 - 51-250 new peak hour trips; two miles from the site
                 - 251 or more new peak hour trips; three miles from the site
Based on the projected trips generated, the preliminary trip distribution, and the anticipated
impacts to the transportation system, the following study intersections are suggested for analysis
(refer to Figure A for the numbering convention of listed intersections):
    2. NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue
    3. NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue
    5. NE 179th Street at NE 50th Avenue
    6. NE 174th Street at NE 50th Avenue
Although considered higher classification intersections within a one-mile radius of the site, the
following regionally significant intersections are not recommended for analysis, with
explanations for removal provided:
    The following intersections will either experience no site trip impacts or will be impacted by
    less than 5 peak hour trips. Therefore, no mitigation can be required as part of the application
    per Clark County Unified Development Code 40.350.020.G.1.c., not-with-standing safety
    improvements which may be necessary per section 40.350.030(B)(6):
    1. NE 189th Street at NE 29th Avenue – no peak hour trip impact.
    7. NE 159th Street at NE 29th Avenue – no peak hour trip impact.

    intersection as part of this development application per Clark County Unified Development

    8. NE 159th Street at NE 50th Avenue – 13 AM and 16 PM peak hour trip impact.

volumes and patterns at the following two suggested study intersections may not currently reflect
typical traffic conditions:
    3. NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue
    5. NE 179th Street at NE 50th Avenue
The most recent set of count data PLS Engineering has available at these intersections that reflect
normal traffic conditions were collected on Tuesday, August 5, 2025. At the time of writing,
these traffic counts have been collected within a 12-month period as required in Clark County
Unified Development Code 40.350.020.B.4. However, in the event the development application
has not been deemed fully complete by early August would it be acceptable to continue utilizing
these counts in this development application's traffic study, assuming roadway closures continue
beyond early August?

     Level of Service Descriptions

                                     LEVEL OF SERVICE
Intersection Level of Service (LOS) is a qualitative measure used to evaluate the performance of
intersections and roadways based on the traffic flow, average control delay, and overall operations. The
Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) defines LOS for signalized and unsignalized intersections as a
function of the average vehicle control delay. LOS may be calculated per movement or per approach for
any intersection configuration, but LOS for the intersection as a whole is generally defined for
signalized, roundabout, and all-way stop configurations.

The LOS metric is categorized using a graded scale from A to F. Descriptions of these LOS grade levels
are provided below:
                                                                             Control Delay Per Vehicle
LOS                                                                         Signalized &
                                   Description                                            Unsignalized
Grade                                                                       Roundabout
                                                                                          Intersections
                                                                            Intersections
        Indicative of relatively freeflow traffic conditions with minimal
        delays and high comfort for drivers. Low intersection delays and
  A                                                                         ≤ 10 seconds   ≤ 10 seconds
        clearing of vehicles occur in a single cycle at signalized
        intersections.

        Representative of reasonably free flow conditions, where speeds
  B     are maintained but maneuverability is slightly restricted. Slightly 10-20 seconds 10-15 seconds
        higher delays at intersections are observed.

        Indicative of stable flow, where maneuverability is noticeably
        restricted, and lane changes require more driver awareness.
  C                                                                       20-35 seconds 15-25 seconds
        Moderate delays at intersections may be observed, and the
        occasional queued vehicle may not clear in a single cycle length.

        Signifies approaching unstable flow, with significant delays and
        reduced comfort. Longer delays and congestion may be apparent
  D                                                                      35-55 seconds 25-35 seconds
        at an intersection. More than one cycle length at a signalized
        intersection may be necessary to service queued vehicles.

        Representative of unstable flow, where traffic is at or nearing
        capacity, leading to long delays. High delays at an intersection
  E                                                                         55-80 seconds 35-50 seconds
        are expected, and extended queuing may be observed. Cycle
        failures at signalized intersections are expected to occur.
        Indicative of forced flow, where traffic demand exceeds
        capacity, resulting in severe congestion and delays. Very high
  F     delays and significant queues are common at intersections.          >80 seconds    >50 seconds
        Frequent cycle failures are expected to occur at signalized
        intersections.

Executive Summary
   1. The proposed Avery Drive project will include the construction of a residential
      subdivision on a single property located at 3504 NE 184th Street in unincorporated Clark
      County, Washington. The proposal will include the construction of a 20 single-family
      detached housing development. As part of this proposal one existing house will be
      maintained, whereby a net of 19 houses will be constructed. Access to the site will be
      provided via a planned north/south roadway (i.e., NE 35th Avenue) that will be
      constructed between the project site and NE 179th Street as part of the in-process Mill
      Creek Terrace Subdivision.
   2. The proposed subdivision is projected to generate 13 net new AM peak hour trips, 18 net
      new PM peak hour trips, and 173 net new average weekday trips.
   3. All study intersections are currently operating acceptably per Clark County standards and
      are projected to continue operating acceptably through the 2028 development year of the
      site. No operational mitigation is necessary or recommended at the study intersections as
      part of the proposed development application.
   4. The roadway segment of NE 10th Avenue between NE 179th Street and NE 189th Street is
      projected to exceed Clark County’s roadway segment v/c ratio threshold under year 2028
      conditions during the PM peak hour. However, no mitigation as part of the proposed
      development application is recommended for the following reasons:
          a. The proposed development is projected to add 0 PM peak hour trips to the high
             demand travel direction of the roadway segment, and therefore, will not impact or
             increase the v/c ratio along NE 10th Avenue.
          b. The study intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue is projected to
             operate at LOS A during the AM and PM peak hours under year 2028 post-
             development conditions. The high roadway v/c ratio is not expected to create
             operational issues at the relevant/applicable study intersections.
          c. Two-lane roadways generally have a base single-direction capacity of 1,700
             pcphpl. The single-direction capacities detailed in Table 40.350.020-1 of the
             Clark County code utilize a similar single-direction capacity but may take into
             consideration how signalized intersections or other traffic controls along a
             corridor influence traffic flow/capacity along a roadway. When reviewing the
             corridor alone using this base 1,700 pcphpl, no capacity issues are expected along
             NE 10th Avenue.




AVERY DRIVE                                                                            6/18/2026
TRANSPORTATION IMPACT STUDY                                                         PAGE 1 OF 33
   5. All other relevant roadway segments are projected to operate acceptably per Clark
      County standards through the 2028 development year of the site during both the AM and
      PM peak hours. No roadway capacity-related mitigation is necessary or recommended as
      part of the proposed development application.
   6. No significant trends or crash patterns were identified at any of the study intersections
      beyond the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue that are indicative of safety
      concerns. The intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue is currently being
      reconstructed as a roundabout, which is expected to reduce the overall number of
      recurring crashes at the intersection. No other crash-related mitigation is necessary or
      recommended as part of the Avery Drive application.
   7. Based on traffic volumes alone, an eastbound left-turn lane is projected to be warranted at
      the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue during the PM peak hour under
      year 2028 pre-development conditions. Although a left-turn lane is warranted based on
      volumes, installation of this turn lane is not necessary or recommended at the intersection
      based on the following:
          a. The segment of NE 179th Street between NE 15th Avenue and NE 50th Avenue
             will be widened with raised medians installed near year 2031, approximately three
             years after the proposed development is constructed and occupied. Installation of
             a temporary turn lane is not expected to have a long-term benefit that outweighs
             the time and cost of installation.
          b. In addition to evaluating traffic volumes WSDOT also considers other factors on
             whether a left-turn lane should be installed at an unsignalized intersection. The
             following suggest a left-turn lane is unnecessary at the intersection:
                  i. The intersection is projected to operate acceptably at LOS C without the
                     turn lane installed.
                 ii. Limited to no crashes are expected to occur at the intersection of NE 179th
                     Street at NE 35th Avenue.
          c. There are currently no left-turn lanes installed along the NE 179th Street corridor
             between NE Union and NE 47th Avenue
          d. When considering the above, an eastbound left-turn lane was determined to be
             unnecessary with approval of the Mill Creek Terrace project. It is reasonable to
             conclude such a determination would be appropriate to apply to the proposed
             Avery Drive subdivision.

   8. The installation of a raised median at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th
      Avenue is not necessary for the roadway in the immediate future to operate safely or
      within acceptable levels of capacity per Clark County standards. Therefore, the County
      may approve the proposed development without the installation of a raised median
      through this intersection.
   9. Although block perimeter and length standards are currently not met for the existing
      block which surrounds the site, the proposed development will be constructing site
      internal public streets which will improve connectivity and promote a completed street
      network in the vicinity. Block perimeter standards can be met in the future; however, this
      is contingent on additional development of lower density/undeveloped properties in the
      area. Since the Avery Drive project will be expanding the public street network and does
      not introduce a street layout which precludes future blocks from meeting required length
      or perimeter standards, no further mitigation or improvements to the transportation
      system with respect to cross-circulation standards are necessary or recommended.

Section A – Project Description

Introduction
The proposed Avery Drive project will include the construction of a residential subdivision on a
single property located at 3504 NE 184th Street in unincorporated Clark County, Washington.
The proposal will include the construction of a 20 single-family detached housing development.
As part of this proposal one existing house will be maintained, whereby a net of 19 houses will
be constructed. Access to the site will be provided via a planned north/south roadway (i.e., NE
35th Avenue) that will be constructed between the project site and NE 179th Street as part of the
in-process Mill Creek Terrace Subdivision.
Based on correspondence with Clark County staff, the report conducts safety and capacity/level
of service analyses at the following intersections:
   1. NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue
   2. NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue
   3. NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue (Site Access)
The purpose of this study is to determine whether the transportation system within the vicinity of
the site is capable of safely and efficiently supporting the surrounding existing and proposed
uses, and to determine any mitigation that may be necessary to do so. Detailed information on
traffic counts, trip generation calculations, safety analyses, and level of service calculations is
included in the appendix to this report.

Location Description
The project site is located north of NE 179th Street, south of NE 199th Street, east of NE 29th
Avenue, and west of NE 50th Avenue in unincorporated Clark County, Washington. Located
within a developing residential area of the County, the site is immediately surrounded by the
under construction Mill Creek Terrace development to the south, and low density residential uses
in all other directions.
The site consists of a single property (assessor parcel 181513000) which encompasses an
approximate total of 6.14 acres. A single-family detached house and ancillary storage structures
are currently built on-site. The existing house will be maintained while all other structures will
be removed following site redevelopment. The site is currently served by a single shared
driveway (i.e., NE 37th Place) along NE 179th Street.
Figure 1 presents an aerial image of the nearby vicinity with the project site outlined in yellow.

Section B – Site Trips

Trip Generation
The proposed Avery Drive subdivision project will include the construction of 20 single-family
detached houses while maintaining one existing house for a total of 19 houses. To estimate the
number of trips generated by the existing and proposed uses, trip rates from the ITE Trip
Generation Manual, 12th Edition1 were used. Data from land use code 210, Single-Family
Detached Housing, was used to estimate site trip generation based on the number of dwelling
units.
The trip generation calculations show that the proposed subdivision is projected to generate 13
net new AM peak hour trips, 18 net new PM peak hour trips, and 173 net new average weekday
trips. The trip generation estimates are summarized in Table 3. Detailed trip generation
calculations are included in the technical appendix.

using the Southwest Washington Regional Transportation Council (RTC) transportation system
model. The Woodbrook Subdivision, Mill Creek Terrace Subdivision, and the project site are all
located in Transportation Analysis Zone (TAZ) #1982 (formerly #547), for which a select zone
analysis was run to determine the distribution of site trips entering and exiting the zone. The
following trip distribution is projected:

       of NE 15th Avenue.

       south of NE 179th Street.
   •   Approximately 13% of site trips will travel to/from the east along NE 179th Street, east of
       NE 50th Avenue.
   •   Approximately 7% of site trips will travel to/from the north along NE 50th Avenue, north
       of NE 199th Street.

   •   Approximately 2% of site trips will travel to/from the north along NE 29th Avenue, north

       of NE 179th Street.

Section C – Traffic Volumes

2025 Existing Volumes
Traffic counts were conducted at the study intersections on the following dates from 7:00 AM to
9:00 AM and from 4:00 PM to 6:00 PM:
   •   Tuesday, August 5, 2025.
   •   Wednesday, August 6, 2025.
   •   Thursday, December 4, 2025.
Data was used from each intersection’s respective AM and PM peak hours.
In addition to collecting traffic counts at the study intersections, data was also collected at the
intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 10th Avenue/Interstate 5 Off-Ramp on Thursday, December
4, 2025. The intent of collecting traffic counts at the intersection was to take into consideration
the planned future realignment of NE 10th Avenue to a location opposite of NE 15th Avenue.
Details regarding this realignment project are discussed in the 2028 Pre-Development Volumes
section below. The existing year traffic counts are shown in Figure B in the technical appendix to
this report.
To estimate traffic volumes at the planned site access intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th
Avenue, major street volumes were balanced with those recorded at the intersection of NE 179th
Street at NE 29th Avenue.
Figure 4 shows the 2025 existing year traffic volumes at the study intersections during the AM
and PM peak hours.

2028 Pre-Development Volumes
Volume Growth
An estimate of future traffic volumes is required to provide analysis of the proposed
development impacts to the nearby transportation system. To approximate the future year 2028
traffic volumes at the study intersections, a compounding growth rate of two percent per year for
over a three-year period was applied to the year 2025 existing traffic volumes.

In-Process Development Data
In addition to the traffic volume growth described above, there are several in-process
developments that are currently approved/proposed for construction within the site vicinity that
are expected to impact nearby study intersections. These in-process developments include the
following:

   •   Four Creeks North Subdivision

   •   Mountain View Ridge PUD

The in-process developments are not currently/fully contributing trips to the transportation
system but may potentially be by the assumed 2028 development year of the site. Additional
trips corresponding to each in-process development were added to the existing year traffic
volumes in addition to the three years of traffic growth at each of the applicable study
intersections. To maintain a conservative analysis of operation at the study intersections, all in-
process developments were assumed to be constructed by year 2028. Figure A in the technical
appendix shows the in-process development trips at the study intersections during the AM and
PM peak hours.
Clark County staff had initially requested that in-process trips associated with the Washington
State University (WSU) Master Plan be considered when developing the future traffic volume
projections. Upon reviewing two Development Agreement (DA) documents associated with this
Master Plan, dated December 11, 1998, and October 31, 2008, both indicate that the terms of the
DA would end at the end of calendar year 2025. This expiration of the DA includes the vesting
of trips associated with the Master Plan; therefore, in-process trips associated with the WSU
Master Plan were not considered.
