Planned Transportation Infrastructure Revisions
Several planned transportation improvement projects were incorporated in the future year
analysis scenarios. According to the Clark County’s Northeast 179th Street Corridor
Improvements project website2, the Washington Department of Transportation’s (WSDOT) I-5 –
179th Street Interchange – Interchange Improvements project website3, and the 2026-2031
Transportation Improvement Program (TIP), these projects include the following:
    •   NE 10th Avenue, just north of NE 179th Street and opposite of the Interstate 5 northbound
        off-ramp, will be closed and reconstructed at a location opposite of NE 15th Avenue along
        NE 179th Street (2026-2031 TIP Project C). Clark County’s 179th Street Circulation and
        Access Management Plan, dated July 2023, and 2026-2031 TIP Project E indicate the
        intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue will be reconstructed as a roundabout.
        The anticipated lane configuration of the intersection was referenced from a WSDOT
        concept design for the NE 179th Street interchange improvement project. Construction is
        estimated to occur between 2028 and 2030.
    •   The intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue will be reconstructed as a
        roundabout (2026-2031 TIP Project F). The initial design will include a single circulating
        lane but will be sized to be expandable as a multilane roundabout once NE 179th Street is
        widened to four lanes. Construction is currently underway.
    •   NE 179th Street will be widened to accommodate two eastbound travel lanes, two
        westbound travel lanes, and a center median/turn lane. This roadway widening project
        will occur in phases:
             o Between NE 10th Avenue and NE 15th Avenue (2026-2031 TIP Project A). The
               project will be constructed in collaboration with WSDOT as part of the Interstate
               5 interchange improvement project. Construction is estimated to occur sometime
               between 2028 and 2029.
             o Between NE 15th Avenue and NE 26th Avenue (2026-2031 TIP Project E).
               Construction is estimated to occur sometime between 2028 and 2030.
             o Between NE 29th Avenue and NE 50th Avenue (2026-2031 TIP Project 2).
               Construction is estimated to occur approximately around year 2031.
    •   There are currently no left-turn lanes installed along the NE 179th Street corridor between
        NE Union and NE 47th Avenue.

Section D – Operations Analysis

Intersection Capacity Analysis
A capacity and delay analysis were conducted for the study intersections per the signalized and
unsignalized intersection analysis methodologies in the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM)4.
Intersections are generally evaluated based on the average control delay experienced by vehicles
and are assigned a grade according to their operation. The Level of Service (LOS) is a qualitative
measure of traffic operational conditions, and can range from LOS A, which indicates little or no
delay experienced by vehicles, to LOS F, which indicates a high degree of congestion and delay.
The volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio is a measure that compares the traffic volumes (demand)
against the available capacity of an intersection or roadway.

Performance Standards
According to Clark County’s Unified Development Code, Title 40.350 – Transportation and
Circulation, Clark County’s performance standards require unsignalized intersections to operate
at LOS E or better unless traffic signal warrants are met. If traffic signal warrants are met, the
intersection is required to operate at LOS D or better. Individual movements at signalized
intersections of regional significance are to operate with average delays of less than two cycle
lengths or 240 seconds, whichever is less.

Delay and Capacity Analysis
The study intersections were analyzed utilizing methodologies and parameters detailed in the
WSDOT Synchro & SimTraffic Protocol document. Of specific note, the following peak hour
factors (PHF) were incorporated in the analysis models:
    •   For existing year conditions, a PHF of no less than 0.80 was applied to each study
        intersection.
    •   For future year conditions, for study intersections where count data recorded a PHF of
        0.90 or greater, the PHF was increased to 1.0.
    •   To better avoid showing a future year scenario with lower delays than under existing
        conditions, for study intersections where count data recorded a PHF of 0.89 or less the
        PHF was increased to 0.92.
Due to the lane configuration at the signalized study intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th
Avenue (i.e., non-NEMA phasing), the HCM 7th Edition methodology utilizing Trafficware’s
Synchro 12 software does not provide capacity outputs for this intersection under existing
conditions. Therefore, the reported results at this intersection are based on HCM 2000
methodologies.

Based on the results of the roadway capacity analysis, the roadway segment of NE 10th Avenue

segment v/c ratio threshold under year 2028 conditions. Although projected to operate with a v/c

development application is recommended for the following reasons:
    •    During the PM peak hour, the northbound travel direction of the roadway segment
         operates with a v/c ratio of 0.922 and the southbound direction operates with an
         acceptable v/c ratio of 0.554. The proposed development is projected to add 0 PM peak
         hour trips to the northbound travel direction of the roadway segment. Therefore, the
         proposed development will not impact or increase the v/c ratio of the high demand travel
         direction of NE 10th Avenue. Since no nexus of impact from the proposed development
         to the high demand travel direction on the NE 10th Avenue corridor can be established,
         no mitigation can be required as part of the proposed development application per the
         Nollan-Dolan test.
    •    The study intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 15th Avenue is projected to operate at
         LOS A during the AM and PM peak hours under year 2028 post-development
         conditions. Therefore, the high roadway v/c ratio is not expected to create operational
         issues at the relevant/applicable study intersections.
    •    According to the HCM 7th Edition, two-lane roadways generally have a base single-
         direction capacity of 1,700 passenger cars per hour per lane (pcphpl), though this
         capacity can vary depending on other factors such as roadway geometry, traffic
         characteristics, etc. The single-direction capacities detailed in Table 40.350.020-1 of the
         Clark County code utilize a similar single-direction capacity but may take into
         consideration how signalized intersections or other traffic controls along a corridor
         influence traffic flow/capacity along a roadway, as described in the Federal Highway
         Administration’s (FHWA) Simplified Highway Capacity Calculation Method for the
         Highway Performance Monitoring System5. Therefore, when reviewing the corridor
         alone using this base 1,700 pcphpl without the influence of intermittent signalized
         intersections, no capacity issues are expected along NE 10th Avenue.

standards through the 2028 development year of the site during both the AM and PM peak hours.

Section E – Safety Analysis

Crash History Review
Using data obtained from the Washington Department of Transportation (WSDOT) Crash Data
and Reporting Branch, a review of the most recent available five to six years of crash history
(January 2020 through late June 2025) at the study intersections was performed. The crash data
was evaluated based on the number of crashes, the type of collisions, the severity of the
collisions, and the resulting crash rate for the intersection.
Crash rates provide the ability to compare safety risks at different intersections by accounting for
both the number of crashes that have occurred during the analysis period and the number of
vehicles that typically travel through the intersection. Crash rates were calculated using the
common assumption that traffic counted during the PM peak hour represents approximately 10
percent of the annual average daily traffic (AADT) at the intersection. Crash rates in excess of
1.00 crashes per million entering vehicles (CMEV) may be indicative of design deficiencies and
therefore require a need for further investigation and possible mitigation.
Regarding crash severity, WSDOT classifies crashes in the following categories:
   •   No Apparent Injury (NA)
   •   Possible Injury (P)
   •   Suspected Minor Injury (SM)
   •   Suspected Serious Injury (SS)
   •   Fatality or Fatal Injury
Table 6 provides a summary of crash types while Table 7 summarizes crash severities and rates
for each of the applicable study intersections. Crash data is included in the technical appendix to
this report.

Per Table 7, the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue had one reported crash that
was classified as Suspected Serious Injury. The crash occurred when the driver of a northbound
left-turning passenger car failed to yield right-of-way to a westbound passenger car. One person
involved in the collision was reported to have sustained injuries.
Additionally, the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue was found to have a crash
rate in excess of 1.00 CMEV. All but one of the reported collisions at the intersection were either
turning movement or angle type crashes. The intersection is currently undergoing reconstruction
as a roundabout. Per WSDOT’s Traffic Safety Methods website6 roundabouts often reduce the
overall number of recurring crashes at signalized and stop-controlled intersections by
approximately 37 percent. Therefore, the overall crash rate at the intersection is expected to
decrease to approximately 0.66 CMEV after this intersection improvement has been constructed.
No additional mitigation is necessary or recommended.
Based on a review of the crash data, no significant trends or crash patterns were identified at any
of the study intersections beyond the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue that are
indicative of safety concerns. The intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 29th Avenue is currently
being reconstructed as a roundabout, which is expected to reduce the overall number of recurring
crashes at the intersection. No other crash-related mitigation is necessary or recommended as
part of the Avery Drive application.

Section F – Warrant Analysis
Left-turn lane warrants were examined for the site access intersection of NE 179th Street at NE
35th Avenue. A left-turn refuge lane is primarily a safety consideration for the major street,
removing left-turning vehicles from the through traffic stream. To evaluate left-turn lane
warrants, section 1310.02(13) Left-Turn Lanes and Turn Radii and Exhibit 1310-9 Left-Turn
Storage Guidelines: Two-Lane, Unsignalized from the WSDOT Design Manual were referenced.
Turn lane warrants were evaluated based on the number of advancing and opposing vehicles, the
number of turning vehicles, the travel speed, and the number of through lanes.
Based on traffic volumes alone, an eastbound left-turn lane is projected to be warranted at the
intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue during the PM peak hour under year 2028 pre-
development conditions. Although a left-turn lane is warranted based on volumes, installation of
this turn lane is not necessary or recommended based on the following:
   •   According to the Northeast 179th Street Corridor Improvements project, the segment of
       NE 179th Street between NE 15th Avenue and NE 50th Avenue will be widened to a four
       to five-lane cross-section with raised medians installed as needed. This will subsequently
       restrict access to/from NE 35th Avenue to right-turns only. Based on correspondence with
       Clark County staff, this widening project is expected to occur near year 2031,
       approximately three years after the proposed development is expected to be constructed
       and occupied. Considering this short time period between installing a left-turn lane
       relative to the eventual restriction of left-turn movements at the intersection, installation
       of the temporary turn lane is not expected to have a long-term benefit that outweighs the
       time and cost of installation.
   •   According to section 1310.02(13)(a) of the WSDOT Design Manual, in addition to
       evaluating traffic volumes WSDOT also considers other factors on whether a left-turn
       lane should be installed at an unsignalized intersection. Some of these factors which
       suggest a left-turn lane is not required include the following:
           o As described in Section D of this report, the intersection is projected to operate
             acceptably at LOS C without the turn lane installed.
           o Referring to Section G regarding a safety analysis that was performed to address
             the Medians and Channelization Policy, limited to no crashes are expected to
             occur at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue.

       impacts from the Avery Drive development. Instead, the volumes that trigger the need for

Section G – Medians and Channelization Policy
Since NE 179th Street is classified as an Urban Minor Arterial roadway, Clark County’s Medians
and Channelization Policy requires a raised median be constructed at the intersection of NE 179th
Street at NE 35th Avenue (Site Access). Clark County Code Section 40.350.030.B.4.d.(3) states
that “In order to preserve capacity and promote safety, urban arterials shall generally include
raised medians to restrict cross traffic movements.” The code section further states that “any
decision by the county that a raised median will not be installed on an arterial will require a
specific determination by the County Engineer that (a) the roadway will operate safely without a
raised median and (b) that the roadway will operate at the required capacity without a raised
median.”
With regard to restricting cross traffic, NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue is a three-legged
intersection with no south intersection leg. Therefore, no cross-traffic travel can occur through
the intersection in the north/south directions. Subsections (a) and (b) of the Medians and
Channelization Policy are further investigated below under the Roadway Safety and Roadway
Capacity subheadings, respectively.

Roadway Safety
For addressing subsection (a), to determine the relative safety of the roadway without a raised
median an analysis of crash history and sight distance was conducted.

Crash Analysis
To evaluate safety at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue without a raised
median, crash data from WSDOT’s online Crash Data Portal7 was referenced. Since the
intersection has recently been constructed, limited to no crash history is expected to be available
at this intersection. Therefore, crash data was evaluated at a comparable three-legged
unsignalized intersection without a raised median, specifically the intersection of NE 179th Street
at NE 47th Avenue. Crash data at this intersection was reviewed over a three-year period between
January 2023 through December 2025, noting the intersection had been constructed between
years 2022 and 2023.
According to WSDOT’s Crash Data Portal, no crashes were reported to have occurred at the
intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 47th Avenue over the three-year analysis period. With
respect to crash history, the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 47th Avenue operates safely,
and by comparison the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue is also expected to
operate safely without a raised median.

 Washington State Department of Transportation. (n.d.). Crash Data Portal.

Sight Distance Analysis
The intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue has recently been constructed as part of
the Mill Creek Terrace residential development. As part of the preliminary and final land use
approval process, the Mill Creek Terrace project would have had to review intersection and
stopping sight distances at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue and found both
to meet minimum standards. Therefore, it is expected that adequate intersection and stopping
sight distances are available at the intersection to allow for safe and efficient operation without a
raised median.

Safety Analysis Findings
Based on a review of crash history and sight distances at the NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue
intersection, NE 179th Street is expected to operate safely without a raised median through the
intersection. Accordingly, subsection (a) is satisfied.

Roadway Capacity
Regarding subsection (b), to determine operation of the roadway/intersection without a raised
median an analysis of intersection and roadway capacity were conducted.
Referring to Section D of this study, under future year 2028 post-development conditions the
intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue is projected to operate at LOS C with a v/c
ratio of 0.18 or less during the AM and PM peak hours. Based on a roadway capacity analysis,
the segment of NE 179th Street, between NE 29th Avenue and NE 47th Avenue, is projected to
operate with a v/c ratio of 0.416 or less during the AM and PM peak hours.
Based on the capacity analysis, the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue is projected
to operate within acceptable Clark County standards without a raised median through the
intersection. Accordingly, subsection (b) is satisfied.

Other Considerations
Under existing conditions NE 179th Street has a varying two to three-lane cross-section without a
raised median for over a one-mile distance to the east and west of the site. Therefore, it is
expected that the roadway within the immediate vicinity of the site will operate safely and with
sufficient capacity without a raised median.
According to TIP Project 2, NE 179th Street is planned for widening to a four to five-lane cross-
section between NE 29th Avenue and NE 50th Avenue with the installation of a raised median as
needed. Construction is estimated to occur approximately around year 2031. Once reconstruction
of the roadway occurs, it is recommended the County evaluate whether a raised median or a turn
lane be installed at the intersection.

Based on the findings presented above, the installation of a raised median at the intersection of
NE 179th Street at NE 35th Avenue is not necessary for the roadway in the immediate future to
operate safely or within acceptable levels of capacity per Clark County standards. Therefore, the

through this intersection.

Section H – Circulation Plan
In accordance with Clark County’s Unified Development Code section 40.350.030.B.2
Circulation Plan, a Circulation Plan was prepared to verify if the County’s block
length/perimeter standards can be met following buildout of the proposed subdivision, and to
evaluate the nearby transportation system/facilities within 600 feet of the site.
Per Clark County’s code, block lengths shall be between 100 feet to 800 feet, measured between
the nearside right-of-way lines between public roadways. The block perimeter shall not exceed
3,200 feet unless an accessway(s) for pedestrian or bicycle circulation is provided where
topographic or other physical constraints preclude meeting the perimeter standard.
Based on the existing transportation infrastructure surrounding the project site, block length and
perimeter standards were evaluated for the area enclosed by the following roadways:
   •   NE 179th Street (Urban Principal Arterial)
   •   NE 199th Street (Urban Minor Arterial)
   •   NE 29th Avenue (Urban Minor Arterial)
   •   NE 50th Avenue (Urban Minor Arterial)
Upon reviewing the impacted block area, the current block perimeter was measured to be in
excess of 3,200 feet. The current block lengths were measured to be in excess of 800 feet except
for the segments of NE 179th Street between NE 44th Avenue and NE 50th Avenue. Although
block perimeter and length standards are currently not met for the existing block which
surrounds the site, the proposed development will be constructing site internal public streets
which will improve connectivity and promote a completed street network in the vicinity. Block
perimeter standards can generally be met in the future; however, this is contingent on additional
development of lower density/undeveloped properties in the area. Since the Avery Drive project
will be expanding the public street network and does not introduce a street layout which
precludes development or connectivity for other adjacent properties to the north, south, and east
of the site, no further mitigation or improvements to the transportation system with respect to
cross-circulation standards are necessary or recommended.
Note that connectivity with properties to the west of the project site cannot reasonably be
provided due to an off-site stream and associated buffer areas and steep slopes. These
topographic and physical constraints preclude the practical construction of east/west streets
across the steam without potentially creating unnecessary environmental impacts and financial
costs to future development in the area. A road modification memorandum was prepared and
submitted under a separate document which seeks an exception to cross-circulation standards
with respect to these adjacent properties to the west.
A circulation plan detailing the nearby transportation system to the project site is shown on the
following page.

   •   The installation of a raised median at the intersection of NE 179th Street at NE 35th
       Avenue is not necessary for the roadway in the immediate future to operate safely or
       within acceptable levels of capacity per Clark County standards. Therefore, the County
       may approve the proposed development without the installation of a raised median
       through this intersection.
   •   Although block perimeter and length standards are currently not met for the existing
       block which surrounds the site, the proposed development will be constructing site
       internal public streets which will improve connectivity and promote a completed street
       network in the vicinity. Block perimeter standards can be met in the future; however, this
       is contingent on additional development of lower density/undeveloped properties in the
       area. Since the Avery Drive project will be expanding the public street network and does
       not introduce a street layout which precludes future blocks from meeting required length
       or perimeter standards, no further mitigation or improvements to the transportation
       system with respect to cross-circulation standards are necessary or recommended.

Introduction
This memorandum details a proposed scope of work for a Transportation Impact Study (TIS)
related to the Avery Drive subdivision project. The project site is located on a single property
(assessor parcel 181513000) addressed at 3504 NE 184th Street in unincorporated Clark County,
Washington. The proposal will include the construction of a 23 single-family detached housing
development. As part of this proposal one existing house will be maintained, whereby a net of 22
houses will be constructed. Access to the site will be provided via a planned north/south roadway
(i.e., NE 35th Avenue) that will be constructed between the project site and NE 179th Street as
part of the in-process Mill Creek Terrace Subdivision.

Site Trips
Trip Generation
The proposed Avery Drive subdivision project will include the construction of 22 single-family
detached houses while maintaining one existing house for a net total of 23 houses. To estimate
the number of trips that are and will be generated by the existing and proposed uses, trip rates
from the Trip Generation Manual, 12th Edition1 were used. Data from land use code 210, Single-
Family Detached Housing, was used to estimate site trip generation based on the number of
dwelling units.
The trip generation calculations show that the proposed subdivision is projected to generate 15
net new AM peak hour trips, 20 net new PM peak hour trips, and 200 net new average weekday
trips. The trip generation estimates are summarized in Table 1. Detailed trip generation
calculations are included in the technical appendix.

        administrative manual. A traffic impact study shall analyze impacts according to the
        following:
                 - 50 or less new peak hour trips; one mile from site

                 - 251 or more new peak hour trips; three miles from the site

     Level of Service Descriptions

        Sidra Capacity Results
                                     LEVEL OF SERVICE
Intersection Level of Service (LOS) is a qualitative measure used to evaluate the performance of
intersections and roadways based on the traffic flow, average control delay, and overall operations. The
Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) defines LOS for signalized and unsignalized intersections as a
function of the average vehicle control delay. LOS may be calculated per movement or per approach for
any intersection configuration, but LOS for the intersection as a whole is generally defined for
signalized, roundabout, and all-way stop configurations.

The LOS metric is categorized using a graded scale from A to F. Descriptions of these LOS grade levels
are provided below:
                                                                             Control Delay Per Vehicle
LOS                                                                         Signalized &
                                   Description                                            Unsignalized
Grade                                                                       Roundabout
                                                                                          Intersections
                                                                            Intersections
        Indicative of relatively freeflow traffic conditions with minimal
        delays and high comfort for drivers. Low intersection delays and
  A                                                                         ≤ 10 seconds   ≤ 10 seconds
        clearing of vehicles occur in a single cycle at signalized
        intersections.

        Representative of reasonably free flow conditions, where speeds
  B     are maintained but maneuverability is slightly restricted. Slightly 10-20 seconds 10-15 seconds
        higher delays at intersections are observed.

        Indicative of stable flow, where maneuverability is noticeably
        restricted, and lane changes require more driver awareness.
  C                                                                       20-35 seconds 15-25 seconds
        Moderate delays at intersections may be observed, and the
        occasional queued vehicle may not clear in a single cycle length.

        Signifies approaching unstable flow, with significant delays and
        reduced comfort. Longer delays and congestion may be apparent
  D                                                                      35-55 seconds 25-35 seconds
        at an intersection. More than one cycle length at a signalized
        intersection may be necessary to service queued vehicles.

        Representative of unstable flow, where traffic is at or nearing
        capacity, leading to long delays. High delays at an intersection
  E                                                                         55-80 seconds 35-50 seconds
        are expected, and extended queuing may be observed. Cycle
        failures at signalized intersections are expected to occur.
        Indicative of forced flow, where traffic demand exceeds
        capacity, resulting in severe congestion and delays. Very high
  F     delays and significant queues are common at intersections.          >80 seconds    >50 seconds
        Frequent cycle failures are expected to occur at signalized
        intersections.

TO: Councilors Marshall, Fuentes, Little, Yung and Belkot, County Manager Otto, Community
Planning Director Orjiako

Cc: Rebecca Messinger, Staff

Dear Clark County Councilors and Staff:

Friends of Clark County congratulates the Clark County Council and its staff for the completion
of the 2025 Comprehensive Plan Update, scheduled to be adopted on Tuesday, October 13,
2026.

We are submitting final comments below:

   ●   We remain in support of the Growth Management Act that protects and preserves
       agricultural land and we continue to oppose the Council’s majority that does not seem to
       understand the law’s requirement to protect that land by not allowing de-designation of it.

   ●   We remain in support of the many voices you heard from the community decrying the
       unnecessary expansion of the Cities of Ridgefield and La Center. We remain in
       opposition to the unnecessary expansion, leading to sprawl and urbanization of our rural
       areas. Three cheers for rural residents, who avoided business park expansion in the
       rural and environmentally sensitive areas east of WSU and north of 199th Street.. .

   ●   We support the denial of expansion into ALLTCS east of Camas

   ●   We believe that the expansions allowed, especially as to residential lands, will
       unnecessarily create a surplus of housing units by thousands of units where the current
       UGAs can, with few exceptions, be accommodated within the existing UGAs.

   ●   Cheers to no more clustering of residential development on resource land. We support
       extending that decision to all rural parcels in Clark County.

   ●   We strongly support the need to take action on the Ag Study showing lands that meet
       the legal criteria for Ag of Long Term Commercial Significance and issue a moratorium
       as recommended by the Agricultural Advisory Commission until the County can address
       those lands that meet the legal criteria

   ●   As an ongoing issue, a review of the equestrian code is encouraged, along with the
       expectation that there be solutions that can be implemented within a reasonable
       timeframe.
                                                2

   ●   We agree on the importance of updating a Clark County Framework Plan prior to the
       next Comprehensive Plan Update. We would be interested in contributing to that effort.

   ●   We support a Public Benefits Rating System as a tool to protect farm businesses.

   ●   We support the recommendation to consider Ag 40, passed to the Ag Commission and
       to the Community Planning staff.

   ●   Friends of Clark County supports the approval of a mobile home overlay and suggests a
       more aggressive timeline for implementation.

   ●   We support BPAC's recommendations regarding active transportation projects, in line
       with FOCC's stated priorities and their inclusion in the Multi-Modal Update.

   ●   With no data from the Department of Natural Resources with which to update mineral
       resources in rural areas of Clark County, the implementation of a “Mineral Resource
       Commission” or “task force” is premature. FOCC supports consideration of such a
       commission at a later time and not as part of this Comprehensive Plan Update.

   ●   We hail the Council’s approval of the Climate Chapter and, in particular, applaud the
       amendment matching the County’s greenhouse gas emission goal to the City of
       Vancouver’s more aggressive goal. Setting a target date of 2040, instead of 2050, to
       reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, reducing vehicle miles and the use of gas
       powered items in our own communities, is critical to equitably enhancing resilience to the
       impacts of climate change.

Friends of Clark County looks forward to continuing to work with the Council and its staff on the
implementation of an updated Comprehensive Plan for our communities.

Regards,

Ann Foster, President
Friends of Clark County

comp plan amendments

Comment
Hello council and staff,
State law requires you to reduce climate pollution as part of the planning process.
I proposed 3 amendments to the comp plan to help do that.
1. Consider amending your Comp plan to reject requests from the gas company to use your
public right of way for more gas lines. We can’t reduce climate pollution by expanding its
infrastructure.
2. Consider charging rent or franchise fees to the gas industry for use of your land for their
pipes. In December 2019, the Washington Supreme Court ruled in favor of King County,
upholding a county ordinance that allows the county to charge utility companies franchise fees
(or rent) for using public rights-of-way to lay infrastructure like natural gas pipelines. [1, 2].
You could earmark the income to help low income residents convert to more efficient heating
systems.
3. Time sensitive, before November 9, 2026
• Direct your federal lobbyist to ask our Congresswoman to protect Federal policies that
require automakers to sell a modest number of zero emission vehicles in the State of
Washington. Ask her to vote No on HJR 205.
• Also ask Congresswoman Perez to protect federal policies that require automaker fleets to
meet fuel efficiency standards and emissions standards by voting No on H.J.Res. 202 &
H.J.Res. 211

Message Subject
Official Opposition to the Proposed R32 Rezoning at NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue

Comments
I am writing as a resident of the Pleasant Valley neighborhood to formally state my strong
opposition to the proposed R32 (High-Density Multi-Family) rezoning of the 88-acre property
located at NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue.
• Inconsistency with the Comprehensive Plan: The city’s Master/Comprehensive Plan designates
this area for low-density residential use to preserve neighborhood character. Granting this
rezoning would constitute "spot zoning," setting a dangerous precedent that undermines the
city’s long-term land-use vision.
• Severe Traffic and Public Safety Concerns: Our existing street infrastructure consists of narrow,
residential roads designed for low-volume traffic. Adding a multi-family complex will introduce
hundreds of daily vehicle trips, leading to gridlock, blind-spot hazards, and increased safety risks
for neighborhood children and pedestrians.
• Strain on Public Infrastructure and Utilities: Our local infrastructure—specifically stormwater
management, sewage capacity, and neighborhood schools—is already operating at or near
capacity. This sudden spike in density will overburden these vital systems without a viable
mitigation plan from the developer.
• Incompatible Neighborhood Scale and Character: The surrounding area is composed entirely of
single-family homes. A multi-story apartment complex introduces a stark architectural mismatch,
creates severe privacy intrusions for adjacent backyards, and disrupts the established quiet and
aesthetic of our community.
For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Planning Commission deny this rezoning
request and Sincerely, Connie Komomua

Subject
Ordinance 2026-10-01 — Preserve rural lands near SE 296th Avenue

Date of Hearing
Tue, 10/13/2026

Comment
Chair Marshall and Members of the Clark County Council:

I am writing regarding 1502 SE 296th Avenue, Washougal, and the surrounding rural area. I
ask the Council to preserve the area's rural character and oppose further urban expansion into
neighboring rural and agricultural lands.

1. Retain the Nevin expansion denial

The proposed ordinance records the Council's denial of the agricultural de-designation and
eastward Camas UGA expansion for the Nevin property. Please retain that decision in the
adopted ordinance and ensure the final comprehensive-plan and zoning maps reflect it.

2. Limit growth induced by infrastructure

Please also address the potential for urban infrastructure to induce further growth beyond the
adopted UGA. Any infrastructure associated with the Grove Field expansion should have
clearly defined service boundaries and safeguards against facilitating urban development on
surrounding rural lands. I oppose additional urban expansion into this area and request a
written explanation of the safeguards the County will apply.

3. Assess local and cumulative impacts
Before approving changes that could affect this corridor, please provide an assessment of local
and cumulative effects on traffic, rural road capacity and maintenance, stormwater, water
resources, and wildfire evacuation. That assessment should identify any anticipated effects on
SE 296th Avenue and neighboring properties, together with mitigation and funding
responsibilities.

4. Confirm the status of the property

Please provide written confirmation of the current and proposed comprehensive-plan
designation, zoning, and UGA status for 1502 SE 296th Avenue, including whether this
adoption package changes any of them. Please identify any proposed road improvements or
utility extensions that could affect the property or the SE 296th Avenue corridor.

5. Implement voluntary conservation options

Finally, I support implementation of the voluntary Transfer of Development Rights program
described in proposed Policy 1.1.24. Please explain the implementation schedule, funding, and
process for identifying eligible sending areas, including whether this property or surrounding
rural lands could qualify. Please identify other voluntary conservation options available before
that program becomes operational.

Please enter this comment into the record for Ordinance 2026-10-01 and confirm receipt.

Chris Teso
1502 SE 296th Avenue
Washougal, WA 98671

assessment should identify any anticipated effects on SE 296th Avenue and neighboring
properties, together with
mitigation and funding responsibilities.
4. Confirm the status of the property
Please provide written confirmation of the current and proposed comprehensive-plan
designation, zoning, and
UGA status for 1502 SE 296th Avenue, including whether this adoption package changes any
of them. Please
identify any proposed road improvements or utility extensions that could affect the property or
the SE 296th
Avenue corridor.
5. Implement voluntary conservation options
Finally, I support implementation of the voluntary Transfer of Development Rights program
described in proposed
Policy 1.1.24. Please explain the implementation schedule, funding, and process for
identifying eligible sending
areas, including whether this property or surrounding rural lands could qualify. Please identify
other voluntary
conservation options available before that program becomes operational.

Message Subject
Official Opposition to the Proposed R32 Rezoning at NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue

Comments
Dear Mayor and Members of the City Council,

I am writing as a resident of the Pleasant Valley neighborhood to formally state my strong
opposition to the proposed R32 (High-Density Multi-Family) rezoning of the 88-acre property
located at NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue.
While I understand the regional need for diverse housing options, the extreme scale and density
of this specific R32 proposal are entirely incompatible with the existing character, safety, and
infrastructure of the Pleasant Valley community. I request that the Council reject this zoning
change based on the following severe impacts:

• Excessive Density and Incompatible Out-of-Scale Design: The proposed construction of high-
density apartment complexes totaling an estimated 2,464 units will fundamentally alter our
single-family neighborhood layout. These towering structures do not integrate with the
surrounding residential architecture and will permanently strip away the suburban character of
Pleasant Valley.
• Overwhelming Population Surge: Increasing density to this degree will cause an immediate,
unsustainable population spike—projected at roughly 6,899 new residents within a half-mile
radius. This represents an estimated 500% population boom that our current local services,
neighborhood pathways, and community spaces cannot absorb overnight.
• Severe Traffic and Overflow Parking Infrastructure Failures: The current building code restricts
parking minimums in these multi-family developments to just one space per two apartments. This
leaves a massive deficit. An estimated 3,080 vehicle owners from these complexes will be forced
to look for overflow parking directly on our narrow single-family residential streets, creating safety
hazards for pedestrians, blocking sightlines, and causing severe daily traffic bottlenecks.

The local infrastructure at NE 139th Street and NE 50th Avenue is already heavily burdened. Also
one must consider 131st Street, west of NE 50th Ave down to NE Corbin Road onto NE Salmon
Creek Ave. This roadway is heavily traveled, currently in terrible condition and absolutely could
not withstand the amount of traffic this would create. Introducing thousands of units alongside
drastically reduced parking minimums guarantees permanent gridlock and dangerous overflow
onto neighbor properties.

I urge the Council to prioritize smart, sustainable growth management that respects established
neighborhoods. Please protect the infrastructure and livability of Pleasant Valley by voting NO on
this R32 rezone request.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and service to our community.

Sincerely,

Anthony Komomua
4907 NE 131st St
Vancouver, WA 98686

Thank you for this opportunity to comment on behalf of AMHO, the Association of

It's bad enough that the park owners where I live are in violation of 59.20 most of the time.

of definition or process last time I asked (10.01.26). I urge you to mirror the standards set in

unviability. This approach is backed by federal court precedent (Laurel Park Community, LLC
v. City of Tumwater, 2012), where the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that local
governments can legally mandate mobile home park preservation to protect low-income
housing without violating property rights.

away from the corporate park owners' greed and stand up for your most vulnerable citizens.
